Off line courses lack live peers, so agents may fill that gap. A theory called constructive controversy says folks learn deep by clash and then by fix of views.

The team asks if that gain holds for AI peers. They vary how much an agent fights a point. They also vary if the agent's design is told to the student. Both picks may sway how much a student trusts and learns. For course teams, the finds guide how frank an AI peer should be.
arxiv-2601-13679:
Sangwon Park, Dongjun Kim, Sung-Hoon Byun, and Sangwook Park build a tiny sound classifier for ships in 2026. Ships give off sounds as they move, and those sounds can reveal the ship type. Small devices at sea must do this job with little power and weak chips. Heavy AI models do not fit that task well.

Their model, ShuffleFAC, uses frequency-aware convolution tuned for low cost. It splits work into light steps and shuffles channels to mix traits cheaply. Tests on the DeepShip dataset showed strong results with far less complexity. Light tools like this suit long, quiet watch at sea.
arxiv-2601-14079:
Paul Walker and co-authors model natural light so 3D scenes can be relit in a true way in 2026. Inverse rendering works backward from an image to the scene and light behind it. The problem is ill-posed, with many possible answers. Illumination priors simplify it by favoring plausible light.

Past work either ignores the spherical, rotation-equivariant nature of light environments, or lacks a well-behaved latent space. Their VENI is a rotation-equivariant variational autoencoder for natural illumination. It models light on the sphere without 2D projections. True light models aid film, design, and robot vision.
arxiv-2601-14279:
Brady Steele reports a negative result on speeding up language models in this 2026 paper. The target is KV cache compression, a way to shrink the memory a model keeps while it writes. His method is Speculative Importance Prediction, a scorer with 1.7 million parameters. It predicts how much each token will matter, from the cache alone.

The scorer does not look at the live query, by design. It has bold parts, such as multi-horizon lookahead and cross-attention. Still, it does not beat simple baselines, not even random selection. Steele ran five seeds, four retention levels, and three tasks. His study marks a clear limit for this kind of learned scoring.
arxiv-2601-14679:
Yiran Zhang, Xingpeng Sun, and Aniket Bera work on virtual reality walking in this 2026 paper. Natural walking enhances immersion in virtual environments. Physical space limitations and obstacles hinder exploration, though, especially in large virtual scenes. Redirected Walking techniques mitigate this problem. They subtly manipulate the virtual camera to guide users away from physical collisions within pre-defined virtual environments.

The team's system is HCVR Scene Generation. It generates virtual reality environments with high compatibility for extended redirected walking. In plain terms, the scenes are built so the redirection tricks work over longer walks. The gain is ease of use. A guest can walk a large fake world and still feel at home in a small room. Readers get scene generation designed around the limits of a real room.
arxiv-2601-15079:
Chenyu Liu, Haige Li, and Luca Rossi make graph neural networks cheaper to train. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with networks that learn from graph data, passing messages between nodes. Quantization shrinks such models and speeds them up for small devices.

For graphs, the features matter more than in language models. The authors present LoRAP, short for Low-Rank Aggregation Prompting. It is aimed at training quantized graph networks. The method guides the quantized model with low-rank prompts, so accuracy survives while the model stays small, lean, and quick to train and run.
arxiv-2601-15379:
Sebastian M. Banaszak, Caitlin A. Witt, and Adam A. Miller compare ways to hear the tick of two black holes in orbit. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with supermassive black hole binaries hidden in active galaxies. Simulations say such pairs should make the galaxy's brightness vary in a periodic way.

That signal must beat the galaxy's own random flicker. The authors simulate binaries with damped random walk noise plus an orbital sine wave. They test three detection methods against each other. The study asks which method recovers the true period best, to guide optical searches.
arxiv-2601-15479:
Sydney Anuyah and three co-authors test whether language models can reason about cause and effect in a 2026 arXiv paper. Safe use of these models in fields like biomedicine needs such skill. A model that confuses correlation with cause can mislead care. The team studies one basic task. It is pairwise causal discovery from text: given two things, judge which causes which, if either.

Thirteen open-source language models face the test. The setting spans biomedicine and other domains, per the title. Pairwise judgments are the atoms of larger causal maps. If models fail here, bigger causal claims rest on sand. The benchmark gives builders a clear check. It shows where current models stand on a skill that high-stakes use demands.
arxiv-2601-15579:
Philip Korman studies periodic solutions of first-order problems in a 2026 arXiv paper. He uses continuation methods and bifurcation theory. The goal is exact counts of periodic solutions, not just existence. He also maps the global structure of solution curves. Knowing how solutions appear, merge, and vanish gives a fuller picture. Two applications anchor the theory.

One is a population model with fishing. There, periodic solutions describe seasons of growth and harvest. The other concerns limit cycles, closed loops that systems settle into. Existence and stability of such cycles matter in many models of nature. Exact multiplicity results are rare and valuable. They tell modelers how many steady rhythms a system can truly support.
arxiv-2601-15779:
Liuyun Jiang and five co-authors grow training data for brain mapping in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neuron segmentation in electron microscopy aims to rebuild the full connectome. Deep learning methods lead the field. They depend on large training sets with costly manual annotations. Classic augmentation warps images geometrically or shifts brightness. The results stay highly correlated with the originals. They lack structural diversity, so models still starve for variety.

The team uses diffusion models for augmentation instead. Generative models can create fresh, varied examples. New structures in training data teach models to handle real variety. Connectome projects generate petabytes of imagery. Any gain in annotation efficiency compounds hugely at that scale. This paper adds a generative route to that efficiency.
arxiv-2601-15879:
Jiajun Zhang and a large team benchmark controllable code completion in a 2026 arXiv paper. Code completion is now a central task for language models. It powers the assistants many programmers use daily. Completion skill has improved fast. Evaluation methods have not kept equal pace, the authors note. Their benchmark is C3-Bench. It evaluates and aims to achieve controllable completion in code models.

Controllable means the model completes code as directed, not just plausibly. Length, style, and scope of a completion all matter in real editing. A benchmark that tests control exposes gaps that accuracy scores hide. Tool builders can then tune models for steerable help. For working programmers, a completer that follows instructions beats one that merely guesses well.
arxiv-2601-15979:
W. Kollatschny and a large team follow a restless galaxy over five years in a 2026 arXiv paper. The galaxy is IRAS 23226-3843. Optical spectra marked it as a highly variable Seyfert galaxy. It even qualifies as a changing-look active galactic nucleus. In such objects, the nucleus changes its spectral type over time. The title promises extreme line profile variations in this repeating case. Emission lines shift and reshape as the center brightens and fades.

The team presents follow-up observations from the past five years. They track ongoing photometric and spectral variations. Long baselines are rare and valuable for these objects. They reveal whether changes cycle or wander. Changing-look galaxies test models of how black holes feed. A well-documented case gives those models something firm to match.
arxiv-2601-16379:
Junjie Yang and coauthors speed quantum sums for crystals with a fit trick. Their 2026 preprint deals with sums that join embed steps and local links. Crystals need sums that use the repeat form of the build. The fit trick splits charge clouds in a way that keeps that form. It is built from points that span the cloud with few terms.

Few terms cut the sum cost to a straight growth in size. Straight growth lets teams treat big crystals with high care. High care sums test new stuff for chips and power gear. The work joins two sum paths in one fast frame. It aims at real stuff, not toy sets.
arxiv-2601-16779:
Luke Southall, Joshua Ammermann, Rinor Kelmendi, Domenik Eichhorn, and Ina Schaefer test claims made for quantum compilers. A compiler turns code for one chip to code for the next. Chip firms build their gear in vast, unlike ways. Sellers say their compilers retarget code with ease. Their 2026 preprint checks if those claims hold in real use.

The team runs code through such tools across chip types. They note where moves fail or lose skill. Clear grades help buyers pick tools with proof. They also push sellers to back claims with tests. Sound moves are key as quantum gear grows more mixed.
arxiv-2601-16979:
Dayal Singh Kalra and a team of six co-authors gauge the bend of a net's loss hills. Loss hills guide how a net learns from data. Their steep bends set how stable training is. The chief gauge is the top Hessian eigenvalue. That gauge shifts as the learning rate shifts. Their 2026 preprint builds a bend gauge that scales to vast nets.

Old bend gauges cost too much for big chatbots. Their gauge tracks bend through the full train run. It can flag when training nears a cliff. Such flags help labs tune big runs with less waste. They also deepen our grasp of why nets learn.
arxiv-2601-17279:
Sonu Kumar and four co-authors present SPADE, a compute engine for neural network work at the edge. Edge devices need math units that are exact, lean, and small. SPADE uses posit arithmetic. Posits taper their precision by value size. They span a wide range and resist some numeric flaws of older formats. The engine is built with SIMD lanes, so many values move at once.

The design targets deep network speed on tight power budgets. It must serve mixed numeric formats without waste. Such hardware could help phones, sensors, and small robots run AI on site. Local runs cut delay and keep data private. SPADE shows how new number formats can aid that goal.
arxiv-2601-17479:
Buddhadev Hajra studies how homotopy traits pass down maps between surfaces. He works with smooth complex affine surfaces. The maps are finite and surjective. A key trait is the Eilenberg-MacLane property. Hajra gives a clear counterexample. It shows that trait need not descend under proper maps in general. That negative result drives the rest of the work.

He then defines a weaker trait, finite homotopy rank-sum. The weaker trait may descend where the strong one fails. Knowing which traits survive maps guides algebraic geometry at large. Maps are how geometers link unlike shapes. A sound descent rule saves false proofs. Hajra's counterexample alone redraws the map.
arxiv-2601-17579:
Andreas Buchinger, Kresimir Burazin, Ivana Crnjac, and Marko Erceg study how rough media can be replaced by smooth rules. Their problems use a fractional form of diffusion. The local traits of the medium shift fast from place to place. The team asks which smooth rule the rough one acts like at large scale. Two kinds of convergence give the answer.

One kind covers the local part of the problem. The other covers the far-reaching part, which comes from the nonlocal form. A full answer tells users which end model they can trust. Such rules serve work on mixed materials and flow below ground. The study joins local and far effects in one frame.
arxiv-2601-17679:
Md Sazzadul Islam Ridoy and three co-authors present BanglaRobustNet for Bangla speech recognition. Bangla is one of the world's most spoken languages. It stays underrepresented in top speech research. Noise and speaker diversity make the gap worse. Their hybrid framework builds on Wav2Vec-BERT. It pairs denoising with attention in one design.

Robust recognition serves Bangla speakers in real settings. Streets, markets, and homes are noisy by nature. A model trained for quiet rooms fails there. Denoising up front gives the recognizer cleaner input. Attention then weighs the sounds that matter. The work pushes low-resource language tech forward. It shows gains need not wait for huge datasets.
arxiv-2601-17979:
Ahmad Abdelfattah and Massimiliano Fasi build a faster batch solver for a core matrix task on graphics chips. Their 2026 preprint deals with the singular value decomposition, or SVD. The SVD underpins tools like principal component analysis, low-rank fits, and randomized methods. Many jobs need not one SVD but thousands of small ones at once. That batch regime is where the authors aim.

Small problems behave unlike large ones on a GPU. Launch costs and memory moves can swamp the math. An efficient batch solver packs the work so the chip stays busy. Fast batch SVD speeds up data analysis, signal tools, and learning pipelines that call it again and again.
arxiv-2601-18079:
Edwin J. Son, Kyungmin Kim, and John J. Oh test whether a gap between star types survives a change in gravity theory. Their 2026 preprint works in Hořava-Lifshitz gravity. In general relativity, black holes and neutron stars differ in compactness, with a gap between them. Compactness says how much mass is packed into a given size. The authors show that this gap may vanish in the altered theory, where fermionic matter forms compact dark objects.

If the gap can close, some dark compact objects could be fermionic stars, not black holes. That possibility changes how odd objects in surveys get classified. The work gives observers a new hypothesis to test with mass and size data.
arxiv-2601-18179:
Yimeng Wang and co-authors explore tools that help therapists support clients between sessions. Their 2026 preprint deals with therapeutic homework, the tasks clients do on their own time. Such homework is essential to good therapy. Yet therapists face scattered client logs, assessments, and reflections, with very little prep time to sort them. The team ran a formative study with licensed therapists to learn what support they need. From that base, they explore customizable interactive tools for the task.

Tools that sort and surface the key parts of homework could save scarce minutes. They must still respect the privacy and nuance of care. The study grounds design in real clinic workflow, not in guesses.
arxiv-2601-18279:
Jiale Tang and Bin Zhu estimate the tones hidden in a noisy signal, using a filter bank with many outputs. Their 2026 preprint deals with line spectral estimation. The task is to find the frequencies of complex sinusoids buried in noise. Their estimator uses atomic norm minimization joined with Georgiou's filter bank, known as the G-filter, across multiple output vectors. A prior version of the method was limited to a single filtered output. The new one integrates several outputs at once.

More outputs can steady the estimate when noise is strong. Frequency estimates feed radar, sonar, and communications. A method that uses all filtered views should beat one that throws most away.
arxiv-2601-18379:
Joydeep Roy studies how dark matter may have formed in the young cosmos through a slow path called freeze-in. In that path, dark stuff speaks only in a faint way with the stuff we can see. It builds up bit by bit and never quite joins the hot mix around it. The path stands as a real choice next to the more known freeze-out path.

Roy adds a new part to the cast: a leptoquark, a thing that can link quarks with leptons. In his setup the leptoquark talks both to dark matter and to the known parts of the world. The math then traces how much dark matter such talks would leave behind. A match with the share seen in space would mark the setup as one worth a search at labs.
arxiv-2601-18779:
Yuxiao Qu and four colleagues give hard tasks a new way to train thought tools: let a guide show the path, but never hand it the goal. On hard tasks, a tool that learns from its own tries may make no good try at all. With no good try, there is no gain to learn from, and training stalls. Past fixes train the tool on pro-made solves. That can bend the tool to a style not its own.

Their plan, named POPE, uses pro solves just to steer where the tool looks. The tool still makes all tries in its own style and learns from its own wins. The guide's facts are used as a map, not as a text to copy. That split could free training on the hard-est tasks. It may also keep the tool's own voice whole as it grows.
arxiv-2601-18979:
Supriya Khadka and Sanchari Das set out design rules for extended reality tools for young children. Virtual and augmented reality can draw young learners in, but children change fast as they grow. Tools built without care can overload their minds or clash with their senses.

Their frame, called Augmented Human Development, models the child's mind, senses, setting, and growth stage together. It aims to keep the pull of immersive tech while cutting the risks for the youngest users. Teachers and builders get a way to check a design against how young children truly take in the world.
arxiv-2601-19179:
Qipeng Zhan and four co-authors order the inner codes of an autoencoder so they reveal a data set's true dimension. Autoencoders squeeze data into a small inner code and then rebuild it. In a plain linear case, the right tweaks make that code match the ordered axes of principal component analysis.

The team builds a principal component autoencoder that keeps that order in curved, nonlinear cases too. Ordered codes let them read off the intrinsic dimension, the number of true degrees of freedom in the data. Knowing that number guides how big a model needs to be for a given data set.
arxiv-2601-19379:
Yidong Wu and Luo Luo give an async optimizer that keeps its speed under heavy tailed noise. In distributed training, workers finish at wildly unlike times. Gradient noise can also be heavy tailed, with rare huge spikes that wreck plain methods.

Their method is an asynchronous normalized stochastic gradient descent with momentum. Workers update on their own clocks, and the normalization tames the spikes. The analysis shows the method hits the optimal time complexity under a mild moment assumption. Robust async training matters as models and clusters grow ever larger.
arxiv-2601-19479:
Victoria Catterall, Cise Midoglu, and Stephen Lynch forecast when elite women's footballers will get hurt. Injuries in football carry personal, competitive, and financial costs for players and teams. The team sets a time to injury task: not just whether a player gets hurt, but when.

Their method uses DeepHit, a survival model that handles competing risks over time. Athlete monitoring data and clear visual displays feed the work. A fair warning window lets medical staff ease loads and target prevention, though such forecasts must be handled with care around selection and privacy.
arxiv-2601-19679:
Pooja, Dana Avramescu, and Tuomas Lappi study the first instant of a heavy-ion collision. When two nuclei smash at near light speed, they briefly form the glasma, a state of intense colour fields. Tiny disturbances in those fields grow with time. How they grow controls how fast the chaos spreads and heat begins to form.

The authors show the growth is exponential in the square root of time. They read this rate as a Lyapunov exponent, the standard measure of chaos in a system. A Lyapunov exponent links microscopic chaos to entropy production, the creation of disorder. It also sets the thermalization timescale, when the system starts behaving like a hot fluid. The result sharpens theory of the universe's earliest microseconds, recreated in colliders.
arxiv-2601-19879:
Zach Hunter, Cosmin Pohoata, Jacques Verstraete, and Shengtong Zhang connect two problems in combinatorics. One concerns point-line incidences: points and lines in a finite geometry, and the graph recording which points lie on which lines. The other is the Furstenberg-Sárközy problem from arithmetic combinatorics, about patterns in dense sets of integers.

Using that connection, the authors construct unexpectedly large induced matchings in the incidence graph. A matching pairs points with lines exclusively; induced means no extra incidences sneak in. Large matchings in turn yield small Nikodym sets, sets that contain a full line in every direction. Such constructions test the limits of finite geometry. They often feed back into number theory and theoretical computer science.
arxiv-2601-19979:
Temple He, Jaeha Lee, and Hirosi Ooguri use reinforcement learning to explore a structure from quantum gravity. The holographic entropy cone collects all entropy patterns that holography allows for several regions. A vector inside the cone can be realised by a graph whose minimum cuts reproduce its entropies. Vectors outside admit no such graph.

Their algorithm searches for a graph realisation matching a target entropy vector. When none exists, it finds the graph whose entropies come closest. That near miss helps probe where the cone's boundary lies. Mapping this cone constrains how information can be organised in holographic theories. Machine search reaches cases that hand analysis cannot. The work blends learning algorithms with deep questions in theoretical physics.
arxiv-2601-20179:
Xuanyu Pan, Dingxin Zhang, and Xiping Zhang bound the topology of hypersurfaces inside a possibly singular projective variety. They look at the total Betti number, a count that summarizes the holes and cycles of a shape. For a hypersurface of a given degree inside the variety, they show this count grows in a controlled way with the degree.

Their bound depends on the degree of the ambient variety and an explicit constant that does not depend on the hypersurface. Such bounds matter in algebraic geometry, where they limit how complex a space cut out by equations can be. The result extends control to ambient spaces that are themselves singular.
arxiv-2601-20379:
Zhengbo Jiao and a large team present Policy of Thoughts, a way to scale the reasoning of large language models at test time. Models struggle with long, complex reasoning, and one cause is their frozen policy: their strategy cannot change mid-task. Current test-time methods use execution feedback only to filter or rewrite attempts.

Policy of Thoughts instead lets the model internalize that feedback and evolve its own policy while it works. The reasoning strategy itself improves during the task. If it works, models could handle longer problems without retraining, by learning from their own trial and error in the moment.
arxiv-2601-20579:
Hui-Chun Zhang and Xi-Ping Zhu study a heat flow for harmonic maps in this 2026 math paper. A harmonic map is a map between shapes that stretches them as little as possible. The flow slowly changes such a map over time, much like heat spreads out. Here the maps land in CAT(0) spaces, a broad class of spaces with no positive curve.

The authors trace the line of work behind their question. In 1964, Eells and Sampson proved long-time existence and convergence for flows into spaces that do not curve up. Hamilton later took up the same flow with boundary conditions added. In 1992, Gromov and Schoen built a theory of such maps into CAT(0) spaces. Zhang and Zhu ask how smooth, in the Lipschitz sense, these flows stay.
arxiv-2601-20779:
Théo Delemazure studies a fairness rule for elections in this 2026 paper. The rule is the independence of clones axiom. Two candidates count as perfect clones when every voter ranks them side by side. If they are true clones, removing one should not change who wins. Delemazure asks whether this still holds for approximate clones.

The paper works with ordinal elections, where voters rank candidates in order. Approximate clones are pairs that voters rank nearly, but not exactly, side by side. Real elections often have such near-duplicate candidates. The question is whether the clone rule survives small errors in the rankings. The answer matters for voting systems that want to resist spoiler effects from copycat candidates.
arxiv-2601-21079:
Maximillian Newman builds a new backward-in-time model of family lines in split populations. The 2026 paper concerns the structured coalescent for diploid populations. The model lives on finite graphs, where each node holds a subpopulation. It allows large migrations between nodes. It also allows uneven offspring distributions, where some parents contribute far more than others. Both features strain older models.

The new model is quenched, meaning the environment is fixed before averaging. It generalizes two earlier models. One is the mean-field model of Birkner and co-authors. The other is Möhle's haploid structured model. Diploid organisms carry two gene copies, which complicates ancestry. Newman's framework handles that case with big moves and skewed families allowed. It serves population geneticists who reconstruct history from present-day genes.
arxiv-2601-22279:
E. Lopez-Saavedra and a large team take a deep look at one reaction that fuels X-ray bursts on dead stars. Their 2026 preprint studies how a proton strikes copper and frees an alpha particle, leaving nickel behind. The reaction also runs in winds blown off a fresh neutron star after a collapse.

The team set tight bounds on how fast the reaction runs in real bursts. That rate helps fix the heat and light a burst gives off. It also shapes which new nuclei the burst can build. Better rates mean burst models rest on firmer ground. Observers can then read burst light with more trust.
arxiv-2601-22379:
Bailin Wang, Dan Friedman, Tao Lei, and Chong Wang fix a flaw in fast attention for long texts. Block-sparse attention reads only picked chunks, which saves huge cost. Their 2026 preprint notes that dropped chunks take their context with them, and picks can miss the mark.

Their method, SPLA, picks chunks with a sharper score, drawn from second-order cues. It then keeps a light linear path so dropped chunks still leave a trace. The goal is long memory at low cost. That goal matters for book-length and code-length tasks. The work refines a key speed trick.
arxiv-2601-22479:
Muzzamal Shaukat, Charles Wallace, Anatoly Svidzinsky, and Marlan Scully study paired atoms that fall through space at a steady push. Their 2026 preprint explores Dicke states, where two atoms act as one in how they glow. The pair sit in the right Rindler wedge, the zone of space an accelerated watcher can see.

The team find the terms under which the pair glow as one bright state, or hide in a dark one. Such work tests quantum effects tied to acceleration and horizons. It links lab atom physics to deep claims about space. The states may also serve future sensors.
arxiv-2601-23279:
N. Ahmadiniaz, F. Bastianelli, F. Karbstein, and C. Schubert continue a study of photon-graviton mixing in an electromagnetic field. Einstein-Maxwell theory predicts photons and gravitons can convert into each other inside such fields. At one-loop level, the effect produces magnetic dichroism, a difference in absorption by polarization.

Earlier work assumed only two diagrams contributed to the one-loop amplitude. The authors point out a third, involving a tadpole subdiagram. Complete amplitudes matter for proposals to detect gravitons through light. A constant electromagnetic field is the setting, where the newly noticed tadpole diagram completes the one-loop amplitude.
arxiv-2603-01879:
Chi-Ning Chou, Artem Kirsanov, Yao-Yuan Yang, and SueYeon Chung predict model failure from the shape of its internal representations. Their 2026 work borrows the biomarker idea from medicine: a system-level measure that flags future trouble. Reverse-engineering every circuit gives insight, but rarely a clear early warning for deployment.

The team designs network markers that probe how task-relevant object manifolds sit in representation space. Two geometric measures stand out: effective manifold dimensionality and a utility score for those manifolds. When both shrink on familiar data, performance on shifted data tends to fall soon after. The pattern holds across architectures, optimizers, and data sets in image classification. In transfer learning from a large pre-trained model, the same markers beat plain accuracy at forecasting shifted performance.
arxiv-2603-02179:
Jérémie Bettinelli and Dimitri Korkotashvili link two kinds of maps on surfaces in this 2026 mathematics paper. A map here is a graph drawn on a surface, split into faces. Some maps are bipartite, meaning their points split into two sets with links only across. The authors build a two-way match between general maps and bipartite ones.

Their method cuts along a chosen loop, slides one side by one notch, then sews it back. That small move flips the parity of loops that cross the cut. For doughnut-shaped maps with a single face, loops have a simple form. That makes the full link between the two map types clear. A paired swapping map on even-faced maps supports the argument.
arxiv-2603-02479:
Rituraj Sharma, Weiyuan Chen, and Noah Provenzano guide deep reasoning with step-level scores in this 2026 paper. DeepThink methods generate many candidate solutions, refine them, and merge the best. Without reliable correctness signals mid-search, deeper thought can amplify errors. Correct minority answers get drowned out, and extra compute yields little.

Their algorithm, PRISM, uses a process reward model that grades each reasoning step. Candidates act like particles in a landscape defined by those grades. Score-guided resampling and random refinement concentrate the population on strong reasoning while keeping diversity. On math and science benchmarks, PRISM matched or beat rival DeepThink methods. A mid-size model using it rivaled one six times larger. Analysis shows steady net correction during refinement, even from weak starting pools.
arxiv-2603-02879:
Fiona Spuler, Marlene Kretschmer, Magdalena Alonso Balmaseda, and colleagues separate the tangled influences of two oceans on East African rain. Their 2026 paper targets the short rains over the Greater Horn of Africa, which respond to both Pacific and Indian Ocean patterns. Untangling joint climate signals matters for seasonal forecasts, but model experiments carry model biases.

Their method, DAG-VAE, fuses deep learning with causal reasoning by planting a physics-based causal graph inside an autoencoder's hidden space. Trained on forecast archives, it recovered response patterns matching costly ocean-swap experiments. Trained on observations, it found a different Pacific influence, exposing possible model bias. It can also generate what-if versions of extreme rainy seasons for planning ahead.
arxiv-2603-03479:
Yacob Medhin, Tushar Sial, and Simone Servadio design a spacecraft and its flight path together instead of separately. Electric propulsion missions are usually planned with fixed thrust and efficiency, ignoring how power supply, propulsion, and trajectory pull on each other. Far from the Sun, where light is weak, those shortcuts can doom a design. Their 2026 framework optimizes all three at once as one coupled problem.

A detailed model of the SPT-140 Hall thruster ties thrust and efficiency to the moment-by-moment solar power available, including array degradation. The time-optimal trajectory problem runs on NASA's OpenMDAO and Dymos toolchains with efficient gradient methods. The demonstration case inserts a spacecraft into orbit around asteroid 16 Psyche, a regime where dim sunlight makes power-aware design critical. Results expose the key trade-offs realistic mission planning must respect.
arxiv-2603-03579:
Kunzhe Song, Maxime Zingraff, and Huacheng Zeng sense human movement with radio signals that already fill the air. Radio sensing sees through walls and darkness while preserving privacy, but the useful spectrum below ten gigahertz is scarce and contested. Their 2026 system, Ambient Radio Sensing, refuses to ask for new spectrum. It repurposes live 5G and Wi-Fi transmissions for sensing without disturbing their communication job.

A standalone device passively receives ambient signals, amplifies them to illuminate the surroundings, and captures reflections through a self-mixing radio design. That hardware extracts motion and angle features from ordinary communication waveforms. A cross-modal learning scheme lets a ready-made vision model supervise the radio model's training. The prototype, tested extensively on ambient 5G signals, estimates human skeletons accurately and segments body masks, proving the borrowed-spectrum approach.
arxiv-2603-03679:
Shunhao Ji and three colleagues report a burst of high-energy neutrinos from an exploding star, too powerful for the obvious explanation. The star, supernova 2017hcd, is a Type IIn, whose light comes from ejecta smashing into dense surrounding material. Analyzing public track-like data from the IceCube observatory, their 2026 paper finds a neutrino flare at nearly four-sigma significance. The flare lasted a month or two and was centered about two weeks before the supernova was even discovered optically.

The flare's total energy, spread evenly in all directions, comes out about a hundred times the energy of the explosion's ejecta. The ejecta-into-surroundings scenario cannot pay that bill. The authors instead point to a choked jet, a jet launched by the collapse but strangled inside the star's envelope, as the likely source of the flare.
arxiv-2605-00279:
Zawad Yalmie Sazid, Robert Abbas, and Sasa Maric compare machine learning models for spotting intrusions in intelligent transport systems. Connected vehicles, roadside units, and 5G links widen the surface attackers can reach, while roadside edge nodes have limited computing power. Protection therefore has to run close to the traffic itself.

The paper proposes a trust-aware federated hybrid detection framework. At each edge site, a random forest, a decision tree, and a linear support vector machine each learn their own view of the traffic. A central server then merges the local updates, weighting each site by trust. The design aims at proactive, low-latency defense that can work without constant human control.
arxiv-2605-00479:
Tom Kimpson, Mark B. Flegg, and Jennifer A. Flegg ask whether cheaper math can speed the stochastic simulation algorithm, the exact workhorse for random processes in biology. It crawls event by event, and large runs make it costly. Weather and climate work had already gained from working at fewer bits, which prompted the test.

Across five classic models from biology, their first approach, scoring reaction rates in 16-bit while keeping totals at 32-bit, matched the 64-bit standard closely. Doing it all in 16-bit brought in steady biases under plain rounding, sometimes badly. Rounding that uses chance, plus a scaling step, removed those biases and brought the match back across the board. The payoff is smaller memory footprints and a modest wall-clock speedup on current hardware, with larger gains likely on chips built for 16-bit math.
arxiv-2605-00579:
Kamila Szewczyk speeds up a small, crucial step inside data compression. Fast range coders and asymmetric numeral systems replace slow division with bit shifts, which works only when symbol frequencies are normalized to sum to a power of two. Normalization always distorts the distribution slightly, costing compression ratio, measured as added Kullback-Leibler divergence. Szewczyk shows the methods in current use are suboptimal twice over, in both running time and distortion.

The proposed method runs in time linear in the number of symbols and achieves the smallest divergence any normalization can reach. It rests on solving a separable concave optimization problem, which Szewczyk notes may interest readers beyond compression. The result is a drop-in improvement to a primitive that sits underneath widely used entropy coders: same interface, provably best fidelity to the original frequencies, and a faster algorithm to compute it.
arxiv-2605-00779:
Elsa Barrio-Torres and five co-authors test how well climate models reproduce summer air circulation over the Iberian Peninsula. They examine thirty-six historical CMIP6 model runs for 1979 to 2005 against ERA5 reanalysis, using the Lamb Weather Type scheme to classify daily circulation. Their framework also checks how types persist and change from one day to the next.

Daily frequencies alone kept sixteen runs, but adding persistence and transition checks narrowed the set to twelve. Models from the EC-Earth3 family performed best and most consistently, led by one aerchem run. Skill was stronger in the northwest and weaker in central and southern Mediterranean areas. The authors argue transition checks select models far better than daily counts alone.
arxiv-2605-00979:
Andreas Stergiou and Nicolas P. D. Sawaya prove that hardware-efficient quantum gates are universal for making states inside tight subspaces, such as those with fixed particle number or spin. Simulating physical systems on near-term quantum computers often requires staying inside such subspaces. Using Lie algebra methods, they pin down Pauli Z dressing as the key mechanism: commutators of overlapping gates produce projectors that split rotations into generators spanning the full algebra.

Adding separate complex phases extends the result from real to arbitrary complex state preparation. An efficient Jacobian criterion verifies whether a circuit can explore any direction from almost any parameter setting. Applications include Hubbard models and molecular structure, plus a completeness proof for a particle-number ansatz and symmetry-preserving circuits for a fuzzy sphere model.
arxiv-2605-01679:
Joydeb Kumar Sana detects falls among older people from wearable sensor data without leaking the private activity records behind the training. Falls demand fast response, yet the motion data that teach a detector are deeply personal, and standard privacy noise, spread evenly over all samples, dulls the model.

His framework sizes the noise to the class mix of each training batch instead. Batches rich in rare fall examples are treated differently from routine-activity batches. All this sits under a formal differential privacy guarantee that he proves and prices against utility. The detector itself pairs a 3D convolutional network with a bidirectional memory layer. On the SisFall, UP-Fall, and MobiAct benchmarks, scores rise over the uniform-noise model by clear margins on each set, and signed-rank tests confirm the edge is consistent. Formal privacy guarantees, the author notes, are what most earlier fall studies skipped.
arxiv-2605-01779:
Giuseppe A Orlando and four co-authors write CT scan reports by sending a language model out to gather proof before it speaks. Vision-language models that compress a whole volume into one embedding tend to invent findings and lose the anatomy, a dangerous habit in radiology.

MedScribe treats reporting as sequential decisions. The model forms hypotheses and calls pathology-specific tools that pull localized features from the volume, then queries a retrieval space where each pathology sits beside its textual evidence. Only after this quantitative evidence piles up does it synthesize the report. With no task-specific fine-tuning, the system beats leading 2D and 3D report models on two chest CT benchmarks in clinical accuracy, factual consistency, and interpretability. The authors present hypothesis-driven gathering, not bigger embeddings, as the route to reports a radiologist could trust.
arxiv-2605-01879:
Manuel Hernández and Eduardo Sánchez-Soto propose Sheaf-Theoretic Planning, a new base for planning by groups of autonomous agents. Older systems used logic tools such as event calculus and situation calculus to track action and change. Those tools work well in a closed world, but they struggle when agents act unseen, plans break, or beliefs drift from reality.

Sheaf theory, from category theory, offers a way to join local views into a global picture only when they agree. The report works through the maths, the prospects for building such a system, and its limits. The authors present it as a path toward agent teams that stay coherent under surprise and attack.
arxiv-2605-02379:
Andrea Forster and colleagues propose a design for fair personalisation by language model agents, when several stakeholders want different things. Such agents can talk with users and draw on outside knowledge. They can also negotiate with other agents, human or artificial. In a multi-stakeholder system, each agent may serve one party's goals. How those goals are set and joined decides whether outcomes stay fair.

The authors map open research challenges and propose a conceptual framework. It joins methods to align stakeholder goals with agent goals. It also covers ways to aggregate agent outputs, drawn in part from social choice theory. The aim is balanced personalisation that can be measured, not rule by one party.
arxiv-2605-02679:
Fabio Leoni and four co-authors review computational methods for making ultrastable glasses, solids frozen into exceptionally low-energy states. Such glasses are more stable in energy, motion, and strength than ordinary ones, and experiments have long prized them. Simulations can reach these states with unphysical moves that bypass slow cooling, opening a window on the glass transition itself.

The review lays out the key steps of the most effective algorithms in the field. For each, the authors discuss how well it works, where it falls short, and what it means physically. A comparative analysis then ranks the stability each method achieves. The aim is to give newcomers and experts alike a clear map of current methods and the chances they offer for designing robust glassy materials.
arxiv-2605-02779:
Erkinjon Karimov and Muzaffar Toshpulatov solve an inverse source problem for a mixed equation that blends wave and diffusion behavior, set inside a cylindrical domain. Inverse problems work backward from observed effects to the source that caused them. Here the governing equation carries a time-fractional derivative whose order varies with time, letting the model shift between wave-like and diffusive regimes as conditions change.

The solution is built as a Fourier-Bessel series, the natural expansion for a cylinder, using separation of variables and classic traits of Bessel functions. The authors analyze when the infinite series converges uniformly, a key step in trusting the formula. That analysis leads to a rigorous proof that a solution exists. The paper is a methods contribution to fractional mixed-type equations.
arxiv-2605-02979:
Supriya Khadka and Sanchari Das propose a formal risk-cost model for adaptive login checks in finance, where a small rise in false acceptance can mean huge loss. Adaptive systems blend biometrics, behavior signals, and context risk scores. Current designs are fragmented, though, and often serve compliance first. Explicit modeling of economic and hostile risk is rare. That imbalance is the paper's target.

The model joins three parts. Cost-sensitive risk functions capture fraud loss, lost chance, and tail risk in one measure. Step-by-step decision rules adapt as hostile users probe and patterns drift. Privacy and rule limits sit inside the core optimization itself, not as an afterthought. Login checking becomes a dynamic risk-cost problem with hard limits: grounded in economics and aware of tail risk, rather than a static classifier.
arxiv-2605-03079:
Vamshi Nallaguntla, Shruti Kshirsagar, and Anderson R. Avila propose checking fake speech sound by sound, rather than treating each clip as one block. New voice tools can fake emotion as well as words, which makes detection harder and past methods hard to interpret.

Working with real and converted speech matched for emotion and transcript, they align phonemes and compare WavLM embeddings for each sound. Complex vowels and fricatives diverged most, while simple sounds stayed stable. Sounds with larger gaps were also easier to flag, across emotions and systems, making the approach both effective and readable.
arxiv-2605-03179:
Richard J. Young and Gregory D. Moody build a vetted prompt bank that separates requests for working malicious code from requests for harmful security knowledge. Safety benchmarks often mix the two, so a single refusal rate cannot show which pathway a model actually used.

Five judge models from four vendor families labeled over three thousand prompts from four public benchmarks under a majority rule. Agreement was near-perfect, and no prompts fell below the consensus threshold. The released bank holds over fifteen hundred code prompts plus a knowledge comparison set. Whether the split predicts model behavior is left to a companion study.
arxiv-2605-03379:
Yi Liu studies how much repeated language model sampling helps binary decisions under majority vote, and how to forecast those gains before spending the compute. Extra calls cost money, so sharp bounds on vote accuracy at each budget matter for test-time planning.

Just two independent answers per validation example, Liu shows, pin down a class of latent success distributions consistent with the paired outcomes. Optimizing over that class gives sharp accuracy and gain bounds at every finite budget, plus infinite-vote limits and curve forecasts. On two question datasets, the method separated settings with real voting gains from those with little headroom.
arxiv-2605-03779:
Nathan Findlay and Seshadri Nadathur present VERSUS, a fast, public algorithm for finding cosmic voids, the large spherical underdensities in the distribution of galaxies. The finder is inspired by excursion set theory, which predicts how many voids of each size should exist. It is designed for the Stage-IV survey era.

Checks use a synthetic particle distribution tracing a known void population, plus mock galaxy samples from a large AbacusSummit simulation with a realistic galaxy-halo link and survey-like systematic effects. In all cases VERSUS matched theoretical predictions for the void size function across the tested radius range, with no post-processing of the catalogue needed. Its speed and modular design support simulation-based models for upcoming surveys.
arxiv-2605-04279:
Ayan Pendharkar develops a theory of how tokens move and cluster inside multi-head self-attention, the core mechanism of transformer models. A single attention head can be viewed as a flow that pulls tokens together, but several heads interfere with each other in ways that break simple arguments.

Pendharkar defines a combined energy for the multi-head case and shows when it grows steadily along the flow. He identifies extra radial terms as the key obstacle, gives a condition that restores the steady behaviour, and checks that it survives when heads are only roughly separate. A simplified setting yields an exact threshold for clustering.
arxiv-2605-04379:
Andrey Kupavskii and Georgy Sokolov work on a classic problem in combinatorics about families of subsets that contain no large collection of pairwise disjoint sets. Erdős and Kleitman settled the maximum size of such families for certain set sizes in 1968, but many sizes stayed open for decades.

Later work tied the best examples to a famous matching conjecture for a range of parameters, and conjectured the tie holds more broadly. Kupavskii and Sokolov prove an approximate version of that conjecture for large enough parameters. Their result supports the view that the same extremal structures govern both problems.
arxiv-2605-04879:
Ray Ganardi studies catalysis in entanglement manipulation, where a helper quantum state enables a change that would otherwise be forbidden. The helper must be returned intact at the end, like a catalyst in chemistry. Most earlier work looked at single copies, while Ganardi focuses on preparing many copies of a target state at once.

He constructs an explicit catalytic protocol and shows it can significantly lower the exact entanglement cost of that preparation. The gain is not limited to entanglement alone. Ganardi notes the same idea extends to other resource theories, giving a general catalytic advantage in the task known as resource dilution.
arxiv-2605-04979:
Anvay Shah and three co-authors learn online in tree-shaped decision problems by treating each whole policy as one arm of a bandit problem. Tree decision problems model sequential games with perfect recall against steady opponents. The catch is that the number of possible policies grows exponentially with the number of states, far too many to track naively.

Their innovation is confidence bounds built from data shared across policies, letting known bandit algorithms run with polynomial memory and step cost. The resulting guarantees add a gap term per end state rather than per policy. In tests on hidden-information games, their algorithms consistently beat the available alternatives.
arxiv-2605-05079:
Maxim Shugaev and ten co-authors present a benchmark for fixing video filmed through rough air or water surfaces, where refraction warps each frame. Existing tests mostly cover mild air shimmer, leaving strong and broken-up warping unmeasured. Their benchmark spans from mild warping to extreme refractive bending, using both lab footage and computer-made clips built with physics-based bending.

Methods from simple baselines and classical matching to advanced learning approaches are scored with pixel, visual, and meaning measures. A proposed diffusion-based method is included for the hardest regimes. The authors frame the release as the first large-scale analysis of warping removal, and a foundation for fixing video from badly distorted optical settings.
arxiv-2605-05179:
Wilson Wu and six co-authors question a basic habit in machine learning: estimating a model's expected loss by sampling. Sampling means running many random inputs through a network and averaging the results. For a wide, freshly initialized multilayer network, they show there is a cheaper way.

Their method tracks how signal distributions change from layer to layer, using cumulants and Hermite expansions. It reaches a target accuracy with far fewer operations than sampling needs. The method is especially strong at estimating rare-event chances, and the authors also show it can be used during training itself.
arxiv-2605-05279:
Violeta Leoreanu-Fotea and three co-authors present quasi sdf-absorbing ideals, a new, broader form of a known ideal class in commutative ring theory. Ideals are special subsets of a ring, and absorbing traits describe how products of members are forced back inside them. The authors study when this quasi version of the property survives standard ring builds.

They check whether it lasts under localisation, surjective images, Nagata idealisations, and amalgamations of rings. Rules are set out for the radical of such an ideal to be prime, and a class of rings is named where the quasi property rises to a primary version. The study closes with a sorting of these ideals in the whole numbers, with cases that split them from nearby classes.
arxiv-2605-05479:
Talal Ahmed Chowdhury, Seokwon Choi, Kyoungchul Kong, and Kwangmin Yu simulate a model of interacting particles on real quantum hardware. Their target is the multi-flavor Gross-Neveu model, a one-dimensional theory used to test ideas about fermions. The simulations ran on superconducting processors with more than one hundred qubits.

A new approximation, called LDOA, cuts the cost of the four-particle interaction terms. Circuit depth then grows with the number of flavors rather than the system size. Results matched exact calculations and tensor-network checks across sizes, showing that careful circuit design can make field-theory simulation practical today.
arxiv-2605-05679:
Pulsar timing arrays listen for a background hum of gravitational waves from merging supermassive black holes. Shreyas Tiruvaskar and Chris Gordon use that hum to compare theories of how the binaries evolve. Ultralight dark matter, environmental effects, and pure gravitational-wave emission each predict different low-frequency power.

The authors apply Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation to the five lowest frequency bins. Four models compete, including simplified and realistic dark matter versions. Earlier work had already used the friction effect to bound the dark matter particle's mass and its share of the total. The environmental-hardening model scored best on predictive accuracy, though its margin over the others was small compared with the uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-05779:
Bound states in the continuum trap light with, in theory, infinite lifetime; real fabrication always leaks. Nikolai A. Vlasov and six co-authors test how robust such states are in a metasurface of phase-change material bars. Lithography rarely cuts perfect rectangles, so they model bars as trapezoids and vary the imperfections.

Identical trapezoid shapes, despite keeping the required symmetry, lowered the quality factor in the amorphous phase through absorption changes. Random angle variations from bar to bar, by contrast, left the quality factor largely intact in both material phases. The study separates which imperfections matter from which can be tolerated.
arxiv-2605-06279:
Chengjie Wang and four co-authors measure a hidden risk in code written by language models: the library versions they specify. Generated Python code routinely imports third party libraries pinned to exact versions, and those choices can carry known flaws or break installation. No systematic study of version level risk existed before this large scale measurement on a benchmark of 1,000 programming tasks across ten models.

Models specified versions often, and between about a third and over half of tasks included at least one version with a known vulnerability. Most of those flaws were public before the model's knowledge cutoff, and models converged on the same small set of risky releases. Compatibility failures, mostly at installation, were also common. External version constraints cut both problems sharply.
arxiv-2605-06379:
Yu-Xuan Zhang and Jing-Ling Chen extract exact solutions of Yang-Mills theory with an algebraic tensor ring framework. The theory's nonlinear equations resist direct solution, yet exact classical solutions clarify its nonperturbative vacuum structure. Their method maps the nonlinear partial differential equations into differential algebraic systems that can be resolved systematically. It uses static pure gauge backgrounds as geometric templates. Their forms generate the cross terms that stabilize self interaction in the equations.

Three classes of exact solutions emerge. Relativistic color waves over an elliptic quotient ring split into decoupled and coupled branches, the latter generating a mass gap. Dynamic dyonic flux tubes branch into Coulomb, dyonic, and screening phases with Bessel type decay. A third family covers dynamic configurations of the larger gauge group, whose real branches hide a chaotic oscillator at their core.
arxiv-2605-06479: Sunay Joshi and colleagues do risk-controlled post-processing of decision policies. The doing does. Their doing is risk-controlled post-processing decision policies. The doing does. It is decision theory. The doing of. The policies post-process risk-controlled-decision.
arxiv-2605-06579:
Angus Mingare and Peter V. Coveney show how to load matrix product states onto quantum computers with shallow, log-depth circuits. Such states classically describe many quantum systems and could serve as reference states for algorithms like phase estimation. Loading them efficiently is essential for near-term hardware, where deep circuits decay quickly.

Their method uses a simple tree tensor network renormalization step, with an explicit knob that trades a little fidelity for large depth savings. Extended to operators, it also builds ancilla-free circuits for computing overlap quantities. Those circuits double as verifier circuits, with a use in calibrating quantum devices at the circuit level.
arxiv-2605-06879:
Zhongmou Chao and four co-authors predict protein function while correcting for survivorship bias in natural sequence data. Databases hold proteins only from organisms that lived, so working examples dominate and failed mutations stay unseen. Learning from positive cases alone is a known problem class, but generic methods ignore the process of evolution that decides which sequences ever get seen.

Their Evo-PU framework models nucleotide mutation in plain terms: a missing sequence one step from a common variant is suspect, while one mutation never arose is merely unseen. On flu, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 tasks it beats standard PU methods and one-class classifiers and protein language models, with caveats noted for messier multi-organism data.
arxiv-2605-07079:
Xinyu Zhang and five co-authors build world models that predict future visual features rather than raw video. Feature prediction can be faster and less prone to invented detail than image generation. Yet direct prediction often turns blurry or collapses during complex interactions.

The team found a new latent action signal hidden in differences between visual features, and showed it predicts how scenes progress. Their model generates that signal with flow matching, beating leading feature and video models while running far faster than video diffusion. Two robot methods built on it improve policy learning, including one trained entirely inside the learned world model.
arxiv-2605-07379:
Xin Chen and six co-authors teach visual object trackers to localize targets through reinforcement learning instead of handcrafted heatmaps. Conventional trackers rely on spatial priors that give only surrogate supervision, poorly aligned with the overlap and success measures used to judge tracking. RELO reframes localization as a decision process over positions.

A learned policy picks locations, rewarded by frame-level overlap and sequence-level success together. A token propagation method keeps meaning consistent across frames at negligible cost. Across benchmarks, RELO beat rivals and reached a strong success score on a hard text-guided dataset without template updates, confirming reward-driven localization as a real alternative.
arxiv-2605-07479:
Ziwei Ou, Xiaolong Yang, and Songpeng Pei report extended gamma-ray emission around the young star cluster Berkeley 59, using data from the Fermi space telescope. With updated catalogs and background models, they find significant emission spread over about a degree, well beyond a point source. The team then examines the surrounding molecular, neutral, and ionized gas.

The gamma-ray spectrum and the modest derived gas mass feed a relationship between cosmic ray acceleration efficiency and diffusion. Their results suggest the glow comes from cosmic rays accelerated by the cluster's winds striking nearby gas. The study links a single young cluster's outflows to high-energy emission visible across interstellar distances.
arxiv-2605-07579:
Yunho Choi and five co-authors improve reinforcement learning for reasoning models, where training needs a reliable baseline score to reduce noise. Group methods estimate that baseline from several tries at the same prompt, which crowds out prompt variety. Training a separate critic model avoids that trade-off but roughly doubles the cost.

Their algorithm, POISE, reads the baseline from the model's own internal states using a small probe trained alongside the policy. A cross-rollout trick keeps the gradient estimates unbiased. On two open model families and a six-domain reward corpus, POISE beat other baselines and trained more stably. The probe matched a full separate value model and stayed accurate as the policy grew.
arxiv-2605-07879:
Silvia Gasparotto works out gravitational-wave memory, the permanent low-frequency displacement left by passing waves, in a theory that modifies Einstein's gravity. Memory is a promising probe of strong-field gravity, but it had never been computed from full inspiral-merger-ringdown waveforms beyond general relativity. Gasparotto does so for scalar Gauss-Bonnet gravity.

The deviations from general relativity come out at the percent level, driven mainly by the changed merger dynamics, while the scalar field's own share of tensor memory is strongly damped. Including memory in the waveform greatly increases the mismatch between the modified theory and general relativity. That makes memory an extra observable for testing gravity with the next generation of detectors.
arxiv-2605-07979:
Santiago Cortes-Gomez and three co-authors study how to split a fixed aid budget between algorithm-led targeting and human screening. Machine learning hands out aid by predicted risk, cheaply and quickly, while physical checking sees true need directly but costs more. Even perfect risk scores cannot remove misallocation, because each person's vulnerability carries a chance that cannot be removed.

In their two-stage framework, a screening stage checks a chosen subset before final allocation. The optimal strategy screens the units at the margin of the algorithmic decision, those near the cutoff, while sending aid straight to the highest-risk units without screening. Screening and targeting act as complements or substitutes depending on conditions, and screening's gains grow as group uncertainty rises. Uses in Colombian social protection and humanitarian demining ground the theory.
arxiv-2605-08079:
Pavel Orlov, Rustem Sharipov, and Enej Ilievski refine the eigenstate thermalization picture. That picture explains how lone quantum systems settle down. The standard view ties matrix elements of local quantities to macrostate data. Those data are the densities of conserved charges.

The team shows the spreads can also hinge on the ensemble used to sample eigenstates. They swap fixed energy windows for ensembles with a tunable scale for charge spread. Their test bed is an integrable field theory. It allows fast sampling and clean scaling to large size. One class of states even allows closed-form work. The results reveal a multiscale pattern in thermalization data.
arxiv-2605-08379:
Jonathon Hirschi, Jan Mandel, and Adam Kochanski adapt a fuel moisture model across fuel types by warping time. Dead fuel moisture drives wildfire behavior models. Fuels are classed by their lag time. The classes run from one-hour twigs to thousand-hour logs. Sensors report the ten-hour class richly. The other classes are observed sparsely.

Their method rescales the learned dynamics of a recurrent network with an LSTM layer. It stretches or compresses time. A model trained on ten-hour fuels can then predict the slower and faster classes. Validation uses a landmark Oklahoma field study. That study calibrated the standard Nelson model. The test asks whether time warping is a sound bridge between fuel classes.
arxiv-2605-09279: Streaming volumetric video — 3D scenes you can walk around — eats bandwidth. Daheng Yin, Yili Jin, Jianxin Shi, and others adapt to color and content with CAGS: color-adaptive streaming via dynamic 3D Gaussian splatting. The 2026 paper squeezes 3D video through thin pipes.
arxiv-2605-09479: Image quality metrics usually please human eyes; machine consumers — downstream models — want different things. Feng Ding, Haisheng Fu, Jie Liang, and others measure multi-layer CLIP similarity for machine-oriented quality — ML-CLIPSim. The 2026 paper judges images the way AI sees them.

Bassi, and others build DeepTumorVQA: a hierarchical 3D CT benchmark for medical VLMs and tool-augmented agents. The 2026 paper grades medical AI like a residency.
arxiv-2605-09779: Active fluids — swarming bacteria, flocking cells — flip between collective states in rare, dramatic transitions; a weakly nonlinear reduction captures them. arxiv-2606-04079:
Atom Computing and collaborators report in 2026 a demonstration of repeated quantum error correction using the toric code on their neutral-atom platform, where individual atoms held by laser tweezers serve as qubits. Error correction is the missing step between today's noisy devices and reliable quantum computers.

The team ran many rounds of syndrome extraction, the checks that reveal errors, while measuring qubits mid-circuit and replacing atoms that were lost from a stored reservoir. Logical information survived through repeated reloading of that reservoir. They tracked the logical error rate across up to ninety correction cycles. Comparing two sizes of the code over eight rounds, the larger code showed the lower error rate, as theory predicts for a working correction scheme.
arxiv-2606-04379:
Richard Cloete and Abraham Loeb report in 2026 a candidate interstellar meteor. It crossed over the South Atlantic in April 2026 on a near-polar path. If its speed truly exceeds the Sun's escape velocity at Earth's distance, it came from outside the solar system.

Starting from the satellite-reported velocity, they removed Earth's gravity with a two-body model. Then they added Earth's orbital motion. The resulting heliocentric speed cleared the escape threshold comfortably. The polar component alone exceeded local escape speed. A million Monte Carlo trials perturbed the measurements with a calibrated error model. Not one produced a bound orbit. That puts the interstellar confidence above ninety-nine point nine nine percent.
arxiv-2606-04479:
Hong and Zhou test whether image generators that write text inside pictures are really reasoning, or only copying patterns, in a 2026 arXiv study. Such text serves documents and slides. The open question is whether the models preserve reasoning. This matters when a full solution must appear as rendered text. The authors probe this reasoning fidelity across four areas. They test long text rendering, factual knowledge questions, context understanding, and multi-step reasoning.

They find that current models often produce semantic errors. They also produce logical inconsistencies and wrong intermediate steps. This happens even when the rendered text looks clear. Text-only models handle the same tasks well. So the failures are not about question difficulty. Hong and Zhou conclude that a substantial gap separates visual text generation from procedural reasoning. They motivate work on making image-based text more reliable. A polished page can hide broken logic.
arxiv-2606-04579:
Zhao and colleagues build a reward model that grades each step of a scientific solution, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Process reward models score intermediate reasoning. They work well in mathematics. Science adds factual consistency and precise tool use, where models hallucinate. The authors first build SCIPRM70K. This dataset holds Chain-of-Tool trajectories. They interleave reasoning with executions of scientific tools in biology, chemistry, and physics.

Trained on it, Sci-PRM gives fine-grained supervision in one inference pass. It covers tool selection, execution accuracy, and result interpretation. The model helps in two ways. At test time, Best-of-N selection picks better solutions. Inside reinforcement learning, it supplies a dense reward signal. This mitigates advantage disappearance, the failure where all sampled solutions score alike and learning stalls. The authors report that this lets models break through existing performance ceilings. They release Sci-PRM publicly.
arxiv-2606-04979:
McKevitt, Ugarte-Urra, and Young watch the Sun's corona change across a full solar cycle the way stellar astronomers must watch other stars, in a 2026 arXiv solar physics paper. They compile eighteen scans from the Hinode satellite's EIS instrument spanning 2013 to 2024.

Disk-integrated coronal intensity correlates strongly with the solar cycle, consistent with stellar observations. No clear cycle variation appears in the Doppler or non-thermal velocity distributions, and active region intensity per unit area correlates moderately. Sun-as-a-star intensity variability is driven mainly by the changing fraction of the disk covered by active regions, not by changing plasma properties within them. The known link between upflows and line broadening persists all cycle, implying active region kinematics ignore the global field configuration.
arxiv-2606-05179:
Sungmook Woo, Hyunku Kang, and Chanwoo Kim restore punctuation in streaming speech recognition with a weighted lookahead scoring method in this 2026 arXiv paper. Punctuation makes transcripts readable, but a streaming recognizer must decide online, with little future context. Generation-based fixes, where a model rewrites the sentence, are prone to latency and can break alignment with the fixed transcript. Their method scores without generating: it preserves the input transcript and decides at each word boundary.

It compares punctuation insertion hypotheses against a no-insertion baseline under a lookahead of K subword tokens, calibrated on a validation set, with no parameter updates at inference time. On the IWSLT 2017 benchmark it reached a four-class F1 of 0.893 with no fine-tuning, and 0.937 after fine-tuning, beating a prompt baseline at 0.566 and a fine-tuned ELECTRA baseline at 0.913 under the same budget. Ablations map the accuracy-delay tradeoff of the lookahead budget.
arxiv-2606-05679:
Summers and Wu move data safety rules into the database itself in a 2026 arXiv paper. AI agents now write queries and run pipelines for users. A query can be correct yet still break privacy law or business policy by joining data wrongly. Checking by prompt or after the fact is fragile. Their framework, Data Flow Control, states safety rules over how each row's data may flow and combine.

Rules are written as conditions over provenance, the record of where each value came from. A rewriting layer called Passant enforces them inside the query, with no provenance tables built. The layer runs on five database engines, from DuckDB to SQL Server. Measured overhead came out near zero. It also beat rival enforcers by orders of magnitude. The authors pitch the work as the first step from prompt-level promises to infrastructure-level guarantees for agent data use.
arxiv-2606-05779:
Van Le, Tran, and Tan Le test tiny onboard models for spacecraft cyber defense in a 2026 arXiv paper. Satellites must spot radio and cyber attacks fast, with little computing power to spare. The SPARTA framework catalogs the attack styles, from uplink jamming to command injection. The team compares four small classical models on speed against accuracy. Theory on complexity and scaling sits beside bench tests on corrupted radio spectrograms.

Logistic regression, the plainest model, answered in microseconds. It gave up only about one percent accuracy against random forest, the strongest rival. That trade makes it a strong baseline for onboard autonomy. Support vector machines and small neural nets filled out the comparison. Attack fakes came in three corruption styles, including band erasure and noise bursts. The authors point to richer signal features and multi-timescale learning as next steps. Lightweight math, they argue, already guards a satellite well.
arxiv-2606-06179:
Naïl Khelifa, Richard Turner, and Ramji Venkataramanan argue that diffusion models are being graded with the wrong ruler in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diffusion models generate images by reversing a gradual noising process, guided by a learned score that points toward more likely data. Training minimizes the L2 score matching error, and theory uses it to bound how far generated samples drift from the target distribution.

The authors split the score error into two geometric parts: a gradient part and a swirling solenoidal part. Only the gradient part feeds the dynamics that shape the final sample distribution, so the other part is invisible to sample quality. They prove no monotone function of the full error can lower-bound distribution mismatch, then bound the Kullback-Leibler divergence using the gradient part alone. On CIFAR-10, that part correlated with sample quality near ninety-six hundredths, well above the full error.
arxiv-2606-06479:
Akarsh Kumar and Phillip Isola rethink how recurrent networks learn memory in this 2026 arXiv paper. Recurrent neural networks process sequences step by step, but training them by backpropagation through time is sequential, slow, and plagued by gradients that vanish or explode over long spans. Their Supervised Memory Training avoids unrolling the network entirely. A Transformer encoder first learns what is worth remembering: a compact state that keeps only the past information needed to predict the future.

Those learned states become labels. The recurrent network is then trained by supervised learning to make one step transitions between states, a task that parallelizes across time and keeps gradients stable. Across language modeling and pixel sequence tasks, the method beat backpropagation through time, and the models captured longer range dependencies. Decoupling what to remember from how to update, the authors suggest, could finally let recurrent models scale.
arxiv-2606-06579:
Christopher Yang and co-authors let a material generate its own laser like drive in this 2026 arXiv paper on quantum materials. Floquet engineering reshapes a material's electronic bands with a periodic drive, usually an external laser: power hungry and hard to integrate. Their alternative embeds a semiconductor layer in an optical cavity wired to leads and a phonon bath. Direct current pumping builds a coherent field inside the cavity through light matter coupling, until the system self organizes.

Above threshold, the system settles into a stable time periodic limit cycle. Its strength is set by the cavity's quality factor and dissipation. That home grown field dresses the electronic bands just as a laser would. In a material with broken time reversal symmetry, the dressed bands' geometry changes the anomalous Hall response, measurable through ordinary in plane transport. Electrically controlled quantum phases, with no external light at all, come into reach.
arxiv-2606-06779:
A food delivery app knows what you order for dinner, but not what groceries you might want. Sinha, Saboo, Wang, and Das attack that cold start problem at DoorDash in this 2026 arXiv paper. Newer shopping areas like grocery and retail have thin user histories, while the restaurant side holds years of rich behavior that could hint at wider tastes.

Their framework uses a large language model as a bridge between the two worlds. A retrieval pipeline digs through each user's restaurant orders and searches, then generates features describing long term tastes and short term intent at several levels of detail. Those features feed the production ranking model that decides what each shopper sees. Offline and live tests showed clear gains in personalization and engagement for the newer verticals, strongest for users with no history there.
arxiv-2606-06879:
Scam texts that unfold over many messages are hard to catch, and real examples are scarce. Lochstampfor and Roy expand a synthetic data set for that fight in this 2026 arXiv paper. The crime is smishing, fraud by text message. Their collection, COVA-X, holds almost eleven thousand invented conversations. The scams target older people in eight categories.

The new corpus fixes flaws found in its smaller parent. Generation glitches, mismatched labels, and leaked stage directions were cleaned out. Label corrections fell sharply as the pipeline improved. All classifiers were then retrained on the bigger set. A transformer model called Longformer now beats the older gradient boosting champion. It reached about eighty percent accuracy on the tests. That confirms the team's earlier guess: transformers need larger conversation data before their context skills pay off. Artifact rates in the trickiest scam type also dropped.
arxiv-2606-06979:
Ordinary particles pair quarks with antiquarks, but theory allows stranger bundles of four. Yuheng Wu and co-authors hunt for fully heavy tetraquarks in this 2026 arXiv paper. A tetraquark packs four quarks into one particle. Here all four are heavy: charm or bottom quarks and their antimatter twins.

The team works inside a chiral quark model. They test two internal arrangements for the bundle. Bound state calculations found no truly bound state in either system. A real scaling method, though, revealed resonance states. Resonances are short lived humps rather than stable particles. The charm system showed two, near seven thousand and seventy two hundred million electron volts. Those match candidates for the observed X(6900) and X(7200) structures. The bottom system showed one resonance near nineteen thousand seven hundred. The authors urge experiments to search the double Upsilon spectrum for it.
arxiv-2606-07079:
Diffusion image models usually dirty the whole picture with one noise level at a time. Papa and co-authors let each region follow its own schedule in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their AsyncPatch Diffusion assigns distinct noise levels to different pixels or latent tokens. One patch can be nearly clean while its neighbor is still pure static.

The team proves the asynchronous process is a valid generative model, with the first correct evidence lower bound for it. Training needs care: random per region noise over samples chaotic mixes. A controlled sampler balances average corruption against spatial variety. One pretrained model then generates, fills missing regions, and extends images without retraining. Clean patches can guide the generation of unknown ones, improving local consistency. Quality matched standard diffusion on ImageNet and LSUN benchmarks. Bonus strategies include speeding up easy regions and generating autoregressively, piece by piece.
arxiv-2606-07179:
Streaming a detailed 3D scene to a headset means sending coarse versions first and refining on demand. Yuang Shi and co-authors rebuild that refinement as a family tree in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is 3D Gaussian Splatting, which renders scenes from millions of soft colored blobs. Earlier progressive schemes stacked independent layers of blobs, one per quality level.

Independence wasted bytes and let errors accumulate between layers. EvoGS instead grows an Evolution Tree. Each parent splat refines into children that can correct the ancestors' mistakes, wavelet style. Redundant splats fell from over sixty five percent to under twenty five percent. Transmission payload shrank by up to about two point four times. Graphics memory needs dropped by up to five point five times. Quality also changed smoothly rather than in jumps. The sparse differences between layers compress well for streaming. Immersive scenes on weak connections are the target use.
arxiv-2606-07479:
Karakaş and Şimşek test whether language models can tell idiomatic Turkish expressions from literal ones, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Light verb constructions pair a noun with a verb like make or do; the same surface form can be an idiom or a literal phrase, which makes classification tricky.
