Support fixes aimed at daily service gaps. Wider fixes aimed at rules and systems. Shared referral paths across the border led the list. Worksite HIV rules and flexible funds also featured. Care built for mobile lives is the core plea.
pmc-13290079:
Louise Dupraz and colleagues identify a 2026 gut bacterium, Sutterella, as a quiet troublemaker that worsens intestinal inflammation. Gut microbes normally train immunity and guard against infection, but some harmless residents turn harmful when the gut environment is disturbed. In bowel diseases such as ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease, that disturbed balance drives severe inflammation through pathways still being mapped.

Lab and animal tests show the bacterium directly dampens lymphoid cell output of IL-22 and IL-17, weakening gut defense signals. In a chemical colitis mouse model, it raised inflammation while blocking IL-22 output as well. Secreted protein compounds block a sensing pathway called AhR in the cells. Human lymphoid cells reacted the same way.
pmc-13290779:
Support helps ALS caregivers directly, not by lightening their burden first, Nafiye Turkmenel and Ersin Uskun report in a cross-sectional study from 2026. They tested a stress-process model in 118 informal caregivers of people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

Worse patient function meant heavier caregiver burden, while trouble communicating added little once caregiver traits were counted. Burden dragged both physical and mental quality of life down. Perceived social support, though, stayed positively tied to quality of life even after burden was in the model, and mediation tests found no sign that support worked through easing burden. Turkmenel and Uskun conclude services should attack burden and build support as two separate jobs, since each touches caregivers' lives on its own path.
pmc-13291179:
HIV testing at a cervix clinic in Sheffield is reviewed by Victoria L Parker and colleagues in a 2026 service check. National rules give no clear steer on such testing. Few clinics in England offer it. This clinic began standard testing in early 2023.

The check covered 367 patients with moderate or worse cell changes. Six already knew they had HIV. Rates in this group far topped the city average. Staff offered a test to most patients. Most of those asked said yes. All new test results came back negative. Nurses offered tests more often than consultants did. High uptake supports wider offers, the authors say.
pmc-13291779:
Yang Wang wrote a 2026 editorial introducing a research collection on functional materials and device design for perovskite solar cells. Certified efficiency for these cells has now passed 26 percent, helped by tunable band gaps and strong light absorption. Wang argues that stability problems still block the road to market.

The collection gathers four invited articles. One models a dual-absorber cell pairing MAGeI3 with CsSnI3 in simulation, finding strong voltage, current, and fill factor even with moderate defect levels. A review article covers recent progress with self-assembled monolayers, among the other contributions. Wang frames the set as a snapshot of where materials design and device engineering now stand for next-generation solar power.
pmc-13292179:
Mahkameh Rafiee and co-authors pool a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on metabolic illness among older people living with HIV. Aging with HIV increasingly means managing blood pressure, weight, sugar, and cholesterol alongside the virus. The team searched five databases plus grey literature for English studies from 2013 to late December 2023.

Twenty-six studies qualified, most from North America and other developed settings. Pooled prevalence came to 40.7 percent for hypertension and 47.3 percent for high cholesterol among older patients. Diabetes affected 13.5 percent and obesity 26.1 percent of those studied in the combined estimates. Every condition ran higher in North America than elsewhere. The authors recommend routine screening, prevention programs, and diet and exercise support tailored to this group.
pmc-13293579:
Mengmeng Wang, Ping Zhang, and Min Shen report, in a 2026 case study, a Chinese patient with PAPA syndrome, a rare inherited inflammatory disorder named for joint inflammation, skin ulcers, and acne. The condition stems from changes in the PSTPIP1 gene.

Illness began at age 13, with skin ulcers and acne as the main signs in this patient. Gene testing found a new change in PSTPIP1 that neither parent carried. The report also reviews recent papers on signs, diagnosis, and care for the syndrome. Treatments aim at inflammatory pathways, with drugs blocking IL-1 or TNF signals among the options used. Wider awareness may speed diagnosis.
pmc-13293679:
Daniel Schallmayer and co-authors report, in a 2026 case study, a cracked plastic liner inside a thumb joint replacement that caused almost no symptoms. The patient, a 53-year-old cook, had a Touch prosthesis fitted in early 2024 for thumb base arthritis.

He felt only slight clicking when spreading his thumb, and standard X-rays and exam looked normal. A CT scan and stress X-rays hinted the ball sat off-center. Revision surgery found the fractured liner as the cause, and swapping the head restored smooth, silent motion. Regular checks are urged, since serious implant failure can hide behind mild signs.
pmc-13293979:
Alba Lillo Sierras, Sandro Bräunig, and coauthors give a 2026 protocol that shows RNA and protein together in routine bone marrow biopsies. Samples are formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded, the standard hospital format. Fluorescence methods mark two growth factor transcripts, TGFB1 and PDGFA1, alongside cell surface proteins that separate blood-forming cells from support cells.

The setting is acute lymphoblastic leukemia, where marrow fibrosis predicts worse outlook but its cause is unclear. Seeing exactly which cells make each factor, and where, can test whether support cells drive scarring. Because the method fits stored biopsy blocks, past cases can be studied without fresh tissue.
pmc-13294179:
Kyosuke Hoshikawa and coauthors use ultrasound stiffness tests to watch shoulder muscles make up for cuff tears in a 2026 study. Twenty-four patients with mean age near 66 years lifted the arm to the side. Stiffness, a proxy for muscle work, was read in three muscles at 30, 60, and 90 degrees. Tear size was measured at surgery.

Patients split into normal and odd deltoid work groups by stiffness shape. The odd group kept deltoid work high at each angle, clearly above normal at 30 degrees. Mate muscle shifts were more subtle. Mapping who leans too hard on the deltoid could guide rehab after repair.
pmc-13294879:
Al-Ali Hussein, Soon Huat Tan, and Vel Murugan Vadivelu design a three-part material for cleaning dye from water with visible light in a 2026 study. Single materials often waste light energy because separated charges recombine too fast. Their blend joins polypyrrole, titanium dioxide, and carbon nanotubes in one linked structure.

Polypyrrole harvests visible light, the oxide offers a stable reacting surface, and nanotubes carry electrons away quickly. Screening of acidity, dye level, and material dose found best settings that removed nearly all methylene blue in tests. The material kept most of its activity after five reuse cycles, and chemical analysis traced how the dye broke down.
pmc-13295079:
Dabin Huang and co-authors combine three bedside measures to warn of gut perforation in preterm babies in a 2026 study. Necrotizing enterocolitis can tear the bowel and kill quickly, yet early warning remains hard. Lactate, platelet size, and an organ failure score were tested together as a warning set.

Records covered 110 preterm infants with surgical bowel disease, half with perforation and half without. The perforated group showed higher values on all three measures and died more often before discharge. Lactate and platelet size independently flagged perforation risk, and the three measures together predicted both perforation and death better than any single measure alone.
pmc-13295779:
Marco Gemelli and colleagues link poverty to outcomes after major aorta surgery in a 2026 study. Twenty years of cases at one centre were split by a national deprivation index. Emergency repair of a torn aorta and planned major aortic operations were judged separately.

In the emergency group of 526 patients, the most deprived half died in hospital far more often and survived fewer years afterwards. Deprivation predicted death on its own in adjusted models for that group. In the planned group of 1,320 patients, no such gaps appeared for early or long-term outcomes, suggesting emergency pathways carry the inequality burden.
pmc-13295879:
Jiale Zhu and co-authors build a spatial map in 2026 of immune cells in breast cancer that has spread to the brain. Combining detailed tissue imaging with public single-cell and spatial data, they compare original breast tumours with brain deposits cell by cell.

Brain deposits had lost a welcoming tissue zone rich in memory T cells and other defenders. In its place grew a suppressive zone holding CD163-positive macrophages, invasive tumour cells and tired T cells. Signals that switch immunity off were also flagged. Tests in animals backed the idea that blocking those signals could help treat brain spread.
pmc-13297779:
Chest scans clear more slowly in people with diabetes who are healing from viral lung disease, though diabetes may not be the root cause. Ana Maria Mihai and her team tracked 430 patients in a 2026 study, scoring lung harm on day 1 and day 6 of care.

The diabetes group came in worse off, with a mid score of 2.0 next to 1.0 for the rest. Both groups got better at the same pace, yet the gap was still there on day 6. Why patients left the study split sharply too: most exits in the non-diabetes group were people who left against advice, while deaths drove most exits in the diabetes group. Once the team weighed how sick people were at the start, the diabetes effect lost its force.
pmc-13299279:
Two drug targets, hit at once, could push a harsh form of breast cancer to die. Sergio Assuncao Monteiro and his team reach that call in a 2026 study done by math and code. Their search paired logic nets of cell life with a strict math sieve to hunt pairs worth a drug.

The hunt lit on TK1 and VIM. A joint block on both drove the cell state 99.03% of the way to the death state. The pair beat all rivals and stayed on top at each tweak of the model's knobs. Drugs that hit each one are on hand now. A deep-learn check found plain breast tissue would shrug off the same block, which hints at a safe dose gap. Bench proof must come next.
pmc-13299379:
Professional soccer strains players' hormone balance for days, and responses may differ by ethnic background, synthesize Sandro La Vignera and Rosita A Condorelli in a 2026 review. They analyzed twenty-one studies of testosterone, cortisol, their ratio, growth hormone, and IGF-1 across training and competition.

Cortisol stayed elevated up to seventy-two hours after some matches, and the testosterone-to-cortisol ratio sagged during congested fixture runs. A gene variant affecting steroid excretion, UGT2B17, may partly explain group differences in testosterone measures, though the evidence is thin. About 7.4% of elite junior players developed non-functional overreaching with blunted hormone responses. The authors suggest individualized hormone monitoring and gentler post-match loads.
pmc-13301479:
Women with amyloid in their hearts are found later and fare worse than men, Ilenia Monaco and colleagues argue in a 2026 narrative review of sex disparities in cardiac amyloidosis. The survey covers how the infiltrative disease shows up, how it is caught, and how it is treated, with the male–female contrast running through each stage.

Women tend to be older at diagnosis, with disease that looks milder on standard measures yet carries a poorer outlook. Sex-neutral cut-offs, the authors contend, help explain the misses and delays. They press for sex-specific thresholds, wider use of multimodality imaging, and trials that enroll enough women to define the female pattern of the disease.
pmc-13302279:
Blood cytokines may one day grade the severity of hidradenitis suppurativa, Anna Tekielak and colleagues conclude in a 2026 systematic review. Following PRISMA rules across major databases for studies from 2015 onward, they hunted human work reporting serum cytokine levels in this painful, tunnel-forming skin disease. Only six studies cleared every bar for the final synthesis.

Patients carried higher levels of IL-17A, IL-6, and IL-1β than healthy controls. IL-23, IL-18, and soluble TNF receptors were raised as well. Several markers tracked disease severity, and some shifted under biologic treatment, feeding proposals to split patients into immune endotypes. Small study counts and mixed methods, the authors caution, keep cytokine panels out of routine clinics for now.
pmc-13303179:
Aligning magnetic flakes with a magnet before the glue sets boosts microwave soaking, Guijiang Liu and colleagues show in a 2026 materials study. Iron oxide specks were stuck onto graphene oxide sheets, mixed into epoxy resin, and cured inside a magnetic field that lined the flakes up. Samples varied in graphene share and field use.

At ten weight percent graphene with the field on, the mix absorbed the whole X-band, eight to twelve gigahertz, at just one to three millimeters thick. Its best reflection loss hit minus 40.3 decibels. The authors credit three effects working as one: charge pile-up at flake edges, superparamagnetic relaxation, and the field-set alignment. They pitch the trick for shielding electronics.
pmc-13305679:
José Roberto Vargas-Villanueva surveyed evidence in 2026 on whether pomegranate compounds can prevent or treat parasitic disease. Standard drugs have lost ground through resistance, side effects that stop people finishing courses, and reinfection where sanitation stays poor.

Water and alcohol extracts, especially from peel, showed the strongest activity against several important parasites in the studies reviewed. Benefit was linked mainly to phenolic chemicals such as punicalagin, punicalin and ellagic acid, among others named in the review. Used alone, for prevention, or alongside standard drugs, the fruit showed protective and restorative effects, making its compounds candidates to widen treatment options.
pmc-13306279:
Thanh Binh Ngo built a low-cost crack watcher for working underground tunnels in a 2026 field study. Small edge devices sense crack movement and temperature, process signals on site, and send guarded updates through long-range radio links.

A thirty-day trial at two sites ran the full chain, from sensing through wavelet and Kalman cleaning to cloud storage, under tight power and cost limits. Lightweight coding and encryption kept data moving in real time in the reported checks. Longer trials with more nodes are still needed to prove scale, durability and lasting reliability.
pmc-13306779:
Saida T. Zulfugarova combined body, chemical and cell-level checks on heat stress in wheat in a 2026 study. Four bread wheat types with contrasting heat tolerance were compared for membrane harm, fat oxidation, defence enzymes and gene switching.

Heat raised damage in all types, yet tolerant Murov 2 and Zirva 85 showed less oxidative injury than sensitive Aran and Gyzyl bugda in reported results. Tolerance tied to stronger antioxidant action plus sharper switching of DREB and HSP16.9 genes. The HSP16.9 protein also built up after heating, supporting a protective helper role. Such joint checks may help breeders pick wheat lines that stand heat in dry zones.
pmc-13309279:
Katy Martin and Rose Legg review in 2026 hyperemesis gravidarum, a harsh form of pregnancy sickness that strikes about 3 percent of pregnancies each year. They press its oral toll on dental teams. The sickness starts before 16 weeks, with fierce nausea and vomiting that block normal eating and drinking and shrink daily life.

Long vomiting can starve the body, skew salts, and shed weight, while acid baths raise cavity and wear risk, warp taste, and dry the mouth. Care can run from anti sickness drugs and steroids to tube or vein feeding in grave cases. Tooth care is hard mid illness, so dental staff must know the state to back patients and work mates alike.
pmc-13309579: Yafei Huang is first named on a 2026 correction notice for a study of how the pain drug nabumetone can harm heart muscle cells. The study links that harm to energy-center damage, with SIRT3 activation offering protection. Corrected here are only the legends for figures 4 and 5, which were published incorrectly. The notice reprints both figures with their proper legends, covering a prostaglandin pathway test in human heart cells. No results or conclusions change, since the item exists solely to fix those captions.
pmc-13310379:
Dimo Dimitrov and co-authors report simultaneous liver and chest infection by a mouth bacterium in a 2026 case article. Actinomycosis is a slow infection that crosses tissue planes and often mimics cancer. Spread to liver and lung lining at once is particularly rare.

An 85-year-old woman with kidney disease and diabetes developed fever, muscle pain, and belly pain weeks after recovering from COVID-19, following several dental procedures. Scans found a liver abscess reaching toward the kidney space and fluid around the lung that later grew and pocketed. Cultures from the abscess grew Actinomyces odontolyticus. Long antibiotics and drainage procedures formed the treatment core. The authors highlight dental sources and slow spread as diagnostic clues.
pmc-13310679:
Youlin Song and co-authors judge two software models that predict stomach function and stomach lesions in a 2026 study. Endoscopy is accurate but invasive and costly for broad screening. Models that fuse symptom questionnaires with blood markers of stomach function promise a cheaper first filter.

Data from 1,677 patients with digestive symptoms at one hospital between 2015 and 2023 fed both models, and outputs were checked against lab tests and endoscopy with tissue results. The function model reached 91.16 percent sensitivity with 39.18 percent specificity in the reported scores. The lesion model reached 89.55 percent sensitivity with 33.22 percent specificity on its task. The authors read both as sensitive triage tools that still over-flag healthy stomachs.
pmc-13310779:
Yeyao Wu and co-authors review drugs that block DNA repair in pancreatic cancer in a 2026 paper. Pancreatic cancer is among the most deadly cancers, with few drug choices beyond standard chemo. Some tumors carry faults in repair genes such as BRCA, which leaves a weak point that repair blocking drugs can strike.

Single drugs help only a narrow group and often stop working as resistance grows, with harsh side effects. New plans pair drugs together, add immune or growth blocking drugs, and try fresh targets. Tests with blood samples may track resistance early. Care is shifting toward paired plans matched to each tumor.
pmc-13310879:
Laura Volpi and colleagues examine regulatory science as a field in health care in a 2026 perspective paper. The term is widely used for work that supports drug and device decisions, yet meanings vary by office and lack a shared core. Without a clear frame, the field risks looking like mere rule following.

Regulatory science, they argue, studies regulation itself with sound methods and clear values. Its aim is to test how systems work and how they should grow to meet real market needs. A refined meaning stresses goals set in law, proof based methods, and reform intent. Set terms could help the field stand as its own discipline.
pmc-13310979:
Kaung Myat Thwin and colleagues link self reported oral health to blood sugar status in Japanese adults in a 2026 cohort study. Gum disease, chewing ease, and tooth count may track sugar control, yet links across normal, borderline, and diabetic ranges were unclear. Baseline data from the Uonuma cohort in Niigata were used.

Adults totaled 4,338 in number, all aged 40 years or older, with a median age near 66 years old at entry. Borderline sugar levels appeared in about one third, and diabetic levels in a small share. Gum history links faded after full adjustment, and chewing ease showed no link. Toothless adults held higher diabetic odds in early models.
pmc-13311079:
Shihao Guo and co-authors chart milk sugars in mothers with gestational diabetes across nursing stages in a 2026 study. Human milk oligosaccharides feed infant gut germs and immunity, and pregnancy diabetes may alter their mix. Milk from healthy and diabetic mothers in Danyang City was compared over three months.

Samples totaled 156 in number from 50 mothers, with 26 healthy and 24 diabetic donors. Total milk sugars fell by one and three months compared with first milk. Seven sugars, including a common fucose type, linked to diabetes after full adjustment. Each sugar followed its own time path, which may shape infant feeding advice.
pmc-13311179:
Shun Wen and colleagues screen scent making genes in an agarwood tree in a 2026 study. Agarwood is a prized fragrant resin that forms slowly under stress, which limits supply. Its key scent part agarospirol had no known making gene, so terpene synthase genes from Aquilaria yunnanensis were tested in yeast.

Screening 26 genes yielded 30 distinct scent products in yeast tests. One gene proved to make agarospirol, confirmed by magnetic spectra of the product. Guided changes at two spots in the enzyme shifted the product mix, which reveals how its pocket shapes the ring form. Gene knowledge may enable factory scale scent making.
pmc-13311279:
Roberto Larcher and colleagues release a 2026 dataset and tool set for testing people-tracking software on ground robots. The robot must move among people in a polite, safe way while keeping track of each person.

Recordings were made in a 6 by 6 meter lab space where a robot resembling a smart wheelchair moved among people. Two depth cameras, a flat laser scanner, and a motion capture system logged the scenes. Scenes vary in crowd size, behavior, and obstacles. The tools score trackers on their own, helping labs compare systems and spot where each one fails.
pmc-13311579:
Shannon McNamara and co-authors set out a 2026 protocol for studying how nurses in Quebec move into nurse practitioner roles. New practitioners who feel unready can struggle with solo decisions and job satisfaction.

The plan uses a cross-sectional survey of nurse practitioners in their first post for under twelve months, in English and French versions. At least 50 respondents will complete a role transition scale covering mentoring, purpose, confidence, and pay. Simple regression will test which factors track with smoother transitions. Results should help schools and employers shape support for the first year in the role.
pmc-13311679:
Martin Tze Wah Kueh and co-authors in 2026 analyze a population study on body weight, belly fat, and death risk in adults with fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. United States survey data from 2007 to 2018 supply the base.

The study sorted 6300 adults into four types by obesity and waist-to-height ratio. The largest group, 72.1 percent, had obesity with high central fat in this sample. Death records were followed through the end of 2019. The work asks whether belly fat adds risk beyond weight class alone, a question that shapes how doctors grade danger in this very common liver condition.
pmc-13312079:
Janaïs Delport and Martin Herrer Villet review, in a 2026 article, how the study of pollen in honey can serve both lawmaking and court work. Pollen and spores trapped in honey can confirm or challenge a product's claimed origin and floral source. That matters as honey fraud becomes a medical, economic, and legal concern worldwide.

The authors argue that test results can anchor legal standards for genuine honey and support honest labeling that protects buyers and rewards small producers. Judged against forensic benchmarks, the field passes tests of testability, peer review, written procedures, measured error rates, and community acceptance, and its findings have already been used in court. They note weak spots too, such as private databases that need outside auditing, and case limits that can keep sound evidence out.
pmc-13312579:
Lilan You and colleagues use multi-omics tools, in a 2026 study, to explain how two bacterial strains working together improve low-salt fish sauce made from yellowfin tuna dark meat. Traditional fish sauce ferments for months at high salt, which health trends now push against, and the team wanted the flavor chemistry of a faster, lower-salt co-fermentation mapped out.

Pediococcus acidilactici and Staphylococcus xylosus at a 1 to 2 ratio lifted amino acid nitrogen above 0.7 grams per 100 milliliters, a standard quality marker. Sequencing showed the mixed culture built a distinct microbial community dominated by Lactiplantibacillus and Pediococcus. Chemical profiling found 16 key volatile compounds and 20 reduced non-volatile ones versus unfermented sauce, enriching fruity, fatty, and cheesy notes through transporter and nucleotide pathways. The authors offer the mechanism as guidance for process design.
pmc-13313179:
Yu-Nan Man and Mao-Lin He review what is known about SEC61G in a 2026 paper. SEC61G is a small part of the Sec61 channel that moves new proteins into the cell. Once seen as a mere extra copy made beside the EGFR gene, it now looks like a driver of growth in many kinds of cancer.

The review sorts its cancer roles into three groups. One is control of immune checkpoints. Another is faulty calcium signals. The third covers paths that do not use the channel at all. It maps where SEC61G runs high across cancers and which tumors depend on it most, with cervical cancer standing out on both counts. The authors weigh drugs that block the channel pore against newer plans such as degraders. They back SEC61G as a marker for outlook and for response to immune therapy.
pmc-13313279:
Kai Wang and colleagues pin a small RNA as a driver of prostate cancer in a 2026 report. The RNA, miR-6833-3p, was the focus of a search for the paths that let this cancer grow and keep stem-like traits.

In cancer cell lines, miR-6833-3p and NOTCH1 ran high while NUMB ran low, the opposite of healthy patterns. Reporter tests proved the small RNA binds and lowers NUMB directly. Adding copies of the RNA sped cell growth, movement, and stem-like traits and cut cell death, while extra NUMB reversed those effects. In mice, the RNA sped tumor growth and kept NUMB and NOTCH signaling down. The chain from a tiny RNA to a known growth path gives drug hunters a fresh point of attack in prostate cancer.
pmc-13314779:
Mila Pešić and colleagues study alfalfa root microbes on metal-tainted soil in work published in 2026. The root zone teems with microbes that can ease plant stress under heavy metal load, and the rhizobium Ensifer meliloti feeds alfalfa nitrogen while it lives in its roots.

The team asked whether adding rhizobia changes alfalfa growth and root microbe life in soils rich in nickel, over 2 years and across seasons. Two sites with lower and higher metal loads, mainly nickel with lead and chromium too, hosted six rhizobial inoculants, sampled at three times, as the design states. Counts of key microbe groups and plant growth were tracked. The answer can guide using partner bacteria to farm safely on polluted land.
pmc-13315679:
Jun Matsuda and colleagues describe in 2026 a hard stent-graft delivery through a very twisted liver artery. A man in his 70s had aneurysms of the proper hepatic, right gastric, and right gastroepiploic arteries, and severe lung emphysema ruled out open surgery under general anesthesia.

The plan was coil blocking of the two smaller aneurysms and a stent-graft for the main liver artery bulge, which at 20 millimeters or more needs treatment to prevent rupture. Twisting was extreme, with an index of 1.67, so the team used balloon anchoring, an inner dilator, and partial unsheathing to cross the bends while keeping liver blood flow.
pmc-13315879:
Shibo Zhao and co-authors developed in 2026 a low-carbon road base from industrial leftovers, steel slag, ground slag, and coal gangue, activated with sodium silicate. Mix shares were tuned with a uniform design method, then strength, durability, and inner structure were checked in depth.

The best blend held 52.6 percent coal gangue, 36.8 percent steel slag, 6.3 percent ground slag, and 4.3 percent activator. Microscopy and spectra showed gels forming a dense three-dimensional network as the silicate frame broke down and rebuilt. Seven-day strength reached 6.52 megapascals, meeting high-grade highway needs, and five freeze-thaw rounds kept over 85 percent strength.
pmc-13316079:
Yoshinori Ikehata, Naotaka Nishiyama, and Hiroshi Kitamura report in 2026 a rare urinary tract malformation in a baby girl, combining several faults at once. A two-month-old with congenital kidney swelling proved to have a horseshoe kidney plus a doubled collecting system on the right side.

Dye studies showed a narrowed right ureter and fusion between the lower pelvis parts of the two kidneys, with blockage where pelvis meets ureter. Repeated urinary infections led to surgery at fourteen months, a pyeloplasty plus a new bladder connection for the ureter. No major complications followed, and the swelling eased over about a year.
pmc-13316179:
Yuri Amemiya and Hiroshi Nishiura write a letter in 2026 estimating how Andes virus spread numbers vary by social setting. The South American hantavirus usually comes from rodents, but unlike its relatives it can pass between people. A cruise ship outbreak sailing from Argentina in April 2026 sharpened the need to understand that spread.

Overall reproduction was low, with a basic number of 0.24 in the cited work, yet secondary spread varied greatly and included superspreading. The authors gathered documented human transmission chains from eight studies and one World Health Organization report spanning 1993 to 2026, from Chile, Argentina, and the ship.
pmc-13316279:
Ramya Kumar and a large team characterize in 2026 the Vibrio strain behind translucent post-larvae disease in Pacific white shrimp, a major farmed species. Disease outbreaks keep battering shrimp farming, and this newer syndrome kills young shrimp in hatcheries, so the team isolated strain P40.49 from infected animals.

Experimental infection confirmed the strain causes the disease. Whole genome sequencing found a plasmid of about 69 thousand bases tied to the syndrome, and stomach and intestine tissue proved best for early detection at six hours after infection. Four unique genes on the plasmid may serve as added detection markers.
pmc-13316979:
Haydee Pacheco and co-authors show, in a 2026 materials study, how the same brominated organic molecule can glow bright blue or barely at all depending on how its crystals pack. Blue afterglow from metal-free organics is hard, since high-energy states usually leak away as heat.

Two crystal forms emerged: a head-to-tail pack and a face-to-face pack. The head-to-tail form reached a quantum yield of 38 percent in microcrystals. That dwarfed the face-to-face form's 2 percent in the same test, with glow lasting about 325 microseconds after the light cut off. Bromine's heavy atom pull plus snug halide contacts unlocked the effect. Packing control, they argue, is a design tool for afterglow materials.
pmc-13317679:
Serena Sirigu and colleagues characterize, in a 2026 structural study, a tail-spike protein from a marine virus that infects bacteria. The enzyme chews through the host's sugar coat so the virus can reach the cell wall. Such enzymes help viruses breach the slime that shields many bacteria.

The protein, named Dpo31, degrades its host's exopolysaccharide. Its folded shape matches other tail-spike enzymes closely, even though its letter sequence looks unrelated, a case of same architecture from different ancestry. Detailing its chemistry and structure adds a marine example to a class mostly studied in viruses of disease germs. The work may guide enzyme hunting for tools that strip bacterial biofilms.
pmc-13317779:
Benjamin Lai and co-authors surveyed, in a 2026 repeated study, clinicians at a national opioid conference from 2022 to 2024. They asked how ready clinicians feel to use the CDC's revised 2022 prescribing guidelines. The update stressed personal care and shared decisions after the 2016 rules caused unintended harm.

Across three years, 72.3 percent of attendees answered. Rural and city clinicians matched in familiarity and felt skill, and years of experience did not split results. Academic staff more often reported in-house rules for acute prescribing, and those rating their own skill high, especially in academia, were likelier to see guideline use as expert work. The authors spot teaching gaps for non-academic settings and call for plainer, practical guidance.
pmc-13318779:
Yazhao Sun and colleagues report a 2026 retrospective study of a combined cholesterol and inflammation index. The index joins remnant cholesterol with high-sensitivity C-reactive protein. They test whether it predicts major cardiovascular events after angina patients receive a stent procedure. Follow-up lasted a median of 36 months.

The sample held 2,171 patients, with a mean age of 65.32 years in the cohort. Events occurred in 363 patients, or 16.7 percent of those followed. The highest third of the index carried a hazard ratio of 4.42 against the lowest third after full adjustment. The middle third also ran higher, at 2.87 in the same model. Links held across age, sex, smoking, diabetes, and blood pressure subgroups. The authors propose the index as a risk biomarker.
pmc-13318879:
Konstantin Semash and colleagues give a 2026 case report of recovery after liver transplant in a teenager with Wilson disease. This inherited copper disorder had damaged her brain severely over five years. At fifteen she could not move or speak, with contractures, drooling, swallowing trouble, and liver failure. Many centres would judge transplant too risky.

Her severity score, the UWDRS, stood at 162 on arrival. Transplant was done as a life-saving step. Complications included aspiration pneumonia and a long period of tube feeding. Steady rehabilitation ran from intensive care through outpatient visits. One year later her score had improved to 59 overall. Speech returned, thinking normalised, and she walked with support and returned to school.
pmc-13318979:
Shao Zhengwei leads a large team presenting a 2026 study of auxin signalling genes and watermelon sweetness. Two gene families, ARF and Aux/IAA, steer plant development. Their role in fruit sugar and acid balance was largely unexplored in cucurbit crops. The team combined genomics, metabolite profiling, and gene activity data.

Across eight cucurbit species they found 157 ARF and 275 Aux/IAA genes, mostly under strong stabilising selection. Comparing wild and cultivated watermelons showed sugars rose in stages during domestication. Four candidate genes shifted sharply during the first sugar-building step and stayed fixed later. Spraying auxin raised glucose and fructose by 23 to 35 percent in fruit tests. It also cut malate by 18 percent in the same work.
pmc-13319379:
Xiaorui Peng leads a large team that built a joint sound and light scanner for sore finger joints in a 2026 report. Swollen joints from joint inflammation are hard to score by hand in a fair, repeatable way. Their bedside system uses a robot arm to scan each joint on its own, then smart software marks tissues and counts signs of disease.

Tests covered 43 finger joints from people with joint inflammation, tracked over time. The software matched hand drawn marks well and gave six measures of blood flow, oxygen, and joint size. Blood flow from light based scans tracked most closely with how active patients rated their disease. Grouped measures may help track drug response.
pmc-13319479:
Juan Olvido Perea García leads a team study from 2026 on how eye color shapes where others think a gaze points. Human eyes show a pale ring around the dark center, unlike the dark ring in chimp eyes. One past claim held that the pale ring helps people share gaze, most of all when viewing is hard.

Volunteers judged gaze from a live person wearing lenses that mimicked each eye type, under varied light and distance. Dark ring eyes did best in dim light and at close range, while pale ring eyes did best in bright light from far away. No type won overall. Each eye form may suit the light and range its species uses most.
pmc-13320279:
Zhuhui Tian and co-authors blend a mineral rich germ culture with peanut sprouts to lift yogurt flavor in a 2026 food study. Plain yogurt tastes mostly milky and sour and lacks some health linked compounds buyers now seek. A selenium fed ferment germ plus sprout mix was brewed and set next to sprout only yogurt for taste, texture, and scent checks.

The blend reached high live germ counts, firm set, and strong water hold in the measures reported. Tool noses and tongues scored it richer and fuller with less bitter bite than sprout only batches. Scent scans found fresh grass and fruit notes from the sprouts, while the culture added fruity esters and cut off notes. Deep chemical scans tied the gains to core energy and protein paths.
pmc-13320379:
Débora Pedroza Guedes da Silva and co-authors set out a trial plan in a 2026 protocol on fitness build up before lung cancer surgery. Cutting out part of a lung is the best cure path for early lung cancer, yet lung hassles after surgery are common and stays can stretch long. Short build up plans before surgery have cut those hassles in past trials, but which training type wins is still open.

Two hundred patients set for lung removal will be split by lot into four equal arms of fifty. The arms cover in breath training, out breath training, full body training, and a lone teaching session as control. All arms get one face to face lesson plus a habit leaflet. Checks run at entry, after the two week plan, and a month after going home.
pmc-13323579:
Yuan Fei and co-authors build machine learning models to predict complications of high blood pressure, in a 2026 UK Biobank longitudinal study of 502,166 participants. Protein profiling used the Olink Explore platform, and clinical variables plus outcomes came from electronic health records.

During follow-up, heart, brain and kidney complications developed in 1,232, 166 and 549 participants in their counts. Joint clinical and protein models reached fair to good discrimination, strongest for brain complications. Single proteins stood out for each organ outcome, led by growth differentiation factor 15 for heart events. Interpretation tools explained which inputs drove predictions. The authors present the models as an early warning route for targeted follow-up.
pmc-13324279:
Haitham Salem Baibers and Mohammad Nayef Ayasrah build a scale for teachers' forward-looking readiness to work with AI, in a 2026 study of secondary teachers in Jordan. Items grew from literature and interviews with 22 teachers, then passed expert review and cognitive testing before field use.

An online survey of 640 teachers split into two halves for exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis. Five factors held, covering foresight planning, adaptive instruction control, algorithmic anticipation, human-AI synergy and long-term reflective practice, across 45 items. Reliability and repeat stability rated high in their checks, and validity tests supported the structure. The authors offer the scale as a context-fitted tool for planning teacher development in AI-rich schools.
pmc-13325379:
Priya Pal and co-authors compare raw orange peel powder with two chars made from it for removing crystal violet dye in a 2026 study. Fruit waste could serve water treatment if it binds dye well.

Peel powder hit a top uptake of 49.35 mg per g, far above the muffle furnace char at 19.05 and the nitrogen char at 12.87 mg per g. Rich surface groups on the raw peel explain the lead. The chars traded capacity for wider pH tolerance and steadier behavior. All three followed monolayer binding with chemistry-led speed. Peel uptake released heat and ran on its own at room temperature, while the chars preferred warmth.
pmc-13328279:
Wenwen Liu and co-authors create new membrane-attacking antibacterials in a 2026 study. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus shrugs off many standard drugs, so the team built a family of phthalazine-based quaternary ammonium salts, compounds 2a through 2v, whose chain length could be tuned. Lab tests weighed killing power, safety, and how the best compound works.

Compound 2n led the family, stopping S. aureus, its resistant form, and two other species at 2 μg/mL in the minimum inhibitory tests reported, while sparing red blood cells up to far higher levels. It killed fast, resisted breakdown, and slowed biofilms, and probes showed torn membranes leaking cell contents, with DNA binding as a possible second hit.
pmc-13329979:
Alison Carroll and colleagues show light-driven storage of hydrogen in propane in a 2026 study. Storing hydrogen in chemical bonds avoids high pressure tanks. Propane is cheap and widely available, so the team tested turning propylene into propane at room temperature and pressure with a light-powered catalyst.

The catalyst pairs aluminium light catchers with titanium oxide and single platinum atoms. Light at 450 and 800 nm both drove strong propane output in the reported tests. Theory showed that light-made carriers at either colour hold enough energy for both reaction steps, splitting hydrogen and adding it across the carbon bond. Paired with earlier light-driven release, the cycle could store and free hydrogen under mild conditions.
pmc-13330479:
Pengyu Zhao and Shuai Geng pool studies on pharmacist care in China amid a shift from dispensing to patient care in a 2026 meta-analysis. Searches ran across eight databases to April 2026 for trials and comparison studies of pharmacist work such as prescription review and counselling. Bias was checked with standard tools.

In total, 32 studies entered the pool, with only 5 randomised trials among them. Pharmacist input linked to more single-drug antibiotic use and more sound prescriptions, and to fewer irrational prescriptions in the reported odds values. Spread between studies was wide, which limits exactness. The authors call the gains promising but early, and urge strong trials with patient-centred outcomes.
pmc-13330579:
Yi Zhang and colleagues trace the family history of STAYGREEN genes in tobacco plants in a 2026 study. Those genes steer chlorophyll breakdown, which drives leaf yellowing, maturity, and crop quality. The team compared gene copies across flowering plants, with focus on Nicotiana, whose doubled genome history may have expanded the family.

Family trees placed tobacco copies inside a conserved flowering plant lineage, with extra copies matching the doubled genome past in the reported analysis. Gene activity differed across tissues. Core catalytic parts stayed tightly conserved, while end regions varied by lineage. Most copies kept signals that send the protein to chloroplasts, though strength varied. The work frames how leaf ageing stays stable yet flexible.
pmc-13333279:
Jean Pierre Díaz-Paz and co-authors present a labeled dataset in 2026 for cleaning speckle noise from Sentinel-1 radar images. Radar pictures are grainy by nature, and training smart filters requires matched noisy and clean examples, which are hard to build honestly.

The dataset holds 512 by 512 pixel radar tiles in both VV and VH polarizations, gathered worldwide through an automated Python and Google Earth Engine workflow with random sampling and quality filtering. For each spot, cleaner reference images were made by averaging stacks of 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 passes, letting users study how averaging depth affects speckle removal. Land cover maps from ESA WorldCover v200 and a metadata file ride along, and benchmark scores including ENL, MSE, SSIM, and PSNR are supplied for sample tiles. The set is hosted on Mendeley Data as a reproducible training resource.
pmc-13333679:
Thomas Buttgereit and a large international team report on the first two years of the Chronic Angioedema Registry, known as CARE. Launched in October 2023, the registry gathers clinical and patient-reported data on recurrent angioedema of any type during routine care.

By December 2025, 550 patients had enrolled at 23 centers spread across 18 countries, meeting its early milestones on time. Hereditary angioedema and mast cell related forms were among the diagnoses tracked. A survey of physicians in the specialist center network explored why centers join or hold back, and how communication could improve. The report shows a global registry for a rare swelling condition can grow steadily, while naming practical barriers that slow wider participation.
pmc-13333779:
Jin Han and co-authors looked at ligustilide, a natural compound from Angelica sinensis and Ligusticum chuanxiong, for central nervous system disorders in a 2026 article. Ligustilide draws interest for calming inflammation, fighting oxidation, and protecting nerves.

Three sources were searched for studies through October 2025, and 55 original studies were left after screening. Evidence links the compound to help in ischemic stroke, vascular dementia, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, traumatic brain injury, and anxiety disorders. Its effects run through pathways including PI3K/Akt, MAPK, NF-kB, and Nrf2/ARE, lowering oxidative stress, inflammation, cell death, and mitochondrial failure. The review also covers how the body absorbs and clears ligustilide and what safety data exist, sketching what stands between the compound and clinical use.
pmc-13334079:
Jeong-Ah Yoon and co-authors tested a candidate probiotic strain, Pediococcus acidilactici MBEL10321, in a 2026 study pairing lab tests with genome sequencing. The strain came from Nuruk, a classic Korean fermentation starter.

In culture the strain survived acid and bile salts well and held back several pathogens, beating two control strains, among them Listeria monocytogenes, Bacillus cereus, Escherichia coli O157:H7, and Staphylococcus aureus. It showed no blood-cell-breaking activity. Its genome spans 2,044,106 base pairs with 1,980 protein-coding genes, and screens found no virulence factors, no drug resistance genes, and no transferable plasmid replicons. The paired safety and function evidence backs the strain as a probiotic candidate for food or supplement use.
pmc-13334979:
Chenhui He and co-authors built an ultrasound-driven sticky hydrogel for infected wounds in a 2026 materials study. Long-term infected wounds resist treatment because bacteria persist, tissue states vary, and antibiotics lose ground.

Their hydrogel, PA-ZA, embeds tiny composites of ZIF-8 studded with nitrogen-doped graphene quantum dots in a polyacrylamide-alginate base. Set ultrasound, first at kilohertz then megahertz speeds, triggers tissue sticking, pushes nanoparticles through skin, and switches on sound-driven production of reactive oxygen species that kill bacteria. The gel proved body-safe and sped cell migration and blood vessel growth in vitro. In infected full-thickness wounds in animals, switching it on lowered bacterial burden, sped the end of inflammation, and hastened repair, with similar benefit in a deeper infection model.
pmc-13335479:
Patricia C Hernandez and co-authors showed how small molecules selectively block the DNA-chewing enzyme TREX1 in a 2026 structural biology study. TREX1 clears stray cytoplasmic DNA; losing it causes autoimmune disease, while blocking it in cancer cells can wake anti-tumor immunity.

X-ray crystallography revealed the inhibitors sitting in the active site, competing with the end of the DNA substrate and hydrogen-bonding to a conserved glutamate. Binding also locks a tyrosine, Tyr129, into an alternative pose that cannot grip DNA and opens a deep hydrophobic pocket that cradles part of the drug. That pocket explains why the compounds spare the close relative TREX2 and viral cousins. The structures give medicinal chemists a blueprint for selective TREX1 blockers.
pmc-13336379:
Jianya Luo and co-authors found a compound that resensitizes a dangerous hospital pathogen to an old antibiotic in a 2026 microbiology study. Acinetobacter baumannii shrugs off most drugs, and colistin, a last-resort option, is losing ground too.

A structure-based virtual screen against the bacterium's lipopolysaccharide transport system produced a somatostatin-like peptide, C4. Alone it barely kills, but with colistin the synergy is strong. Lipid and gene analyses showed C4 remodels the membrane, selectively building up phosphatidylglycerol and raising expression of mlaC, a phospholipid transport gene. Deleting mlaC erased both the lipid change and the synergy, while extra copies strengthened it. The work reveals membrane lipid management as a lever for rescuing colistin therapy.
pmc-13336779:
Zhaoqiang Jiang and a large team connect night shift work to higher blood pressure in a 2026 study of people and mice. Shift work scrambles the body clock, and the authors point to failing mitochondria, the cell's power units, as the main link. Mice on simulated night shifts developed higher pressure and disturbed clock genes such as PER1 and BMAL1.

The shifted mice also showed power-unit damage and oxidative stress. Human night workers showed the same pattern: longer shift exposure tracked with higher systolic and diastolic pressure and with disturbed clock and mitochondrial markers. The shared pathway helps explain the heart risks of night work and may guide ways to blunt them.
pmc-13336979:
Yiming Fu and colleagues study why windows for imaging the living mouse brain cloud over in a 2026 methods review and study. Thinned skull and clearing methods let multiphoton microscopes watch brain cells over time, yet image quality fades fast. Systematic tests with adaptive optics compared window types for lifespan, sharpness, and distortion.

Progressive skull regrowth emerged as the core limit across all types, steadily blurring signal and resolution. A local glucocorticoid delivery method stretched good performance to one month. Sealing the window with a drug-loaded hydrogel suppressed regrowth while keeping optics clear. The findings give labs a practical route to month-long, high-fidelity brain imaging and explain what ends it.
pmc-13339779:
Chia-Heng Lin and colleagues compare victim choices among sexual offenders with and without severe mental illness in a 2026 forensic study. Court-referred evaluations in Taiwan from 2009 to 2022 supplied the records. Understanding pattern differences may sharpen risk assessment.

Among 86 men, 21 had psychotic or bipolar disorders and 65 did not as reported. Offenders with severe illness more often had adult and stranger victims in the reported comparisons, with odds near fourfold for each in adjusted models. Substance disorders were more common without severe illness. Small subgroup size urges caution, but distinct patterns suggest assessment should weigh diagnosis alongside victim history.
pmc-13341179:
How nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor blockers protect the kidney from inside is reviewed by Eun Sil Koh and colleagues in 2026. Drugs such as finerenone cut albuminuria and improve outcomes in chronic kidney disease, but the exact vessel-level mechanics remain partly unclear.

The review gathers clinical and lab evidence on sodium handling and pressure inside the glomerulus. These drugs mildly increase sodium excretion, ease aldosterone-driven tightening of outgoing vessels, and restore feedback signals that guard against overfiltration. Whether they beat older steroidal blockers at fixing hyperfiltration is unproven. Their edge may instead be safety and tolerability that let patients stay on treatment.
pmc-13341479:
A gene that pushes colon cancer cells toward iron-driven death is studied by Haiying Sun and co-investigators in a 2026 analysis. RBMS3 had unclear significance, so the team mined pan-cancer and colon adenocarcinoma datasets, then validated findings in lab cultures.

Tumors expressed less RBMS3 than normal tissue, and low levels meant worse survival, supporting a tumor-suppressor role. Expression tracked with tumor stage, and adding it to staging improved a prognostic nomogram. Cell work showed M2 macrophages suppress RBMS3 through STAT3 signaling, weakening ferroptosis. The pathway names both a biomarker and a possible lever for treatment.
pmc-13346079:
Joyce Jebet and co-authors systematically review tools for screening mothers' mental health across Africa in 2026. Pregnancy and new motherhood carry heavy mental burdens that clinics rarely test for. The team gathered African studies from 2014 to 2024 to see which questionnaires actually get used and how they perform.

The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale dominated the shelf, with the PHQ-9 common in Ethiopia and the SRQ-20 favored in West Africa. Studies clustered in South Africa, Ethiopia, and Nigeria, with samples from 37 to 3,311 women. Disorders stay common yet under-detected, and the authors push for screening folded into routine mother-and-child visits, better staff training, and tools fitted to local culture.
pmc-13347079:
Juan Huang and colleagues test whether walking patterns can flag thinking decline in Parkinson disease, in a diagnostic study published in 2026. Patients classed as normal, subjectively declining, or mildly impaired did timed up-and-go walks, both plain and with a second task. While a wearable system recorded 209 motion measures for each trial.

Extra measures captured how much the added mental task cost each walker. Several learning models were trained to sort the three groups, checked with cross-validation and a held-out set. Importance tools were used to show which gait features drove each call. The aim is a low-burden clinic test that spots early decline without long paper testing.
pmc-13347379:
Aarti Gupta and colleagues characterise a doped bismuth ferrite powder for cleaning toxic chromium from water with sunlight, in a study published in 2026. Praseodymium and cobalt were added into the crystal without forming second phases, shrinking grain size. A combined heat-based instrument read thermal flow, energy gap, and charge lifetime in one pass.

Moderate doping improved heat flow and charge separation, while heavy doping added trap sites that sped charge loss and slowed heat spread in the reported measures. Under plain sunlight the best powder cut the harmful chromium form by about 96 percent within 120 minutes, turning it toward a safer form. Linked structure and heat data guide tuning of such cleaners.
pmc-13349779:
Chao Gong and colleagues reported a cohort study in 2026 on whether HDL cholesterol levels predict outcomes in non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy. They followed 297 patients who had cardiac magnetic resonance scans between 2017 and 2024.

Over a median 35 months of follow-up, 41 patients reached the main endpoint of death or heart transplant, and 97 reached a wider endpoint adding heart failure readmission. Lower HDL cholesterol was linked to higher risk in adjusted models, and patients with higher levels stayed event-free longer. Adjusting for estimated pulmonary artery pressure weakened the link somewhat. The authors propose HDL cholesterol as a cheap, routine marker for sorting risk in these patients.
pmc-13349979:
Jiahuan Tang and colleagues fine-tuned a multimodal GPT-4o model in 2026 to write diagnostic impressions for a tricky breast MRI finding. The finding is called non-mass enhancement. Earlier work showed public language models handled breast lesion grading poorly. This lesion type had never been singled out.

Records from 229 patients supplied scan images, reports, and clinical histories. Six model versions were built. Some were untuned. Others trained on text alone, or on images plus text. Their impressions were compared with three radiologists of differing experience. Other experts then graded the outputs. The study tests whether targeted training lifts AI reporting to a clinically useful level.
pmc-13350179:
Jiale Huang and colleagues used combined gene and chemistry profiling in 2026 to explain why blueberries fail after years in the same soil in Dalian, China. Soil was sampled around roots and away from them after zero, two, four, and six years of continuous cropping.

Microbial diversity fell steadily with cropping years, especially near roots, and communities separated clearly by period. Helpful microbe groups thinned while stress-tolerant ones grew, and soil chemistry showed accumulating compounds harmful to the plants themselves. The picture blames a sickened soil community plus self-poisoning as twin drivers of the decline, pointing growers toward soil restoration rather than more fertiliser.
pmc-13350379:
Chun-Ka Wong and a multicentre team reported Asia-Pacific experience in 2026 with cutting heart valve leaflets during catheter valve replacement to stop the new valve blocking a coronary artery. The registry covered consecutive patients at seven centres from 2019 to 2026 treated with two techniques, one slicing the leaflet and one burning through it with a radiofrequency needle.

Success meant completing the cut and implant with no coronary blockage, emergency surgery, stroke, or death. Most published proof comes from North America and Europe. Real-world results from this region tell local teams whether the demanding trick works in their own patients and systems.
pmc-13350479:
Ningbo Yin and colleagues pooled ultrasound strain measurements of the heart's right side in a 2026 meta-analysis, aiming to set normal values. Speckle tracking follows tiny heart muscle patterns to measure how the right atrium and ventricle deform, but healthy ranges were never standardised.

Studies of healthy adults published up to July 2025 were gathered from three databases. Pooled values covered ventricle strain and strain rates plus three phases of atrial strain, and subgroup checks probed race, sex, age, and the software and machine used. Reference numbers that account for equipment differences let clinicians tell true right-heart weakness from measurement noise.
pmc-13350679:
Yuhan Fan and co-authors used deep learning in 2026 to regenerate radiotherapy positioning images that clinics normally throw away. Cone-beam projections for head and neck cancer patients are bulky, so they are discarded after building the three-dimensional scan, yet later checks may need them.

Working from 50 patients, they first computed synthetic X-ray views from the stored scans, then trained networks to convert those into realistic projections. Three network designs were compared, with tests on scatter correction, scan sharpness, and training size. Regenerating discarded images from kept data could rescue old treatment records for review and research.
pmc-13351679:
Chenjia Jiang and co-authors present a 2026 case report on emergency non-heart surgery in a child with Eisenmenger syndrome. The condition marks late, untreated congenital heart disease with fixed high lung pressure, reversed blood flow, and low oxygen. An 11-year-old girl needed urgent surgery under general anaesthesia for a twisted right ovary.

Her lung artery pressure was 105/49 mmHg, and anaesthesia used etomidate, midazolam, vecuronium, and sufentanil, then propofol, remifentanil, and sevoflurane. Readings stayed stable during surgery, but a lung pressure crisis followed with fast heart rhythm, low blood pressure, and low oxygen. Amiodarone, treprostinil, bicarbonate, and oxygen restored normal rhythm, and she went home on day 11.
pmc-13351879:
Sen Lin and colleagues report a 2026 surgical technique for easing pressure on nerves at two neighbouring lower back levels through a single small cut. Endoscopic decompression is a key low-impact option for narrowed spinal canals. Reaching two levels often needs several cuts, so the team set out to do both through one opening.

Working over the top to the far side, they trimmed bone and removed thickened ligament at the L3-4 and L4-5 levels. Surgery took 115 minutes through a 0.7-cm cut with six brief X-ray checks. Pain scores fell from 8 to 0 by follow-up at 2 and 6 months, and the patient walked within 24 hours. The case shows the one-cut route is workable.
pmc-13352479:
Feiyang Liu leads a 2026 project building a scale for the healthy mental effects of exercise in Chinese college students. Existing tools capture only general or narrow mental outcomes after exercise. Scale items were drafted from theory, prior work, interviews, and open surveys, then tested in staged samples.

An early sample of 612 students shaped the item set, and a formal sample of 945 students checked reliability and validity. The final scale holds 55 items in five parts: emotional feelings, self-cognition, frustration coping, control and social efficacy, and social interaction. Variance explained per part ranged from 62.546 to 73.711 percent. A retest group of 597 students after 1 month supported stability over time.
pmc-13353379:
Xiaoyu Ma leads a 2026 review of oxidative enzymes that break down plant biomass. Plant walls are mostly lignocellulose, a tough mix that resists biological dismantling. The review maps how microbes, mainly filamentous fungi, attack with redox enzymes, including newly found AA families.

Laccases and lignin-active peroxidases lead lignin attack, while lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases and their redox partners cut sugar chains. Hydrogen peroxide acts as a shared middleman whose supply and use are tightly timed and placed. Non-enzyme radical systems join the synergy. Structural computing sharpens the picture, and the authors argue the knowledge can speed next-generation biorefineries for a circular bioeconomy.
pmc-13355279:
Mohamad Abou Chakra and co-authors studied in 2026 whether age changes how well two bladder treatments work for high-risk bladder cancer that has not reached the muscle. One treatment uses a weakened germ, BCG, placed in the bladder, and the other uses two chemotherapy drugs in sequence. Records covered 401 patients treated from 2011 to 2024.

Age, split into bands from under 60 to 80 and over, did not clearly predict cancer return in either group. Older patients on BCG showed a mild trend toward more returns, while older patients on the drug pair held steady over time. The authors say the trend in the BCG group deserves more study.
pmc-13355779:
Romana Erblich and co-authors studied in 2026 when traumatic cardiac arrest happens outside hospital and how timing shapes survival. Using records from thirteen helicopter rescue services from 2010 to 2019, they split cases by when the heart stopped: before crews arrived, after arrival at the scene, or during transport.

Nine of ten arrests had already occurred at the scene before the first unit arrived. Survival was highest when arrest came after crews arrived or during helicopter transport. Still, lasting return of circulation was possible even in early arrests, above all when the first heart rhythm was not flat. The authors say resuscitation in such cases is worthwhile.
pmc-13355879:
Abdul Nadim Asil and co-authors review in 2026 how studies define and use two key terms for personal response to ionizing radiation. Radiosensitivity and radiosusceptibility are often mixed up, though they point to distinct ideas: cell-level damage response versus risk of tissue harm and cancer. The team searched two databases and screened studies under standard review rules.

Radiosensitivity was mostly measured by DNA damage and repair tests, while susceptibility tied to normal tissue harm and cancer risk, and was named far less often. Personal response varied widely in all studies. The authors call for clearer definitions and shared methods to support personal radiotherapy and fair risk judgments.
pmc-13357079:
Wei Shi and co-authors mapped in 2026 how mitophagy, the cleanup of worn-out mitochondria, shapes the tumor surroundings in osteosarcoma, an aggressive bone cancer of teens. Single-cell gene data let them group the many cell types by their cleanup activity. They then traced cell-to-cell signals, gene networks, and links to patient survival.

Cleanup-active support cells sent strong blood-vessel growth signals, and cleanup-linked killer T cells looked worn out and less able to fight. Tumors rich in these cell types meant poorer survival, and the patterns also hinted at response to immune therapy. The authors suggest blocking, not boosting, this cleanup could aid treatment.
pmc-13358579:
Qinling Jiang and co-authors test a clever scan trick in a 2026 study on lung adenocarcinoma. Doctors now grade this cancer under a newer system that sorts patients by outlook more sharply. The team asked whether computer analysis of CT scans could predict the grade before surgery, using artificial images sharpened by a generative network.

They compared models built on these enhanced images with models built on normal scans, using patients from two Chinese hospitals. The sharper images were meant to reveal fine tumor texture that plain scans blur. If scan-based grading proves reliable, it could help surgeons plan the size of the operation before the first cut.
pmc-13359879:
Xukai Yang and co-authors measure three key elements across mountain forests in a 2026 study. On the southern slopes of China's Qilian Mountains, forests anchor regional ecology and nutrient cycling. The team compared carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus in leaves, branches, and forest floor material for six common tree species.

Broad-leaved species generally held richer nutrient levels, while conifers stored more carbon per unit of nitrogen or phosphorus. As plant material became forest floor litter, nitrogen and phosphorus fell and the carbon ratios rose, signs that trees pull nutrients back before shedding leaves and that litter quality differs by species. The patterns guide how managers read nutrient health in these forests.
pmc-13361979:
Yoshihito Saijo and co-authors report a 2026 case of heart infection with a puzzling twist. A 24-year-old man with eczema came in with fever and painful skin spots on his hands and feet. Blood tests grew Staphylococcus aureus, and scans found a large, mobile growth on his tricuspid valve, which had torn and leaked badly. Right-sided heart infections usually send infected clots to the lungs, not the body.

His body-wide spots suggested infected material was reaching the left side of the heart. A bubble test showed blood crossing from right to left only after a straining maneuver, and none at rest. No fixed hole between the heart chambers explained it. The team traced the route to a temporary shunt within the lungs, a rare path that let the infection spread system-wide.
pmc-13362079:
Blanca T M Spee and co-authors tested whether Parkinson's disease changes how people judge art in a 2026 study. Parkinson's is now seen as a whole-body disorder touching perception, emotion, and reward. Art programs for patients usually focus on making art, not on viewing it. The team asked whether looking at art, and rating it, works differently in these patients.

Eighty-seven people with Parkinson's and 49 matched healthy controls rated 36 artworks online. They scored liking and beauty and reported emotional and color-linked responses. The study's verdict, reflected in its title, is that aesthetic judgment is largely preserved in Parkinson's. That finding suggests art-viewing programs need little content adaptation for these audiences, a hopeful note for museums and therapists planning inclusive sessions.
pmc-13362179:
Qiang Gao and co-authors used machine learning to predict long breathing support after heart surgery in preterm babies in a 2026 study. The surgery closes a ductus, a blood vessel that should shut after birth but stays open in many early babies. Some babies then need a breathing machine for a long time. The team reviewed 271 infants born at 32 weeks or less, treated from 2021 to 2025.

Babies were split at six days of support: 150 came off sooner and 121 needed longer. Birth weight, age at birth, weight at surgery, duct size, and breathing severity all differed between the groups. A method called SHAP showed which factors pushed each prediction. Flagging high-risk babies early can help teams plan care and counsel parents.
pmc-13362479:
Jan den Boer and co-authors describe a 2026 study of a playful device meant to cut food waste in school canteens. Two primary schools and one kindergarten took part. The device lets children vote with balls after lunch, and the emptier a child's returned plate, the more their vote weighs, which nudges pupils to take only what they will eat.

Plate waste fell at all three sites while the device ran, for both soup and main dishes. Children ate a larger share of what they were served. The authors note that kitchens also cooked less food during the trial, which blurs the exact effect, so they advise holding meal output steady in future tests of the idea.
pmc-13364179:
Caitlin Wenske, Mahnoor Mukarram, and Carlos Gomez-Meade present a 2026 case report on a nonsurgical cure for a skin cancer on the nose of an 80-year-old man. His squamous cell carcinoma in situ, on the right nostril rim, had returned after past care. Kidney transplant drugs, lung disease on oxygen, and poor mobility made Mohs surgery and rebuilding risky. He chose image-guided superficial radiation, planned with high-resolution skin ultrasound.

Twenty sessions over six weeks delivered the full dose. Skin reactions peaked at a moderate grade, scans showed the tumor shrinking away, and six weeks after treatment no tumor could be found. The nostril kept its shape and airway. The authors commend the option for medically complex patients.
pmc-13364679:
Anna Fajardo and co-workers hunt in 2026 for genes that drive the spread of melanoma, a harsh skin cancer. They knock out suspect genes in live mice with a gene edit screen and watch which loss stops spread. One gene, Polr1a, stood out as a strong driver.

High ranks of the gene in patients track with more spread and short life. Blocking it cut cell move, lung spread, and tumor growth in tests. Its pull runs through a cell growth path that drug care can hit. The team sees Polr1a blocks as a pre surgery care path worth trials.
pmc-13364979:
Raquel Behar-Lagares and co-workers read blood fat maps in 2026 for folks with both HIV and liver C germ whose livers fail in steps. Once the liver slips to the worse stage, death risk climbs, even after the germ is cured. The team maps blood fats in 58 such patients.

Wildlife cases can warn of spread before farm outbreaks appear. The piece frames such viruses as a shared concern for farms, wildlife, and trade.
pmc-13415679:
Cyril Thouverey, Isabelle Badoud, and Patrick Ammann test whether strontium strengthens the bone building effect of parathyroid hormone treatment, in 2026 rat experiments. Female rats lost ovaries to mimic postmenopausal bone loss, then received strontium, intermittent PTH, both, or neither for eight weeks. Bone structure, density, and strength were measured in spongy and cortical bone.

PTH alone reversed much of the spongy bone decay. Strontium alone raised tissue level density without adding spongy mass. Combined treatment beat PTH alone on thickness, density, and strength measures in both bone types. Cell cultures matched, with stronger bone forming gene signals under the pair.
pmc-13415979:
Lanlan Wei, Ziyi Qin, Sichen Li, and Congsheng Yan spray blueberries with a living chemistry coating to slow decay, in 2026. Their film blends gelatin with a cellulose derivative and loads it with the cell free liquid left from lactic acid bacteria fermentation. Spraying suits small fruit better than dipping or brushing, which waste solvent and mark skins.

Film analysis showed the parts mixed compatibly, blocked more light, and let through more water vapor than the plain film. The full strength spray killed four test microbes, including E. coli and Listeria. Sprayed berries decayed less, lost less weight, and kept firmness statistically unchanged.
pmc-13417479:
Yuanyi Wang and co-authors review records of heavily pretreated metastatic breast cancer patients given vessel blocking therapy plus chemotherapy, in a 2026 multicentre study. Options run thin after many prior treatments. Records for 348 patients were matched into 174 pairs comparing combined treatment with chemotherapy alone.

Matched patients on combined treatment went a median 122 days without progression, versus 90 days on chemotherapy alone. Side effect rates were similar, and most events were mild or moderate. Results varied by which vessel blocking drug and chemotherapy base were used. Dose comparisons were descriptive only, the authors caution, and cannot prove lower doses work as well.
pmc-13418479:
Mathis Neuhaus and colleagues compare belly fat and under skin fat from patients with obesity, in a 2026 study. Paired samples came from 22 patients during weight loss surgery. Fat cell size, gene activity, glucose uptake, and fat release were measured in whole tissue and isolated cells to see how the two depots differ in expandability.

Under skin fat cells were larger and released fat faster at rest, with more flexible scaffolding proteins. Belly fat cells responded more strongly to stimulation for both fat release and glucose uptake. One skin fat gene tracked with insulin resistance across a public dataset. Depot specific biology may shape metabolic risk.
pmc-13418879:
Francesca Lessi and colleagues study tumor cells found in the blood of people with glioblastoma, the most aggressive common brain tumor. Such tumors almost never spread outside the skull, yet loose tumor cells show up in the blood again and again. That puzzle raises the hope of a blood test that tracks the disease without brain surgery.

The team examined blood-borne tumor cells from 27 patients, both in bulk groups and one cell at a time. The grouped cells shared many gene changes with the matched brain tumors. Single cells varied widely, and some carried no clear gene copy changes at all. The mix suggests that blood cells sample many parts of the tumor, a useful trait for watching the disease over time.
pmc-13419179:
Valério and colleagues present a 2026 computational study of lunar calendars across East Polynesia, including Rapa Nui, also called Easter Island. Communities kept lists of about thirty named moon nights. The team compared 48 such lists from every major island group, measuring how their words and structures differed, and built a family tree of the calendars.

The tree splits into two main branches. One joins the Marquesas with Mangareva and Rapa Nui; the other joins the Cook Islands, New Zealand, Hawai'i, Tahiti, the Tuamotu group, and the Austral Islands. That split matches a recent grouping of East Polynesian languages into Distal and Proximal branches. Since calendars and languages both pass down within communities, the match suggests the calendars divided early, mirroring the first voyages and language splits that settled the region.
pmc-13419879:
Baramett Somtha and colleagues profile the bacteria riding on dialysis catheters of patients with chronic kidney disease, using gene sequencing instead of culture alone. Kidney failure patients face high infection risk, and catheter lines raise the danger of deadly blood infection further. Slow or missed germ naming can leave treatment off target.

Sequencing of a ribosomal gene named the microbes present and ranked their shares in each sample. Known troublemakers appeared in the list, including Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, and Acinetobacter baumannii, among other named species. A full census of catheter life shows which germs to expect before culture results land. That foresight can shape first antibiotic choices and line-care practice in dialysis units.
pmc-13420479:
Kaushal Patel and colleagues report two patients with a stubborn bladder pain condition, marked by ulcers inside the bladder wall, who improved under an Ayurvedic oil treatment given through the urethra. Standard care for interstitial cystitis often brings only short relief and can scar the bladder over time. Both patients were tracked with pain scales and quality-of-life questionnaires for two years.

Each patient showed major clinical improvement, and quality-of-life scores pointed to near-complete settling of symptoms in the report. The gains held stable across the full two-year follow-up, an unusually long window for a case series. Two patients cannot prove a therapy, yet durable relief in a condition known for relapse earns attention. The authors present the method as a candidate for formal trials beside standard care.
pmc-13421079:
Le Gao and colleagues test whether a pre-trained model can guess where a person is looking during a film, using brain scan data alone. Eye tracking is often missing in older and shared scan sets, yet gaze shapes what the brain is doing during natural viewing. The model was applied cold, with no retraining, across three independent data sets.

Predicted gaze matched the true gaze modestly, with correlations between 0.24 and 0.37 across the sets in the reported range, and the brain maps it produced hugged the visual cortex. Age effects on the predictions wobbled between sets. The authors judge the cold model too weak for person-level claims without local training. The work still maps what can be salvaged from legacy scans that never recorded the eyes.
pmc-13421279:
Titherington and colleagues present a 2026 review of high-volume blood filtration for children in septic shock, a life-threatening infection state. The treatment runs blood through a filter at high flow to clear inflammatory signals, alongside standard kidney support. The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign gave it a conditional backing, despite low-certainty evidence. The review tests that stance against the data.

The targeted signals are small enough, in theory, for high-flow membranes to clear. But pediatric studies are small, single-center, and use mixed dose definitions, so their estimates are fragile. The largest observational data sets in children show no consistent benefit, and adult evidence is also weak.  The idea is sound, the proof is not, and routine use should wait for stronger trials.
pmc-13421379:
Lukas C Bal and six colleagues map, in a 2026 study, how the brain's outer layer rewires its gene activity during daily torpor in the Djungarian hamster. Torpor lets warm-blooded animals slash their metabolic rate for hours to survive harsh conditions, and the cortex's response had not been charted at single-cell resolution.

Sequencing RNA from individual cell nuclei in hamster cortex across seasons and metabolic states, the team found a division of labour. Non-neuronal cells adjusted mainly with the seasons, through clock genes, while neurons changed during torpor itself, favouring RNA breakdown programmes. The cortical pattern diverged from the hypothalamus during metabolic depression. The authors frame torpor as a coordinated, cell-type-specific programme rather than a uniform shutdown.
pmc-13422879:
Aylı and colleagues add up the environmental bill of dialysis in this 2026 national modeling study of Türkiye, where in-center hemodialysis keeps thousands alive at heavy resource cost.
