They combined international per-session parameters with measurements from two Turkish centers running 4,000 sessions a month, then scaled to the country's 9.27 million sessions in 2023.

The literature-based estimate lands at 4.57 million cubic meters of water a year, up to 181.8 gigawatt-hours of electricity, and greenhouse emissions between 45.3 and 171.1 thousand tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent annually. Turkish measurements came in kinder on water, about 390 liters per session against the international 493, a 21 percent saving, while electricity use sat mid-range. Electricity dominated emissions at up to 72 percent of the total, making grid decarbonization and waste segregation the biggest levers.
pmc-13423079:
Grace Van Winkle and six colleagues describe the CHAMP trial, a pragmatic randomised study at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. The trial compares two ways to monitor intravenous heparin, a widely used blood thinner whose effects vary sharply between patients. One protocol adjusts the dose by the aPTT clotting test; the other uses an anti-Xa assay. The two have never been tested head to head in a prospective trial.

Running inside the hospital's learning health system from June 2024, the trial randomises inpatients who need heparin infusions to one monitoring protocol or the other. Outcomes will show which approach keeps levels in range more reliably. The authors designed the study to answer a daily dosing question with ordinary ward data.
pmc-13423479:
Fan, Wei, and Yan introduce in 2026 a special issue on nanozymes, engineered nanomaterials that act like enzymes. After nearly two decades of growth, the field now stretches across chemistry, physics, biology, and medicine.

The issue gathers 40 papers from research groups worldwide. Themes include sharpening catalytic performance, sensing, environmental cleanup, and therapies that fight oxidation, infection, or immune imbalance. The editors highlight several directions. One is tuning the small molecules attached to carbon dot iron nanozymes to control two enzyme-like activities at once. Another is a cerium nanozyme built on renewable lignin that stayed stable when heated and broke up bacterial biofilms. A third is an iron framework grown directly on a 3D-printed metal support to make a reusable glucose sensor. Together, the collection shows design shifting from discovering activity to engineering it deliberately.
pmc-13425579:
Thyago de Moraes and coauthors compared peritoneal dialysis modalities in a 2026 analysis of the PDOPPS cohort covering 9,463 patients in six countries or regions. Automated dialysis dominates in many high-income settings and is spreading elsewhere, yet survival differences against continuous ambulatory dialysis remain unclear. Patients entered the analysis within three months of starting peritoneal dialysis.

Cox models with intent-to-treat handling examined survival, permanent transfer to hemodialysis, and time to first peritonitis, adjusting for patient and facility factors. Clinicians and policymakers gain large-scale comparative evidence for a modality choice often driven by habit and resources. The scale of the data set lets small gaps show up that a single site could not hope to spot on its own at all. The pool is vast, with men and women from six lands and all walks of life in the mix of those who took part.
pmc-13425779:
Bennet Rohan Fernando Devasahayam and coauthors used nanopore sequencing to study barley roots and their microbes together in a 2026 multi-omics project. Wild, landrace, and modern barley types host different rhizosphere communities, a legacy of domestication, yet two-way influence between root and microbe stayed unclear. Long-read metagenomics was combined with root gene expression and plant genome data across genotypes and seasons.

Microbe communities shifted with genotype, while core functions such as amino acid metabolism and energy production stayed shared. Genotype-dependent differences in carbohydrate handling point to breeding targets for crops that recruit helpful root microbes. Roots and germs trade food and cues both ways, so a change on one side soon shows up on the other side as well.
pmc-13425879:
Dan Ziegler and colleagues critically appraise two modern diabetes drug classes for diabetic neuropathy in a 2026 review. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors transformed type 2 diabetes care through heart and kidney benefits shown in outcome trials. Animal and early human work hints they might also ease nerve damage and neuropathic pain.

Human evidence so far rests on small, short phase II trials of mixed design and quality, without clear gains in clinical or nerve conduction outcomes. Real-world responses also vary widely, so the authors caution against assuming nerve protection from glucose or organ benefits alone.
pmc-13426379:
Lyra C. Ceblano, Benilda C. Sanchez-Gan, and Patricia C. Orduña studied caregiver burden and well-being at Philippine General Hospital in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Their participants were 95 primary caregivers of children with neurological conditions admitted to the pediatric neurology ward between December 2024 and January 2025, chosen by purposive sampling. Long hospital stays push caregiving demands well beyond ordinary parenting and can damage caregiver health.

Structured questionnaires gathered social, demographic, and clinical details alongside a modified caregiver burden measure and well-being ratings. Linking burden scores with well-being shows where hospital support for families should focus. Moms and dads who stay at the bed side for weeks feel strain in body, mood, and purse, and the poll takes all three in view.
pmc-13427079:
Zaman and colleagues built and field-tested in 2026 HerCare, a women's health chatbot. It answers from two sources at once, expert medical knowledge and peer stories, and shows the source of each answer. Health chatbots tend to be either dry and clinical or warm but unreliable. Showing where an answer comes from is meant to let users judge trust for themselves.

In a single-session online study, 243 women completed the test. Usability scores ran high, and seven in ten users said they would recommend it. Text analysis found the bot's tone stayed warmly positive even when users wrote in distress. It followed a validate-then-guide pattern: first naming the feeling, then steering to advice.
pmc-13427479:
Abdishakur Mohamed Abdi and colleagues report a newborn whose neck tumor critically squeezed his airway in a 2026 case study. The boy was delivered at 38 weeks by planned cesarean because prenatal scans showed a large neck mass with excess amniotic fluid. He developed severe breathing distress soon after birth and required a breathing tube. CT measured a heterogeneous mass of 10 by 12 by 13.5 centimeters spanning mouth, jaw, neck, and upper chest, mixing cystic and solid parts, fat, and calcium.

The mass compressed and displaced the trachea without reaching inside the skull, and the tumor marker alpha-fetoprotein was markedly elevated before surgery. Complete surgical removal of such cervical teratomas is the goal despite their usually benign tissue type.
pmc-13427779:
Vieira and colleagues reported in 2026 on pain catastrophizing, a pattern of expecting the worst from pain, in people with knee osteoarthritis. They asked how this pattern relates to anxiety and low mood, and whether brain-wave patterns add any signal. The team studied 62 patients from a rehab cohort, recording resting brain activity and scoring mood, catastrophizing, and clinical details with standard scales.

Vieira found that catastrophizing was linked on its own to both higher anxiety and higher low-mood scores, across both standard statistics and machine learning checks. Low mood also tied to stronger slow brain waves over the back of the head, lower education, and higher body weight. Brain-wave data alone were weak predictors, but they added a small amount when combined with clinical details. Most patients had mild symptoms, so the findings describe gradual links, not diagnosed illness.
pmc-13428179:
Dakota Van Parys, Sarah Williams, and Catherine Haase studied how bat groups changed at a military base after a deadly fungal disease reached North America. White-nose syndrome, caused by a fungus, has killed millions of hibernating bats since 2006.

The team used 30 years of netting records from Fort Campbell, on the Tennessee and Kentucky border, covering four bat species the disease spares. Some spared species rose after the disease arrived, but the pattern varied by species and by scale of analysis. Forest cover and how broken up the forest was explained capture rates better than the loss of rival species did. The authors say habitat and disease act together, so bat conservation must plan for both at once.
pmc-13429279:
Adam and colleagues measure how many women in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have heard of cervical cancer, a preventable disease that kills widely where screening is rare. Their 2026 study analyzes the Demographic and Health Survey of 2023 to 2024, covering 27,583 women aged 15 to 49. The team weighs which traits, from schooling to media habits, separate women who know the disease from women who do not.

Only about one woman in five had heard of cervical cancer. Awareness rose with age, city living, schooling, paid work, radio listening, internet use, and recent contact with health facilities. The strongest link was a past breast cancer exam, which came with nearly five times the odds of awareness, a hint that any cancer contact teaches. Facility based childbirth and Christian affiliation also tracked with knowledge. Campaigns should aim hardest at young, rural, unschooled women, the authors conclude.
pmc-13430179:
Qiong Wu and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a low-cost gene test panel tailored to a protected Chinese chicken breed. Hetian chickens are prized for richly flavored meat and hold national protection status, yet breeders lacked a dedicated genetic tool. The team sequenced 50 birds deeply and found over 16 million variable spots in their DNA. Strict filters for reliability, frequency, and even spacing across the genome shrank that list to 5,781 chosen markers.

Those markers form a liquid chip panel using targeted sequencing, a cheaper route than full genome reads. Validation on 307 birds returned a call rate of 99.9 percent, near perfection. The panel also sorted birds into families accurately and estimated relatedness well, the two jobs conservation breeding needs most. Indigenous breed programs elsewhere can copy the recipe for their own protected stock.
pmc-13430479:
Thomas and co-authors describe the career bottleneck facing early-stage investigators in diabetes translational research. That is the work of turning laboratory findings into real prevention and treatment. The bottleneck hits as they try to reach mid-career independence. Input came from 34 early investigators and 19 senior faculty at 23 United States institutions. All attended the inaugural national enrichment conference of the diabetes translational research centers.

The group catalogued challenges, opportunities, and needs across the transition. The backdrop is a nation where diabetes affects over 38 million Americans. It costs more than 327 billion dollars yearly. Only around half of patients have met glycemic targets over the past two decades, despite strong care guidance. That underscores why the field needs these researchers to persist. The authors aim to keep multidisciplinary early investigators engaged. They offer guidance for strengthening and sustaining their careers within the center network.
pmc-13431879:
Huynh and colleagues reported in 2026 a gentle way to purify boron nitride nanotubes, thread-like tubes prized for heat and strength uses, using slow spinning rather than harsh acids or fast centrifuges. Raw batches carry compact impurities, and standard cleaning can damage the tubes. Their method rests on settling physics: dense lumps sink fast, while long thin tubes drift down slowly.

By spinning slowly in water with common stabilizers, the team let impurities settle out while the tubes stayed suspended. The cleaned batches reached an estimated purity near 95 percent, with a good share recovered and no visible damage. The purified tubes still formed aligned structures when filtered, a trait needed for heat-spreading films. The authors offer slow spinning as a green cleaning route for thin nanomaterials.
pmc-13436079:
Zijin Zhou and Yutong Shao wrote a 2026 letter questioning the numbers in a trial of needle-knife treatment for tennis elbow. The trial, by Zhang and colleagues, compared treatment aimed at deep versus shallow tissue layers under ultrasound guidance.

Zhou and Shao show that the trial's reported ratios mix up two different measures, which changes how strong the benefit looks. They also note that the pain threshold used to judge real benefit came from shoulder research, not elbow research. The letter flags clashing claims about whether all 70 patients finished treatment, plus missing detail on how gaps in the data were filled. The authors ask for corrected figures and clearer reporting before the trial's claims are trusted.
pmc-13436279:
Feng Jiang and a large team grade five coronavirus variants descended from the JN lineage for entry skill and immune escape in 2026. Cell tests weigh infection rates, receptor grip, and membrane fusion for each variant. Blood serum from prior cases tests how well antibodies still block them.

Two of the variants infect cells far better than their kin. One grips the ACE2 receptor tightest, while the other fuses membranes best in key cells. All five dodge antibodies better than the parent strain. All still enter cells bearing animal versions of the receptor. Vaccine updates should track this fast moving family.
pmc-13436679:
Kyunyeon Kim and coauthors ablate a faulty heart pathway in a 57 year old man whose heart sits shifted right in 2026. The man survived a ventricular fibrillation arrest tied to early excited atrial rhythm. Scans confirmed the heart is displaced, not mirrored, which keeps vessel layout normal.

Shifted landmarks made the extra pathway hard to map with X ray views alone. Three dimensional mapping plus ultrasound from inside the heart guided the burn. The pathway was cut without harm to the normal conduction node. Rare anatomy need not bar standard cure when imaging stacks up. Case lessons aid teams facing displaced hearts.
pmc-13437979:
Caris Bogdanov and colleagues used brain wave recordings to test whether ear rehabilitation truly changes the brains of adults with cochlear implants. The implants bypass damaged ears, and structured practice can sharpen what users make of the signal. Their 2026 study enrolled adults with one implant and late-onset deafness into a ten-week guided listening program.

Speech scores told one story and brain waves another. After training, the program group recognized sounds and words better than controls, in the implanted ear alone and both ears together. Yet the cortical response peaks the team recorded, a standard sign of sound reaching the brain, did not shift at all. The gains were real but modest, arriving without a measurable change in that brain signal. The authors draw a careful lesson: absence on the trace does not cancel progress. Clinics should weigh behavior and brain measures side by side .
pmc-13438179:
Boustani and colleagues, writing for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, update the evidence behind Medicare's coverage rules for amyloid-targeting Alzheimer's drugs in this 2026 paper. Since 2022, Medicare has covered these drugs only under coverage with evidence development. That policy requires further proof. A 2024 review addressed the regulator's stated questions. This update adds extension data for donanemab and lecanemab and newer safety findings.

The extension studies show the treatment benefit continuing to build over time, with no new safety signals appearing during the longer follow-up periods covered. Safety analyses identified baseline traits that raise the risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, the brain swelling or bleeding side effects of these drugs. A slower dose-escalation schedule for donanemab lowered the risk of the swelling type, and the authors argue the evidence now justifies reconsidering the coverage policy.
pmc-13438379:
Chunyu Chen and colleagues trained machine learning models to flag which scrub typhus patients will turn severe. The mite-borne fever is common across Asia-Pacific and can crash into organ failure. Their 2026 study reviewed 492 patients in Jiangmen, 2013 to 2025. Standard statistics first picked candidate risk factors, then seven learning models were built and checked on held-out patients, .

Needing a breathing machine topped the list, a sign lung failure sits at the core of severe disease. High bilirubin, slow blood clotting, and low platelet counts followed as close markers. The strongest model, a boosted tree method, separated severe from mild cases with high accuracy in both its training and check groups. The authors argue such models could sort patients early at hospitals where the disease is common, steering intensive care toward those heading downhill. They note the models grew from one city's records and need outside testing.
pmc-13440979:
Pereira and colleagues presented in 2026 a shortened version of the MBGR protocol, a structured exam of the mouth, face, and swallowing structures used by speech-language pathologists. The full protocol is thorough but long, which limits its use in busy clinics. The team set out to cut it down while proving the short form still measures well.

A draft of 36 items went through two rounds of expert review, and 17 items were dropped. Expert agreement on the kept items reached a strong level. Eleven trained clinicians then applied the short form to 11 patients and judged it clear and workable, with most calling the original too long for routine care. The authors conclude the short protocol keeps validity with a shorter testing time.
pmc-13444279:
Yngve Forslin and colleagues report a routine drain swap that turned life-threatening in an 88-year-old man in a 2026 case paper. He had lost his left kidney to surgery and grown a deep abscess that needed a drain. During a planned swap to a larger drain tube, the tube nicked the stump of his renal artery and massive bleeding followed.

An emergency vessel team raced in to stop the flow. A stent graft alone could not seal the bleed, given the stump's tight shape. Coil plugs added through the graft path sealed the stump at last, while the graft kept coils from drifting. The authors stress that routine swaps in post-surgery bellies need full plans and rescue gear at hand, even in expert hands.
pmc-13444479:
Rishav Kumar and colleagues compare two broiler stunning methods by the chemistry they leave in breast meat in a 2026 research note. Gas stunning and electric stunning both precede slaughter, yet their early meat chemistry had scant head-to-head data. Breast fillets came from Ross 708 birds under pilot plant terms, six per method.

Fillets were drawn about 30 minutes after death, with sourness read at 15 minutes and color logged before deep freeze. Gas-stunned meat ran more sour than electric-stunned meat, at p below 0.001 in their tests, while color marks matched. Wide chemical scans found 508 compounds, with five split by method at raw p below 0.05 in the screen. The authors share the split as a lead for meat quality work.
pmc-13445379:
Pharis B. Sasa and colleagues report a small case series on a weight-loss artery procedure done in an office lab, with patients going home the same day, published in 2026. The procedure blocks select stomach arteries to curb hunger signals, and past reports kept patients in hospital overnight. The team asked whether that stay is truly needed for safety.

Six patients with at least class II obesity had the procedure at one accredited office lab between December 2024 and August 2025. Flow to the target stomach arteries stopped in every case, and all six went home the same day with no unplanned hospital stay. No side effects of any grade appeared over a median follow-up of nine months. The authors urge a larger planned trial.
pmc-13446179:
James Williamson and colleagues weigh a new computing workflow that aims to make base editing, a precise gene tweaking method, easier for labs to plan, in a 2026 commentary. Base editors swap single DNA letters without cutting both strands, which trims stray damage. Yet many labs still default to older CRISPR cutting, in part for want of friendly design tools.

The workflow under review, from Eaton and co-workers, joins existing design tools with a fresh analysis platform for knockout experiments with adenine base editors. It walks users through editor choice, guide design, delivery, and proof checks, with immune targets as the worked case. The commentary sets the tool in context and asks how far such pipelines can widen careful use of base editing.
pmc-13447079:
Xiaoying Li and colleagues review how the tumor's neighborhood rebuilds itself under treatment and breeds drug resistance, in a 2026 paper. Resistance was once blamed on tumor cells alone, yet the stroma, immune cells, vessels, and matrix around them shift under fire and carve safe niches. Those niches block drug entry, hide tumors from immunity, and shelter stem-like cells.

The review sorts the machinery: stiffening matrix signals, low-oxygen switches, gene mark changes, fuel rewiring, and bubble messages between cells. Counter-plans follow the same map, from softening stroma and retraining macrophages to fixing vessels and loading drugs in nanoparticles. The authors tie hope to place-aware gene reads and organ-like lab models that sort patients for paired attacks.
pmc-13447179:
Farah Yasmin and co-authors compare rural and city hospital care in a 2026 United States study of patients who had both heart failure and liver cirrhosis. Together the two conditions raise the risk of kidney injury, infection and long stays. Whether place of care widens those risks on a national scale was the question.

Hospital records from 2016 to 2022 yielded close to half a million stays meeting the study rules. About fifteen percent occurred in non-city hospitals. Death during the stay was slightly higher in rural settings, while city stays ran a little longer and cost more after price adjustment. Matched comparisons gave the same picture. The authors call for better regional access and support for complex care outside large cities.
pmc-13447279:
Mao and colleagues studied in 2026 why subtropical broadleaf trees release very different scent chemicals.  The team measured seven tree species from distinct lineages using cut branches in controlled settings. They combined gas analysis with measures of photosynthesis, meaning how leaves turn light into food, and with leaf traits.

Trees fell into two camps based on which chemical dominated their emissions. Trees rich in isoprene showed higher photosynthesis rates and stronger electron transport, the flow that powers food making. Trees rich in monoterpenes had heavier leaves and relied more on stored chemicals released for defence. Emission profiles tracked leaf weight and photosynthetic capacity closely across species. The authors suggest future emission models should include leaf weight and electron transport as inputs. That change would sharpen forecasts of forest emissions under climate change.
pmc-13447379:
Yun-Hee Kim, Seyoung Shin and Jinuk Kim review brain rewiring after stroke and what it means for rehabilitation in 2026. Stroke often leaves lasting movement loss, while recovery leans on neuroplasticity, the brain's ability to remodel connections and reroute signals. Two forms anchor the account, one strengthening active links through use and one keeping overall network balance.

Intensive, task-focused practice taps the use-driven form, and repeated goal-directed training improves movement in animal and human studies. Robots, sensor feedback, brain stimulation, drugs and stem cells aim to boost the same processes with high, personalised doses. Results across those add-ons stay uneven, the authors note. They urge matching treatment to lesion features, brain markers and recovery stage, with combined approaches and precise tools as the way forward.
pmc-13447479:
Seyedeh Ala Mokhtabad Amrei and colleagues test a behaviour scale for executive problems in a fragile X related tremor disorder in 2026 work. The disorder stems from a moderate repeat expansion in a gene and erodes planning, control and thinking with age. A scale based on observed behaviour is widely used for executive function, yet its tie to brain scan markers in this condition was unexamined.

Fifty-six carriers with and without the disorder completed the scale, a brief mental test and computerised executive tasks, alongside brain scans. Worse scan scores tracked with worse scale scores in a strong pattern that survived adjustment for age, sex and repeat length. Computerised executive tasks rose with scan burden in a smaller complete sample, while the brief mental test moved the other way. The scale earns a supporting role beside other measures.
pmc-13448079:
Filip Milisav and co-authors test how nested modular structure shapes computation in brain-like networks in a 2026 modelling study. Brains organise into specialised subnetworks nested inside larger ones, yet what that layered layout buys computationally was unclear. A simple generator for multi-level modular networks let the team build artificial reservoirs, networks whose internal dynamics do the computing, with controlled structure.

Layered modular reservoirs remembered more, handled several tasks at once and produced richer timing patterns than strictly modular or random rivals. Recurring loop motifs enriched in the layered design explained much of the advantage. Human brain wiring data showed the same benefits when its natural layered layout was used, including brain-like timescales of activity. Hierarchy itself, not just modularity, emerges as a functional asset.
pmc-13448279:
Battalapalli and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract DSAI-09, a head-to-head test of an interpretable imaging signature against two black-box artificial intelligence models. The puzzle is classic: telling recurrent tumor from radiation necrosis, dead tissue from earlier radiosurgery, on MRI scans of treated brain metastases.

The team assembled 233 scans from three institutions, most with pathology confirmation, and computed 944 texture and spatial features per lesion for their SMART-Risk signature. On the held-out Wisconsin test set it reached an accuracy in the high seventies. It clearly beat a standard deep network and a fine-tuned medical imaging foundation model, which managed only the low-to-mid sixties. Importance analysis showed recurrent tumors display greater spatial complexity than necrotic tissue, giving clinicians an explanation, not a bare score. The authors argue such transparency could cut unnecessary surgery for what is only treatment damage.
pmc-13448579:
Sidiki Kaba and Alexandre Avdeev trace movements between contraceptive states among women in Guinea in a 2026 analysis of survey calendar data. Understanding when women start, switch or stop methods matters more than a single snapshot of use. Monthly calendars from the 2018 national survey let the team rebuild five years of contraceptive and pregnancy histories for women aged fifteen to forty-nine.

A recurrent-event survival model handled repeated transitions per woman across non-use, traditional methods, modern methods and pregnancy states. Monthly movement chances were low during contraceptive states, rose during pregnancy and jumped after pregnancy outcomes. Age, education and wealth shifted the chances only slightly, while media exposure and residence showed no clear link. Reproductive events, not social background, drive switching in this setting, so support around pregnancy and delivery moments is emphasised.
pmc-13448679:
Anmol Mathur and co-authors present in 2026 an electrochemical system that pulls carbon dioxide straight from the air. Instead of treating a bulk liquid, the device makes hydroxide right at the air-facing electrode, where capture happens. A porous layer spreads that reactive surface through a three-dimensional volume.

Captured carbon dioxide is later released in pure form through a mediator that moves protons and electrons together, keeping regeneration energy low. With a tuned porous layer and pulsed current, the system ran steadily for over 50 hours at current densities about ten times higher than earlier devices of this kind. Modeling and cost analysis in the paper sketch how the design might scale.
pmc-13448879:
Sean Wharton and colleagues pool in 2026 the liver safety data from seven phase 3 trials of orforglipron, a once-daily GLP-1 pill for obesity and type 2 diabetes. The analysis covered 11,220 participants, 6,920 on the drug and 4,300 on placebo or active comparators, followed for up to 104 weeks. Liver enzymes were tracked over time, and cases were screened against the standard pattern for serious drug-induced liver injury.

On average, liver enzyme levels fell during orforglipron treatment, a pattern consistent with the metabolic gains of weight loss. Marked enzyme elevations occurred at equal low rates in both arms, six participants each, and every orforglipron case had another explanation, so none met the injury criteria. Liver-related side effects were likewise balanced. Results held for participants whose enzymes started normal or elevated, easing a key safety question for the drug class.
pmc-13449479:
Wenhao Bao and colleagues show in 2026 that a routine stained tissue slide can reveal a pancreatic cancer's stromal stiffness program, a trait normally invisible without molecular testing. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma wraps itself in dense, cross-linked scar tissue that squeezes vessels and blocks drugs, one reason survival barely improves. The team trained foundation models, large pretrained image networks, on standard hematoxylin and eosin slides to predict that remodeling program from appearance alone.

External validation on an independent national cohort, CPTAC, confirmed the transcriptomic predictions. Spatial gene mapping then checked where the model looked: its attention landed on tissue zones expressing COL12A1, LOX, and LOXL2, the very genes that build and cross-link the matrix. The authors offer the result as a histology-derived biomarker candidate, a way to read stromal biology from slides every pathology lab already produces.
pmc-13449779:
Mohammed Said Bouya, Hamza Najout, and Najib Bouhabba propose in 2026 a new way to think about patients who cannot come off a ventilator after surgery. Hospitals usually record liberation failure as a single late yes-or-no event, yet the authors argue vulnerability accumulates quietly through anesthesia, the ventilator itself, paralysis drugs, pain control, fluids, and surgical stress. Their conceptual review builds a framework from four interacting dimensions of that vulnerability.

The four are weak respiratory muscle contraction, diaphragm injury from effort, suppressed central breathing drive, and a cardiovascular system that cannot bear the load. Mapped across readiness checks, the stress of a spontaneous breathing trial, and life after the tube comes out, these dimensions form stage-specific risk trajectories. The authors are explicit that the model is a testable architecture, not a validated bedside score, meant to define patient phenotypes and aim future trials at mechanisms.
pmc-13452279:
Yaroslav Chushak, Teresa Sterner, and Rebecca Clewell build in 2026 learning models that guess whether a chemical can cross the brain's gate wall. Lab tests can flag brain-active chemicals, yet only those that cross the blood-brain barrier act the same in a body. The team trained varied models on molecular traits and checked them with split tests that guard against easy wins.

A merged consensus model proved steadiest, with balanced accuracy near the top range on the hard split. One trait, the polar surface share of the molecule, mattered most, and nitrogen rings showed often in crossers. Run over 6,000 brain-receptor blockers from lab assays, the model warned that over a quarter likely never cross, triage news for testers.
pmc-13452379:
Ahmed and colleagues measured fat hormones and trace elements in 2026 in the blood of patients with papillary thyroid carcinoma, the most common thyroid cancer, before and after treatment. The hormones leptin and adiponectin link body fat to cancer biology, and several minerals shift in illness. The team asked whether these blood patterns could help diagnose the cancer or follow it after care.

Fifty new patients and fifty healthy volunteers were compared. Before treatment, patients carried higher leptin and lower adiponectin than both treated patients and controls. Zinc, selenium, and magnesium ran low, while manganese, copper, and iodine ran high. Levels largely settled after treatment. A ratio of the two hormones separated patients from healthy people with excellent accuracy, and the authors suggest it as a cheap marker for diagnosis and follow-up.
pmc-13452479:
Mateusz Wróbel and six co-authors measure how well ultra thin layers built from ring shaped carbon compounds block electric current. These single molecule layers, made from a class called N heterocyclic carbenes, could serve as insulation in organic electronic parts. Their 2026 study tests a matched set of such layers and checks their strength as blockers.

Every layer in the set blocked current strongly, even one just 3.3 angstroms thick, a span far below a nanometre. That thinnest layer blocked current about 100,000 times better than a standard layer of the same length built from chain like molecules. Math checks ruled out one quantum effect that some blamed for low flow in ring compounds. The result points to a simple route to very thin, strong insulation for gate parts in future devices.
pmc-13453479:
Liu and colleagues tackle in 2026 a weak point of lithium batteries: the solid electrolyte interphase. This thin film forms on an electrode and controls how long the battery survives repeated charging. Uneven films cause uneven lithium deposits and early failure.

Instead of adding more film-forming chemical, the team applied 45 kilohertz ultrasound during a narrow voltage window of the very first discharge. The film then grew as a two-layer structure with a compact mineral-rich inner layer. Graphite cells treated this way kept about four fifths of their capacity after 500 charge cycles at a fast rate. Cells made without ultrasound began a rapid capacity decline after roughly 250 cycles.
pmc-13454079:
Li and collaborators compared blood levels of chemerin in 160 Chinese breast cancer patients and 160 matched controls. Chemerin is a fat-derived signaling protein. They tested whether the adipokine tracks cancer risk, and whether blood lipids carry part of any effect. Risk factor questionnaires accompanied the blood measurements in this one-to-one matched case-control study.

Patients had higher chemerin than controls overall and within both menopausal subgroups examined separately in the analysis. Women above the control median for chemerin had 2.217 times the odds of breast cancer, rising to 4.713 among premenopausal women and 2.103 after menopause in the stratified results. The dose-response relationship was linear across the measured range rather than threshold-like in spline modeling. Triglycerides statistically mediated part of the link, accounting for about 15.0 percent of the total association between chemerin and breast cancer odds.
pmc-13454279:
Jeffery A. Jones and John F. Houde wrote the 2026 editorial that opens the third volume of a series on how sensory feedback guides speech. Earlier volumes dealt first with hearing and then with touch and body sense. The new volume asks how the brain weighs errors from each sense and how that balance shifts in speech disorders.

Contributions summarized here report that speakers correct sound shifts more strongly when the shift moves a vowel toward a nearby natural category. One study found that pitch adaptation faded fast with repetition, dropping by about two thirds after a second exposure. The editors use such findings to argue that error size alone does not drive correction.
pmc-13454579:
Shuyuan Zhang and Alexei A. Lapkin propose, in a 2026 methods study, a transformer model that reads molecules through two graphs at once. Predicting a molecule's properties drives work in chemistry, materials, and drug hunting. Standard models lean on atom maps alone, which can miss what the bonds themselves carry.

Their dual graph transformer fuses atom features, bond features, overall shape, and three-dimensional geometry inside one attention system. Benchmarks across standard datasets showed clear gains over the best current models. Follow-up tests credited the dual view, the position and structure codes, and the geometry input for the lift. The model also highlights which parts of a molecule drive a prediction, aiding interpretation. The authors aim the tool at faster, more transparent screening of candidate compounds.
pmc-13455379:
Zeng and colleagues trained a deep learning network to clean up PET scans taken faster or with half the usual radioactive tracer dose. The aim was to cut patient radiation exposure and scanner time without losing detail. They studied 322 patients, faking half-dose imaging and scan times from 30 to 90 seconds per position.

A residual U-Net rebuilt the noisy images, lifting reader quality scores in the half-dose group from 3.45 at baseline to 4.33 after processing, on the five-point scale used. Numeric similarity climbed too, with structural similarity rising from 0.75 at the low end to 0.87 at the high end and peak signal-to-noise from 37.65 decibels before to 41.37 decibels after in half-dose reconstructions. Even the fastest 30-second protocol recovered strongly after processing in the reported metrics. Detection of small lesions improved by up to 16.3 percent in shortened scans, judged by two nuclear medicine physicians, supporting efficient AI-enhanced protocols.
pmc-13456379:
Hongmei Yang and seven colleagues write, in a 2026 letter, about estimating a key lung severity ratio without repeated blood draws for ventilated patients at high altitude. The ratio of arterial oxygen to inhaled oxygen guides care in acute respiratory distress syndrome, a lethal lung failure. Drawing arterial blood often is painful, costly, and hard where staff and equipment are thin.

A fingertip saturation ratio has been proposed as a stand-in, with formulas built mostly on sea-level patients. Thin air changes how saturation maps to blood oxygen, so those formulas may mislead in the mountains. The team's earlier work in non-ventilated patients showed promising agreement. Their letter sets out a systematic check in the sickest group: patients on invasive ventilators at a hospital in Lijiang. The goal is a validated, needle-free severity read for high-altitude intensive care.
pmc-13457079:
Courtney Bartel leads a sixteen-author study, from 2026, hunting blood clues that show whether a child's Crohn disease has truly healed inside the gut. Healing seen by scope, not just calm symptoms, predicts fewer setbacks. Eighty-seven patients aged one to twenty-two, all on anti-TNF biologics for over six months, had drug measures and scope checks at several centers.

About 55 percent had healed. Three members of a marker family called CD64 ran lower in the healed group, each with a usable cutoff. Standard drug trough levels did not differ, but children clearing infliximab faster healed less. A combined model using clearance, platelet count, and albumin sorted healing with an accuracy score of 0.90. The authors say the split matters: slow drug clearance calls for dose changes, while a drug that is present yet failing calls for a switch.
pmc-13457379:
Aliaa Khalili and five colleagues published this 2026 case report of one patient, a 73-year-old man with high-risk antiphospholipid syndrome, an immune disorder that promotes clotting. He developed fast-spreading leg ulcers with active MRSA and Pseudomonas infection, alongside severe thrombocytopenia, a shortage of platelets. Steroids risked feeding the infection, and blood thinners risked bleeding, so standard options were blocked.

The team used intravenous immunoglobulin, a pooled antibody treatment, as a bridge: it calms immune attack without broad suppression, and it also raises platelet counts. He received a dose every three weeks with targeted antimicrobials, while blood thinners were paused and another immune drug stopped. Once platelets recovered past the safety threshold, anticoagulation resumed. Over five months the ulcers steadily resurfaced with skin and closed completely. The authors present the sequence as a workable template for similarly trapped cases.
pmc-13460179:
Wei Gan and colleagues report in 2026 early experience with EndoFusion, a system that overlays a patient's three-dimensional scan model onto the live camera view during keyhole lung surgery. Finding small, faint nodules inside the lung is notoriously hard, and the usual needle localization is invasive. Fifteen patients carrying nineteen peripheral nodules, most of them pure ground-glass shadows with a median size of eight millimeters, underwent assisted resection at one center.

Every nodule was removed without converting to open surgery, through wedge cuts or segment removal. Registration of the model took a median of just over two minutes, blood loss was minimal, and no complications occurred during surgery. Two patients had minor problems afterward, and the median stay was four days.
pmc-13461179:
Fabiana Pereyra-Goday and co-authors weighed the trade offs of Uruguayan farms that rotate crops and cattle pasture together, judging them on profit, environment, and food security at once. Integrated crop and livestock systems promise greener intensification, but single score claims hide real tensions. In their 2026 evaluation drawing on long term experiments, the team scored rotations for productivity, gross margins, soil erosion, emissions, and nitrogen gains. It also scored the protein produced for human food.

The long rotation, alternating pasture and crops over more years, emerged as the most eco efficient system, emitting 9.6 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent per dollar of gross margin in the indicator reported. Legumes in the pasture phase fixed nitrogen biologically, lifting how well nitrogen was used, and erosion stayed well below the regulatory tolerance limit of seven tonnes per hectare yearly. Combining pastures with crops can raise productivity while improving environmental performance.
pmc-13461579:
Qing Zhang and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, how to get the best results from teduglutide for children with short bowel syndrome. In that condition much of the gut is missing or fails, so children cannot absorb enough food and depend on nutrition given into a vein. Teduglutide copies a natural gut hormone and helps the remaining bowel adapt. New trials and clinic reports update older advice on timing and dose.

Recent work finds that up to 30 percent of treated children reached full feeding by mouth or tube, well above an earlier figure of 16 percent. Children who started with lower volumes of vein feeding and fewer infusions each week tended to gain the most. The authors argue against one fixed start rule, urging plans fitted to each child. They also advise giving the drug for at least a year before judging whether it works, since gains build slowly.
pmc-13462079: Neil Bowley and colleagues issued a 2026 correction notice in the journal Eye for their article on the environmental cost of a higher-dose eye drug. The notice is a correction only and carries no new findings. One printed measurement for the larger-dose syringe packet was wrong: the middle dimension should read 165 millimeters, not 135 millimeters as first printed. With that size fixed, the claim stands that many more units fit on one shipping pallet, cutting transport emissions by about one third. The journal states the original article has been updated.
pmc-13462679:
Yuyu Hua and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a risk model for neck lymph node spread in patients who have both Hashimoto's thyroiditis, an autoimmune thyroid inflammation, and papillary thyroid cancer. Judging node spread is hard because the inflamed gland distorts ultrasound pictures of nodes. The team reviewed 261 patients whose diagnosis was confirmed after thyroid surgery at a hospital in Guizhou between 2018 and 2023.

Seven traits stood as independent risk factors: age, a blood enzyme, calcium spots and blood flow in the main tumor, and shape, brightness, and calcium spots in the nodes. Four models were built from feature mixes: tumor ultrasound alone, node ultrasound alone, both together, and a full model adding clinical data. The full model sorted patients best, with accuracy in internal checks and risk estimates matching real rates. The authors offer the model as an aid for surgery and follow-up in this patient group.
pmc-13463379:
Yagmur Unsal leads a 2026 case report of, the authors say, the first known patient whose CD70 deficiency appeared as severe type 1 diabetes. CD70 is an immune signaling protein; lacking it brings immune dysregulation, runaway inflammatory episodes, abnormal lymph cell growth, and cancer risk. The child arrived with severe diabetic ketoacidosis, failure of several organs, and later puzzles: repeated ketoacidosis, skin lesions, and celiac disease.

Gene testing confirmed a double-copy missense variant in CD70, and family studies backed the finding. A stem cell transplant from a donor treated the immune defect. After transplant, sugar control improved, with the median long-term sugar marker falling and daily insulin needs dropping. The authors argue the case shows an intact CD27 and CD70 signaling pair guards against immune attack on the pancreas's insulin-making cells. They point to that pathway as a candidate target for immune therapies against type 1 diabetes.
pmc-13463479:
Fu and co-authors described in 2026 a faster way to multiply a rare medicinal orchid, Anoectochilus roxburghii. The plant is highly valued, endangered in the wild, and slow to reproduce on its own. Starting from stem segments with nodes, they built a lab culture system. The system grows protocorm-like bodies directly from buds. These are small cell clusters that behave like orchid seeds, and no messy callus stage intervenes.

On the best hormone mixture, each starting piece produced more than 30 new bodies. The authors call that multiplication rate rare for this species. The full cycle ran about 110 days to prepare sterile material and 160 days of body induction. Rooting took 90 days, and hardening off took 60 more. Every plantlet rooted on the strongest rooting medium. More than 95 in 100 survived the move to normal conditions. Chromosome checks showed no genetic drift at any stage.
pmc-13463579:
Alba Díaz González and four co-authors study death risk in dogs with acute pancreatitis, a sudden swelling of the pancreas. Some dogs heal in days, while others grow gravely ill. The team followed 134 owned dogs seen at a hospital and compared them with healthy dogs.

Two scores built from routine blood tests, both tied to creatinine, stood out at intake. One score pairs creatinine with albumin, and the other pairs white cell counts with creatinine. Dogs with higher scores died in hospital more often, and the scores beat single blood values at sorting risk. Since the tests are already routine, vets can flag fragile dogs early at no extra cost.
pmc-13463979:
Karel Huard and six co-authors review how to judge venous congestion, backed-up blood in the veins, in critically ill patients. Congestion can injure many organs and can shift within hours. No single test captures it well, so the authors join three ultrasound methods at the bedside.

Heart ultrasound grades how stiffly the heart fills, vein ultrasound scores excess flow in organs, and lung ultrasound spots fluid in the lungs. Worked examples and flow charts show how the three views correct each other's blind spots. A stiff heart with quiet veins tells a different story than swollen veins with dry lungs. Intensive care teams gain a fuller, faster read on fluid overload and organ risk.
pmc-13464079:
Luping Wang leads a team that targets SIRT6, a gene-tuning enzyme, to calm blood cancers with runaway neutrophil growth. A screen of gene-tuning compounds flagged a SIRT6 activator, MDL-800, as a strong brake on the excess growth. Zebrafish bred with a faulty sirt6 gene developed a like disease on their own.

Sirt6 trims a chemical mark at the switch of c-myb, a growth gene for early blood cells. Without Sirt6, young blood cells and neutrophils multiplied out of bounds, while extra Sirt6 calmed them. The activator boosted the standard drug imatinib in fish and mouse leukemia models. It even restored drug response in resistant mouse tumors, which marks a fresh pairing for hard cases.
pmc-13464279:
Aguiar and Mioto wrote this 2026 editorial about a heart tumor that was misdiagnosed as benign. They discuss the case of a woman 31 weeks pregnant. She developed acute heart failure from two large left atrial masses. Three years earlier, surgery had removed a tumor labeled a myxoma. Re-examination of both the original and the new tissue showed cardiac myxofibrosarcoma, a rare cancer that mimics myxoma.

Fewer than five percent of primary cardiac sarcomas are this type, yet it tends to grow invasively and recur, so the label matters greatly for outcome. The authors explain that scans, however advanced, cannot reliably separate the two tumors, which both appear gelatinous and mobile in the left atrium. Only microscopic and immunostaining examination settles the diagnosis, and they argue the case was most likely a misclassification from the start, not a cancerous transformation.
pmc-13464879:
Xu and co-authors examined tumor tissue from 25 patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma in 2026. They tracked how immune cells inside the tumor change after chemotherapy combined with immunotherapy given before surgery. Samples taken before treatment and from the removed tumor were stained for three lymphocyte types. Lymphocytes are the white blood cells that attack cancer. Patients whose tumors vanished completely were compared against those whose did not.

Seven patients, 28 percent, achieved a complete pathological response. No living cancer remained at surgery for them. Only in that group did the shares of helper CD4 and killer CD8 lymphocytes climb after treatment. Their post-treatment levels also stood significantly above the non-responders' levels. B cells, marked CD20, barely moved in either group. Patients destined to respond started with relatively more CD4 cells. That starting share may help predict who benefits, independent of the commonly used PD-L1 test.
pmc-13464979:
Wenbin Xiao and six co-authors screen nine essential oils from Chinese medicinal herbs against food poisoning germs. Foodborne bacteria and their slimy biofilms resist many cleaners, so plant oils draw interest as natural guards. Four target germs, including Staphylococcus aureus and Listeria, faced each oil in growth and biofilm tests.

Honeysuckle oil led the pack, halting the widest germ range at low doses. It stripped mature biofilms of three germs by roughly half or more, though staph biofilms resisted. Scent analysis found 156 compounds across the oils, with honeysuckle rich in linalool and borneol. Growth curves and microscope views showed the oil stalling growth and wrecking cell surfaces, which backs its use as a food guard candidate.
pmc-13465079:
Mihai Adrian Păsărică and four co-authors review how uveal melanoma, a cancer inside the eye, rewires its chemistry to survive. Local treatment often clears the eye tumor, yet half of patients later face spread, chiefly to the liver, years down the line. Flexible fuel switching sits at the center of that staying power.

Tumor cells flip between sugar burning and oxygen-based burning as conditions demand. Fat handling and redox balance, the cell's rust defense, shift in step with the fuel choice. Each switch helps cells outlast drugs and outgrow rival clones. Set beside other cancers, the eye tumor's tricks look partly shared and partly its own. The authors map the switches as targets for stopping late spread.
pmc-13465679:
Huang and co-authors re-engineer a traditional Kyrgyz pastry to carry less fat. Their 2026 paper optimises Katima, a spiral-rolled layered pastry from Xinjiang normally made with abundant clarified butter. The tools were single-factor trials and response surface methodology. That is a statistical technique for tuning several ingredients at once. Butter, yeast, and salt emerged as the variables that mattered, judged by sensory score.

The validated optimum used about 12.7 grams of butter, with under a gram each of yeast and salt, per hundred grams of flour. It scored about 95 on sensory testing while cutting fat by about 37 percent against the traditional full-fat version. The reduced-fat pastry came out moister, harder, and chewier, with markedly lower peroxide and acid values, indicating better fat stability in storage. The authors offer the parameters as a standardised route to industrial production of a healthier ethnic pastry.
pmc-13466179:
Xueyan Liu and a large team built patient-specific lab models of hereditary angioedema, a swelling disorder caused by faults in the SERPING1 gene, reporting in 2026. The faults cut production of a blood protein that normally keeps swelling pathways in check. Human models that mirror each patient's own mutation have been missing.

Blood cells from four patients, each carrying a different kind of gene change, were reprogrammed into flexible stem cells and then grown into liver-like cells. Those cells matured properly and released the protective protein at near-normal baseline in form, yet each patient's cells faltered in mutation-specific ways. Gene-editing checks validated the platform, which the authors offer for testing tailored treatments.
pmc-13467679:
Özokan compared two ways in 2026 of building a family of ring-shaped molecules called decahydroacridine-1,8-diones, used as dyes and drug starting frames. One route mixed all parts at once in a single pot. The other prepared a key middle piece first, then finished in a second step. Six molecules were made by both routes.

The two-step route won on yield: after counting the first step, it returned roughly three fifths to two thirds of product, against about two fifths for the one-pot route. The one-pot mix also spun off side products. Özokan reads the gap as sequence control: forming the middle piece first steers parts into the desired ring, while lighting all reactions at once opens rival paths.
pmc-13467779:
Prieto Palomo and colleagues combined lab spectra, quantum calculations, and statistics in 2026 to read the vibrational fingerprints of four phenolic acids, plant compounds valued as antioxidants. Raman spectroscopy reads how molecules vibrate, giving a fingerprint of structure. How each chemical group shapes that fingerprint was the open question.

The four acids were measured as solids and in an alcohol-water mix, and their spectra were matched against computed ones. Solid samples gave the sharpest fingerprints and the clearest split between compounds. The three acids built on a longer chain shared strong bands from their linked double bonds, while gallic acid, built differently, sang a distinct tune led by its oxygen groups. Computer maps showed oxygen sites as the most reactive spots, which explains why solvent shifts those bands most.
pmc-13468479:
Zhen Li, Jinhui Hu, and Jian Xing design in 2026 the signal shaping for a wireless system that senses and communicates at once, aided by an active intelligent reflecting surface. Such surfaces, studded with tunable elements, can amplify and redirect radio waves, creating virtual line-of-sight paths for radar targets and phone users alike. The wrinkle is hardware imperfection at the base station transmitter, which injects distortion noise that couples with the surface own amplification noise.

The goal is to maximize radar signal quality while guaranteeing communication users their service levels and respecting two power budgets. Because the optimization problem is non-convex with coupled variables, the authors solve it by alternating: fixing some parts, optimizing others, and iterating. Future 6G base stations are expected to double as radar sensors, and designs that survive real hardware flaws, rather than assuming perfect radios, are the ones that will ship.
pmc-13468679:
Jie Gao, Liheng Li, Qi Liu, Ning Zhang and Yan Li published this 2026 review on plant polysaccharides as a treatment route for Alzheimer's disease. These sugar molecules from traditional Chinese medicine protect nerve cells in lab studies and seem safe. Yet they are barely absorbed from the gut and hardly cross into the brain, which clashes with their reported benefits. The authors argue the gut microbiome resolves that paradox.

In their account, the sugars act like prebiotics: gut bacteria ferment them into short-chain fatty acids and other small products. Those products enter the blood, cross into the brain, and calm inflammation through metabolic and immune pathways. Reviewed studies report less amyloid buildup, less tau protein change, restored synapse function and better cognition in disease models. The authors frame the sugars as gut-oriented agents rather than brain-targeting drugs, and lay out what this means for future therapies.
pmc-13469579:
Jiandong Zhao, Honghua Zhao, Benwang Li, and Xuyin Gong review in 2026 how deep reinforcement learning helps indoor robots dodge moving obstacles. Fixed rules cope poorly with cluttered, changing rooms where people and carts move at random. Learning agents that earn rewards through trial and error have become a popular alternative.

The review sorts the main algorithms into three families based on how they value actions, choose actions, or combine both roles. It then works through five technical problem areas, comparing the fixes each family has produced and what those fixes cost or gain. A shared reference frame for choosing algorithms is one stated aim. The authors close by naming the directions they judge most promising for indoor navigation research.
pmc-13469679:
Su and colleagues in China built in 2026 a rig and method to line up circuit board shots, so a robot can find each solder joint. Big boards fight back: parts crowd in one zone and thin in the next, light glints, and shapes warp. Stock match tools use one fixed rule for the whole board, which cracks on such mixed ground. Their rig holds the board still under a ring light, while the code bends its search by local crowd load.

The method tags board marks with a set code, then finds each tag's mate with a search that widens or trims by how dense the zone is. In cut tests, near nine in ten mates were true inliers, the sound core of a match. Line ups held firm through shifts in height, zone, and view. The team pitches the rig for plant checks and robot soldering.
pmc-13469879:
Ha-Neul Jo and colleagues report in 2026 that a calcium pump helps control blood vessel growth and barrier function in the brain and retina. The receptor Frizzled4 receives signals from Norrin and WNT proteins and is required for these vessels to form and seal properly. How the receptor itself is regulated had stayed unclear despite its importance as a drug target.

Using a proximity labeling method that tags nearby proteins, the team found the pump ATP2B1, also called PMCA1, sitting next to Frizzled4 in vessel lining cells. Removing the pump raised cell calcium, switched on a calcium driven program, and weakened Norrin signaling. Mice lacking the pump in vessel lining showed brain vessel defects matching weak Frizzled4 signaling. The authors suggest high calcium states may quiet this pathway in disease.
pmc-13470279:
Alam Ahmad Hidayat and colleagues publish in 2026 the full genome of a heat tolerant bacterium pulled from an acidic hot spring in Indonesia. The strain, named Pseudobacillus badius WCB-1, came from sediment at Kawah Putih in West Java. It was grown in culture, checked with a marker gene, and then confirmed by whole genome comparison methods.

Two sequencing technologies, a short read Illumina run and a long read nanopore run, were combined for the assembly. The genome spans just over four million DNA letters with a moderate share of the letters G and C. Annotation found 4,106 protein-coding sequences plus transfer and ribosomal RNA genes. Mining the sequence flagged several clusters that may produce useful natural compounds. The dataset is offered for comparative genomics work.
pmc-13471179:
Ataoğlu and co-authors interviewed internists in Türkiye in 2026 about deprescribing, deliberately stopping the acid-blocking stomach drugs called PPIs that patients often take for years needlessly. Twelve doctors, ten residents and two specialists, gave in-depth interviews in spring 2023, anchored by two patient vignettes. Answers were mapped onto a standard behavior framework.

Influences spanned twelve domains, with barriers piled on the system side: a fragmented health system, heavy workloads, and poor provider coordination. Patients also resisted, treating the pills as rescue drugs they expect to keep. Knowledge gaps and doubts about consequences added friction. Yet enablers existed too: doctors intended to deprescribe and held clear goals. Beliefs about consequences cut both ways, motivating and restraining. The authors conclude that good intentions are not enough. System fixes, shared records, clear guidelines, and patient education must carry the behavior change.
pmc-13471379:
El Ayat and colleagues tested whether eye-tracking patterns, measured while people view images, can help detect autism spectrum disorder with artificial intelligence. Their 2026 multi-site study combined two European datasets, 57 participants from France and 27 from Italy, giving 84 people in total, 40 of them autistic.

Four model types were compared, and a memory-based LSTM network scored highest, with an AUC of 0.859 on the ranking scale where 1.0 is perfect. A graph neural network with attention nearly matched it at 0.855 and reached the best specificity, correctly clearing 93.2% of non-autistic participants. Attention mechanisms, often assumed helpful, did not significantly lift the graph model's results. The authors argue either design could support objective screening where specialists are scarce.
pmc-13472979:
Mamode and colleagues present a 2026 commentary on the collapse of kidney care in Gaza during the war that began in October 2023, arguing that not to act is itself an act. Before the war, Gaza had performed over one hundred living-donor kidney transplants and hoped to grow the program. Transplantation has now stopped entirely.

The main hospital in Khan Younis had thirty-one working dialysis machines for 238 patients in December, with no peritoneal dialysis supplies at all: no catheters, no fluid, no sterile space. Kidney failure patients who miss dialysis die within days to weeks, so rationing by scarcity is a death sentence delivered slowly. The authors, transplant professionals, write as witnesses and colleagues. Their plea is that medical neutrality cannot mean silence when a whole treatment system is dismantled.
pmc-13474879:
Shuhei Nomura and a broad team ask in 2026 why healthy life expectancy figures disagree across Japan. Three national metrics plus a global model estimate were compared for forty-seven prefectures from 2001 to 2019. Survey-based metrics rely on self-reported limits, while one national metric uses care insurance records. Panel math linked gaps to disease burden, risks, and social traits.

Survey metrics matched the global model well for men but weakly for women. The records-based metric matched well for both sexes across the span. Mental disorders and body weight helped explain survey-model gaps in men. Knowing what each metric misses helps leaders pick the right gauge.
pmc-13475379:
Simone Rota and co-authors pool trial evidence on HER2-targeted treatment for metastatic colorectal cancer with HER2 amplification, a subgroup with poorer prognosis and resistance to standard EGFR therapy. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis includes phase two and three trials of anti-HER2 regimens without added chemotherapy.

Ten trials covering 467 patients tested five combinations built around trastuzumab. Across them, about a third of patients responded and just over two thirds achieved disease control, with weighted median survival of 13.4 months and time without progression of five and a half months. Two regimens stood out: trastuzumab deruxtecan and trastuzumab with tucatinib showed higher response and control rates than the older dual blockade of trastuzumab plus pertuzumab. The authors conclude anti-HER2 therapy works in pretreated patients, while noting further studies are needed to confirm the ranking.
pmc-13476479:
Ronald S. Samia and four colleagues published this 2026 brewing study tracking thiols, the sulfur compounds that give hop-forward beers their fruit aroma, through pilot fermentations. Thiols occur at trace levels but smell potent, and steering release from hop precursors is hard. The team followed thiol levels daily in a lager yeast and an ale yeast, with and without dry-hopping, alongside yeast gene expression.

Without dry-hopping, thiol production peaked on days one to three, matching peak fermentation activity. The lager strain released more of one thiol, 3SH, than the ale strain, while another thiol showed no strain effect. Dry-hopping raised thiols, but 3SH did not rise in proportion to hop dose. Both thiols kept climbing during later processing. Candidate enzyme and transporter genes switched on and off in waves, yet their expression failed to explain the patterns, leaving precursor supply and metabolism as co-drivers.
pmc-13477279:
Yongyu Huang and coauthors published a 2026 cohort study asking how the mix of moderate and vigorous exercise relates to death rates in United States adults. The team used national health survey data from 1997 to 2018, linked to death records through 2019. Adults were grouped as inactive, active at moderate intensity only, active at vigorous intensity only, or active at both.

Nearly 587,000 adults were followed for a median of ten years. Every active group had lower death rates than inactive adults, and the combined group fared best. Among people who mixed intensities, those who got more than a quarter of their activity from vigorous exercise had the lowest risk. The authors say intensity mix matters alongside total activity time.
pmc-13477379:
Xianglin Long and coauthors published a 2026 multiomics study identifying spondin-1, a protein tied to tissue scaffolding, as a candidate driver of atrial fibrillation. The team combined genetic analyses of blood proteins and atrial tissue gene activity with heart rhythm genome data. Follow-up work used single-cell and spatial gene mapping plus experiments in fibroblast cells.

Spondin-1 activity concentrated in fibroblasts, the cells that build scar-like tissue in the heart. In a UK Biobank group of about 39,000 people, higher blood levels of the protein were linked to more new atrial fibrillation cases and larger left atria. Among people who already had the rhythm disorder, high levels also marked higher risk of heart failure and death. Adding the protein to fibroblasts pushed them toward a scarring behavior.
pmc-13478179:
Eduard Petrosyan and coauthors published a 2026 study of PHGDH, an enzyme that starts serine production in cells, and its unexpected role in low-oxygen lung tumors. Oxygen-poor regions resist radiotherapy, so researchers hunt for metabolic weak points. Patient datasets linked higher enzyme levels with known low-oxygen gene patterns, and lab-grown lung cancer cells raised the enzyme when oxygen dropped.

Removing the enzyme with gene editing did not make cells more radiation-sensitive when serine and glycine were available in the medium. Sensitivity appeared only under complete removal of those nutrients. Surprisingly, enzyme loss helped cells tolerate low oxygen, with faster sugar fermentation, more lactate output, and stronger activity of a key oxygen-response factor. The authors warn that blocking this enzyme could backfire unless nutrient conditions are controlled.
pmc-13478479:
Ante Plečaš and coauthors published a 2026 study comparing brain cell development in Down syndrome across human tissue and stem cell models. Down syndrome, caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21, is the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability. The team grew neurons from matched stem cells that differed only in chromosome 21 count, including three-dimensional cortico-striatal assemblies.

Cells with three copies formed clumped cell bodies tied together by thick neurite bundles, unlike the even networks of normal cells. Their neurites were shorter, wider, and less branched, with fewer endpoints. Energy organelles looked abnormal, synaptic markers ran low, and cell spheres stayed smaller. The same shape problems appeared in fetal and postnatal human brain tissue, supporting the models as faithful tools for studying the condition.
pmc-13478879:
Liu and colleagues in China reviewed in 2026 nickel based anode stocks for potassium ion batteries, a cheap stand in for lithium cells. Potassium is rich in the earth, and its cells suit grid scale storage. Nickel compounds hold much charge on paper, but two flaws block their use. They swell a lot as potassium ions move in and out, and they pass electrons poorly, which slows charge.

The review sorts the field by kind: nickel oxides, sulfides, selenides, and more, down to mixed metal forms. For each, it weighs test scores from the newest lab work. Three fix paths stand out across the set: wrap grains in carbon, shrink parts to nano scale, and shape the inner build with care. Blends that mix all three scored best. The authors close with the gaps that stay, chiefly swell control over long cycle lives.
pmc-13479579:
Dongling Lian and coauthors published a 2026 cross-cultural audit of allergic rhinitis videos on YouTube and Bilibili, the Chinese platform. More than 500 million people live with this condition, and video sites are now first stops for health advice. The team pulled the top 200 videos per platform from January 2022 to January 2025, then applied exclusion rules.

The final set held 240 videos, 91 from YouTube and 149 from Bilibili. Trained scales scored understandability, information quality, and overall quality. Engagement counts and posting seasons were compared with real-world allergy seasons to see whether uploads chase symptom peaks. The comparison exposes how two platform cultures handle the same disease, and where misleading or low-quality content concentrates.
pmc-13479979:
Shraddha Khanke and co-authors report a 2026 study of a learner-led teaching method called SNAPPS in pathology training. Thirty-five residents at three levels of training took part. SNAPPS asks learners to sum up a case, narrow the choices, weigh the options, ask questions, plan next steps, and set their own study goals.

Scores on choice-based tests rose after the teaching at every level, with the largest gains in the third year. Checklist scores for the first five SNAPPS steps rose from a median of 3 to 4, while the self-study step rose from 1 to 2. More than nine in ten feedback replies were positive, though time pressure was a concern. Readers gain a clear test of a structured format for case teaching in pathology.
pmc-13480079:
Ken Kojo and co-authors describe a 2026 early-phase trial of a short treatment course before surgery for advanced lower rectal cancer. Fifteen patients got five days of focused radiation paired with two drugs, S-1 and irinotecan, over two weeks. The aim was to find the highest safe dose of irinotecan for later use in full pre-surgery therapy plans.

All patients finished the course. At the top dose every patient hit dose-limiting harm, so that level marked the ceiling. At the middle dose two of six patients hit such harm, and the team set that level as the dose to carry forward. Diarrhoea was the most common severe side effect. Among eleven who had surgery, all had clean margins, and most tumours had shrunk in stage. Three patients showed full clearing on scans and skipped surgery. A larger trial can now test the chosen dose.
pmc-13483379:
Sun and co-authors field-tested a new bracing system for deep digging in soft city ground, where nearby metro tunnels rule out anchors drilled outward. Their 2026 study examined inclined steel-composite piles set at 45 degrees, paired with deep-mixed soil columns, at a Nanjing excavation about six to seven meters deep. Load tests pushed three piles to failure while sensors tracked the pit walls during construction.

The test piles carried between 1,350 and 2,090 kilonewtons before failing, settling only about 14 to 15 millimeters under load. Wall movement peaked at just 6.36 millimeters, far less than conventional unsupported designs allow in comparable ground. Extrapolation suggested the piles could ultimately hold much more than the failing loads measured. Sun concludes the slanted bracing changed the wall into a better-supported structure and offers the numbers as a design benchmark.
pmc-13483479:
Yan Wang and co-authors describe a 2026 study of how white spot syndrome virus, the scourge of farmed shrimp and crayfish, bends the cell's power plants to its will. Working in red claw crayfish, the team found the virus switches on mitophagy, the disposal of worn mitochondria, through one of its own proteins, wsv156.

That protein gathers mitochondria into clumps and calls in the cell's tagging machinery to start disposal. A second viral protein then jams the final shredding step, freezing the clean-up halfway. The stalled state pays the virus twice: sugar burning speeds up to feed new virus building, and cell suicide stays suppressed so the factory keeps running. Few animal viruses show such precise two-handed control of cell upkeep, and the lead protein offers a target for future defences.
pmc-13483579:
Alozie Emeonye leads a 2026 prospective study of eye damage from high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy at a teaching hospital in Owerri, Nigeria. One hundred fifty antenatal patients enrolled between March and December 2023 received physical and eye examinations. The team then tested whether retinal changes tracked with outcomes for mother and baby.

Retinopathy, meaning damage to blood vessels at the back of the eye, appeared in 58.7 percent of participants. Its presence correlated significantly with maternal seizures, early delivery, and low birthweight. No clear link appeared for delivery method, overall newborn outcome, or Apgar score. Because an eye exam is quick and noninvasive, the authors suggest retinal findings can flag pregnancies needing closer watch, alongside stronger maternal and child health education.
pmc-13483679:
Yuletta Adny Ambarsari and co-authors report surgical results for a four-part congenital heart defect in a developing country setting. Published in 2026, the retrospective cohort reviews 43 patients who had complete repair between April 2024 and April 2025. Records capture age, nutrition, oxygen levels, bypass times, hospital stay, complications, and deaths.

Most children arrived late, at a mean age above nine years, with two thirds underweight and most showing low blood oxygen. Deaths reached 11.6 percent overall and occurred only in children under two years old. Narrowing below the pulmonary valve lengthened bypass times. Limited intensive care capacity and late referral likely worsened results. The authors argue that late repair should still proceed, since careful preparation and aftercare can bring outcomes closer to global norms.
pmc-13484879:
Jake Grange and co-workers review if forms filled in by patients steer care choices in joint diseases marked by swelling. Their 2026 review searches four databases to February 2025. It covers three diseases: rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and axial spondyloarthritis. From near seventeen thousand records, 29 studies made the cut, most on the first disease.

The forms helped care in three ways. Most often, they guided drug changes in treat-to-target plans. They also aided talk in clinic visits and checks done at home. Staff followed form-based plans less well for complex patients. Home checks matched standard care results, though thin services cut their worth. Scores also built trust between patients and staff. Wide gaps in how forms are used waste much of what patients report.
pmc-13486679:
Simegn and a large team charted how blood sugar control evolves in Ethiopian patients who carry both type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure, a pairing that multiplies complication risk. Their 2026 study pulled records for 600 such patients followed at Debre Markos hospital between 2014 and 2023. A flexible statistical model traced each patient's glycated hemoglobin, the three-month average sugar marker, over years of visits.

Average glycated hemoglobin ran high compared with the target range of the American Diabetes Association cited by the authors. Seven factors predicted worse trajectories, including injected medication use, obesity, kidney damage, heavier weight, and family history of diabetes. Uncontrolled blood pressure and more than six years of treatment also tracked poorer control over time. Simegn recommends tighter combined management of sugar and pressure rather than treating the two conditions in separate silos.
pmc-13487679:
Tiffany Tu and Alejandro Ochoa warn that pooling genome studies can quietly break when the studies share relatives. Published in 2026, the theory and simulation work starts from a live proposal to fix participation bias with sex-stratified pooling, which ignores that men and women from one population are heavily related. Between-study relatedness correlates test statistics and inflates false positives.

Simulations across family and population structures show ordinary pooling inflating badly whenever family links cross study borders, with inflation growing as samples grow. Genomic control patches the symptom yet costs real power in high-signal settings. The authors' correlated meta-analysis method, shipped as the metalcor package, models the correlation directly and restores calibration. Real data confirm severe inflation inside family studies and negligible effects in population studies up to ten thousand people.
pmc-13488279:
Shuyuan Zhang and co-authors build an artificial intelligence tool to spot cardiac amyloidosis in a 2026 multicenter study from China. The disease thickens the heart wall as abnormal protein deposits build up, and it is often mistaken for other causes of thickening. Heart tracings and ultrasound measures came from a Beijing hospital cohort, with patients from ten other hospitals held back for outside testing, and a learning system combined eleven model types.
