Seven features carried the diagnosis, mixing tracing measures, wall thickness, blood pressure, and pumping indices. The combined model separated amyloidosis from its mimics with very high accuracy, and performance held up in the outside hospitals in the reported tests. A simplified score built from the same features also performed well for bedside use.
pmc-13488579:
Shala Cunningham and colleagues evaluate stroke rehabilitation training for physiotherapists in Myanmar in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Conflict and disruption have cut access to rehabilitation, although stroke is a leading cause of disability worldwide. Seventeen professionals took blended training mixing online coursework, live mentoring, and hands-on clinical sessions, with surveys before training, after each stage, and at six months, judged against a four-level training evaluation model.

Self-rated knowledge and skill rose significantly, strongest for methods needing little equipment in the reported comparisons. Follow-up surveys showed evidence-based assessment and treatment entering routine practice for many participants. Seven therapists joined focus groups at six months to explain how changes held under local constraints. The authors present the tailored design as a model for fragile settings.
pmc-13490379:
Sun and co-authors sped up the scheduling mathematics for neighborhoods that share electricity and heat with each other. Community energy systems juggle power, heating, and cooling, and sharing between communities raises efficiency, but central scheduling is slow and exposes private data. Their 2026 study built a day-ahead stochastic model, which plans under green-power uncertainty, with dynamic prices set by an operator. They solved it with a new distributed algorithm that splits the problem apart.

Case simulations showed the sharing model and pricing scheme cut operating costs and carbon emissions for individual communities and the whole system. The new algorithm converged faster than the standard distributed approach it improves on, according to the comparisons reported. Privacy survives because each community solves its own sub-problem and exchanges only limited signals. Sun presents the scheme as ready for multi-community energy markets.
pmc-13491579:
Hai Wang and four co-authors examine a 2026 multicenter records study on blood pressure medicines during acute kidney injury. Drugs called ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers protect the heart and kidneys long term, yet doctors disagree about stopping them when kidneys fail suddenly. The authors sorted patients by whether these medicines were stopped, continued, or newly started.

The records covered 1,285 patients across several hospitals. People who stayed on the medicines had lower odds of kidney injury worsening within fourteen days than people who stopped them. A survival advantage seen before adjustment faded once other factors were counted, and starting the drugs looked no different from stopping them. The authors call for prospective trials because deaths were few and estimates were unstable.
pmc-13491679:
Eglė Šidlauskaitė and four colleagues set out in 2026 to derive bonding radii, the standard sizes chemists assign to atoms when deciding which atoms in a crystal are bonded. X-ray crystallography gives atom positions but rarely shows bonds directly, so distance rules do the everyday work. Existing radius sets lean on a commercial database or on hand-adjusted values, which limits open checking.

Their unsupervised workflow learns radii from crystal structures in the free Crystallography Open Database instead. Two atoms count as bonded when their distance is no more than the sum of their radii plus a small tolerance. Published sets can disagree by more than an angstrom for some elements, so an openly derived set matters. The paper lays out the method and the resulting radii for reuse by other researchers.
pmc-13492279:
Leonardo Bernal and eight colleagues combine chemistry software with machine learning in 2026 to hunt for old drugs that might fight aggressive prostate cancer. Advanced, treatment-resistant disease still kills many men, and repurposed medicines arrive with known safety records. Their workflow filtered candidates by chemical similarity and used applicability checks to weed out false leads before laboratory testing.

Screening the DrugBank library produced five candidates that slowed cancer cell growth in both flat cultures and three-dimensional models. An antifungal medicine, chlormidazole, performed best, acting mainly by pausing cell division rather than killing cells outright, and sparing non-cancer cells comparatively. It raised a cell-cycle brake protein and pushed cells into arrest. Chlormidazole also boosted the chemotherapy drug docetaxel, matching its effect at much lower docetaxel doses.
pmc-13493779:
Lavecchia and colleagues map how stress is arranged inside the rocks of peninsular Italy, work that feeds directly into earthquake hazard estimates. Their 2026 study rests on roughly 8,200 measurements of fault slip, the scratches and offsets left where rock masses slid past each other, gathered at outcrops across the country. From these they rebuilt the directions and relative sizes of underground stresses over roughly the last three and a half million years.

The team outline a belt of stretching crust about 1,000 kilometres long running through the Apennines, where the ground is being pulled apart. Stress directions form nested arcs at several scales, from single faults up to the whole crust, and they bend in line with the deep boundary beneath the crust. Modern earthquake records and satellite measures of ground movement point the same way, suggesting the old pattern still drives today's deformation.
pmc-13493879:
Joerg F Hipp leads a nine-author team probing in 2026 a brainwave signature of Dup15q syndrome, a rare genetic condition causing developmental delay, autism features, and epilepsy. Extra copies of a chromosome segment overload certain calming receptors, and children's brain recordings show unusually strong beta rhythms as a result. The team isolated that rhythm cleanly from background noise in fifty-two affected children and fourteen typically developing peers.

The beta excess was large, nearly two standard effect sizes above typical children. Among children without epilepsy, stronger excess meant lower cognitive scores and weaker everyday adaptive skills, both correlations solidly significant. That dose relationship supports the idea that overactive calming receptors drive real functional loss, not just a pretty signal. A measurable brainwave that tracks severity could help future trials judge whether treatments actually help.
pmc-13494079:
Shunming Zhang and co-authors ask, in a 2026 cohort study, whether people whose lab results clash with their body mass index face a different risk of heart failure. Body mass index, or BMI, gauges weight for height but says little about inner health. The team used UK Biobank data on 394,198 adults. They grouped people by how far markers such as blood sugar, blood fats, and C-reactive protein, a sign of inflammation, sat from what their BMI would predict.

Over a median follow-up past twelve years, groups whose inflammation or blood sugar ran worse than BMI suggested developed heart failure more often, in both men and women. Some other groups, such as women with higher than expected blood pressure, showed lower risk. Liver enzyme groups showed no clear link. The authors argue that sorting people by these marker patterns could sharpen efforts to prevent heart failure.
pmc-13495279:
Sufen Wang and colleagues run, in a 2026 randomized study, a teaching trial that blends problem-based learning with medical humanities in a pathology lab course. The course went to anesthesiology undergraduates at a Chinese medical university. Four classes were assigned by lot: two got the blended model and two got standard lecture-based teaching, with 115 students in all.

Both groups improved on theory exams, and final theory scores did not split clearly between them. A microscope image test leaned toward the blended group without quite reaching the bar for proof. Blended students did score higher on drive to learn, self-directed study skill, and communication, and they rated the teaching better overall. Ethics awareness and social responsibility scores did not differ. The authors offer the blend as a reference for reforming lab teaching, with gains in engagement rather than raw exam points.
pmc-13499879:
Zwirner and colleagues explore whether squeezing the spleen can tell forensic doctors how long someone has been dead. Temperature-based methods fail once a body equilibrates with its surroundings, leaving a gap at longer intervals. Their 2026 study collected spleen samples from 53 adult cadavers, spanning roughly two days to three weeks after death. The team measured the tissue's squishiness with an instrument that wiggles samples and records how they store and lose energy.

One measure, the loss modulus, which captures how much energy the tissue dissipates, fell significantly as time since death grew, while the storage measures showed no useful pattern. A threshold value on that measure gave strong evidence for death within about 200 hours, performing well on the authors' diagnostic accuracy analysis. The team presents spleen mechanics as a promising addition to the time-of-death toolkit, pending larger studies.
pmc-13500079:
Austin Erickson, Jennifer Griffith, and Trushar Patel chart in 2026 when and where urology conferences gather across the United States, using public listings from 2022 to 2025. Conferences anchor education, networking, and research sharing in the specialty, yet their calendars had never been mapped. Working from a Florida medical school, the team collected events from organiser sites and calendars, recording dates, frequency, and location for each meeting.

Eighty-five organisations held 293 events across the four years. Texas and California hosted the most, and the Western regional section led the sections, followed by the Southeast and South Central. Meetings lengthened slightly on average, and autumn dominated the calendar, with October the busiest month and July the quietest by a wide margin. The authors suggest spreading events more evenly across months and regions to ease scheduling clashes and improve access.
pmc-13500379:
Miku Goto and co-authors profile in 2026 the liver enzymes that break down drugs in squirrels, a group frequently treated with veterinary medicines despite almost no baseline data on their metabolism. The team combined gene sequencing, gene expression measurement, and functional tests on liver microsomes, tiny cell fragments carrying the enzymes, focusing on two enzyme families central to foreign chemical handling. Three squirrel species were compared with mouse and rat laboratory rodents, using the flea treatment fipronil as a test substance.

No clear squirrel-specific loss or major divergence appeared in the two focal enzyme families, and fipronil breakdown efficiency did not differ significantly among the species examined in the reported analysis. Wider expression profiling did show distinct patterns, with one enzyme family making up under one percent of major expression in the Eurasian red squirrel, below rodent levels. The work supplies baseline data for comparative wildlife drug metabolism studies.
pmc-13501779:
Mario Giuseppe Zotti leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 diagnostic study linking electrical nerve tests to muscle wasting seen on MRI in chronic lower back problems. The cohort took 100 consecutive eligible patients with chronic lumbar symptoms, drawn from 119 who underwent electrodiagnostic testing. Needle electromyography sorted them into confirmed chronic lumbar radiculopathy, a pinched or damaged nerve root condition, versus a symptomatic control group with normal electrical findings. Two independent observers graded multifidus muscle atrophy on MRI using a modified Goutallier scale and fat measurements.

Atrophy appeared in 98 percent of the confirmed radiculopathy group but also in 64 percent of the symptomatic controls, a significant gap with an odds ratio of 27.2 on that comparison. Grading showed most confirmed cases at mild to moderate levels, with 11 percent at the severe grade 3, which never appeared among controls. The authors propose the wasting pattern as a supporting biomarker, not proof on its own.
pmc-13504779:
Xiangyang Li and three colleagues ask how few muscle sensors a rehab glove system needs to read hand gestures, in a 2026 study. Wearable muscle-signal gear often uses eight or more channels, which adds bulk, power draw, and discomfort. Fewer channels would ease daily use if accuracy holds.

Their check plan rests on clean signal capture, a full search of all channel subsets from six sites, and stress tests with degraded signals. Data came from 24 healthy adults, judged by leaving one person out in turn. Three channels passed a 90 percent accuracy bar on average but failed badly for some users. Four channels scored higher and left no user stranded. The winning four sites sit on forearm muscles that drive the wrist.
pmc-13504979:
Timms and colleagues ran a feasibility study for a bigger question: can painting silver diamine fluoride on children's rotten baby teeth beat usual NHS dental care? The fluoride compound arrests decay without drilling, a prize for treating small children, but a trial inside British practices faces recruitment and retention hurdles. Their 2026 study randomised children aged one to eight with decay across eight practices, following them for a year and interviewing families and dentists.

Eight sites recruited 54 children, and nearly every eligible family approached agreed to join, an encouraging sign for willingness. The obstacles lay elsewhere: recruitment ran slower than the team planned, and keeping the randomised allocation intact inside busy practices proved tricky. The standard decay-scoring system also looked weak as the main outcome measure. Their verdict is a conditional yes: a definitive trial is feasible, with slower timelines, stronger randomisation support, and a better primary outcome.
pmc-13508279:
Zhengqing Bao, Jiaqi An, Guizhong Li, and Jianwei Wang pool studies on whether a simple blood ratio forecasts survival in urinary tract cancers, in 2026 work. The ratio compares fibrinogen, a clotting protein tied to inflammation, with albumin, a nutrition-linked protein. Earlier pooling had covered bladder and kidney cancers only thinly. The team searched three databases through March 2026 and found six studies with 1,603 patients in all. They combined risk figures for overall, cancer-specific, and disease-free survival.

Patients with a high ratio before surgery fared worse on every survival measure. The combined risk of death was more than double that of patients with lower ratios. The pattern held when kidney cancer and bladder cancer were judged apart. Disease-free survival also suffered in the high-ratio group. The authors argue this ratio offers a cheap warning sign for planning follow-up after surgery.
pmc-13510279:
Yuyang Wei, Weijie Fei, Jiarong Wang, and Luzheng Bi present Mechanics-AI, an open-source system that pairs physics simulation with machine learning for engineering design, in 2026 work. Direct simulation gives clear physical answers yet runs slowly and ignores real-world context, while machine learning runs fast yet needs much data and hides its reasoning. The design copies living bodies, where sensors read physical signals and the brain places them in context.

A first learning layer stands in for costly simulations, producing readable measures such as stress, strain, and heat or moisture fields. A second layer blends those measures with outside data to predict outcomes and suggest designs. The system tests eight methods, keeps the best for each task, and shows which physical factors drove each answer. Trials spanned brain injury prediction, a tissue-growth device, and low-carbon building design with recycled concrete.
pmc-13512979:
D'Amato and colleagues tested two things in hospitalized heart failure patients. First, whether a staging system called HLM, which grades heart, lung, and multiorgan involvement, predicts outcomes. Second, whether starting an SGLT2 inhibitor drug during the hospital stay helps at every stage. Their 2026 prospective multicenter study enrolled 711 consecutive patients admitted between late 2022 and mid 2025 and followed them for six months.

D'Amato found the combined endpoint of cardiovascular death or heart failure readmission in 82 patients, rising clearly with each HLM stage. Each stage step carried roughly forty percent higher risk regardless of drug status. Starting the SGLT2 inhibitor during the index admission was independently linked to about forty percent lower endpoint risk. The drug class also protects kidneys and metabolism, and benefit showed no weakening in advanced stages. The authors support combining whole-body staging with early drug initiation in routine heart failure care.
pmc-13515479:
Md Imran Hossain, Sitansu Sekhar Nanda, and Dong Kee Yi review, in a 2026 article, surface-engineered magnetic nanoparticles for rebuilding skeletal muscle. Lost or damaged muscle needs scaffolds that copy its aligned fibres, softness, and high energy use, and ordinary cell culture falls short. Tiny magnetic particles, tuned by their coatings, answer outside magnets without contact, which opens several tricks at once.

The review covers coating choices, both organic and inorganic, and the weaving of particles into scaffolds that respond to magnets. Aligned fields can line muscle cells up, guide stem cells and drugs to a target, and stiffen or move a construct on cue. Magnetic resonance imaging can then watch the implant without cutting. Hossain's team weighs the safety record and the body's handling of the particles. Regulation and long-term fate remain the gates between this platform and patients.
pmc-13516679:
Biondi and colleagues profiled oxidative stress and inflammation in horses naturally infected with Theileria equi, a tick-borne parasite that lives inside red blood cells and causes equine piroplasmosis. Their 2026 study enrolled thirty-five infected horses and twenty healthy controls, confirming infection by antibody testing and gene amplification. Measuring inflammatory signals plus markers of cell damage and antioxidant reserves in blood.

Biondi found infected horses had lower platelet counts and higher liver enzyme activity than controls. Two inflammatory messengers were clearly raised, showing persistent immune activation, while a damage marker from fat oxidation rose and the key antioxidant glutathione fell, consistent with worn-down defenses. The damage marker tracked with clinical severity scores and lower red cell counts, and antioxidant levels fell as white cell counts rose. The authors conclude chronic infection couples oxidative stress with sustained inflammation, and combined markers could help monitor disease and treatment.
pmc-13518479:
Xuan Xuan Song and four colleagues open the mail of a parasitic tapeworm larva in a 2026 study. Spirometra mansoni larvae burrow through human tissue, causing blindness or paralysis, and biopsy diagnosis is hard. Like many parasites, the larvae shed extracellular vesicles, tiny membrane parcels. The team cultured larvae, harvested the vesicles, and profiled their proteins and small RNAs.

The parcels measured eighty to one hundred fifty nanometres and carried the classic vesicle markers. Their protein cargo ran to twenty-seven hundred entries, rich in transport, secretion, and signalling roles. The RNA haul held thirty-seven known and one hundred eighteen new microRNAs, with targets touching cell death, cholesterol handling, and host interplay. Rabbit serum against the vesicles stirred a mixed but mainly Th1-style immune answer. Song's team offers the catalogue as a base for diagnostics and for decoding how the larva talks to its host.
pmc-13518879:
Chengming Ma and six colleagues build a mechanics-based method in 2026 for choosing how fast to flow back fracturing fluid from coalbed methane wells. Crews today pick rates by experience, which transfers poorly between wells. Flowing too fast drags out proppant sand and coal fines, damaging the fractures that carry gas.

Their model balances forces on particles before and after fracture closure, using measurable inputs such as particle size, fluid thickness, and pressure difference. Calculations for two wells gave critical proppant velocities spanning wide ranges depending on closure stage. Particle size, density, and pressure difference dominated the results. Ma and co-authors offer the workflow as a screening tool, openly noting no new lab validation.
pmc-13518979:
Barbara Szymanik, Sam Ang Keo, Franck Brachelet, and Didier Defer refine in 2026 a harmless way to find steel rebar hidden inside concrete. Crews must locate rebar and judge its state without harming buildings. Their method heats the concrete with microwaves and watches the surface with an infrared camera, since steel warms at another rate than concrete.

The study pairs fine computer models of a microwave source, broadband antenna, and steel-laced concrete block with matching bench tests. How the source fired and how the antenna sat against the sample both shaped the heat patterns on the surface. Matching mock and real heat maps, the team works toward settings that make rebar spotting precise and repeatable.
pmc-13520379:
Sylvester R Groen and colleagues compare in 2026 three questionnaires for adults living with faecal incontinence, asking whether a broader well-being measure adds anything beyond symptom and quality-of-life scales. Patients often value independence and stability, not only fewer accidents.

Data came from 72 trial participants, mostly women, with an average age near 67 years. The capability measure scored higher on its scale than the generic health measure and showed good agreement with related scores. Each tool separated known groups somewhat differently, with no single winner across all checks. Clinicians gain guidance on matching questionnaire choice to the question asked.
pmc-13522479:
Nawab John Dar, David Soriano-Castell, and Pamela Maher describe a long-lasting stress state in nerve cells exposed to excess iron in a 2026 laboratory study. Iron builds up in brain areas harmed by Alzheimer and Parkinson diseases, yet the effect of prolonged exposure was unclear. Cultured neuronal cells received either a brief exposure of hours or a chronic exposure lasting nine days.

Brief exposure caused little change and did not make cells more fragile. Chronic exposure raised iron-storage protein, damaged fat molecules, depleted a key protective chemical, and lowered a protective enzyme, while cells stayed alive. Those chronically stressed cells then died more easily when faced with further oxidative challenges. The authors name the state chronoferroptosis and present it as an early vulnerability stage.
pmc-13522879:
Juan Pablo Frias wrote a practical guide for doctors on spotting and treating hypercortisolism, a state of excess cortisol, the body's stress hormone. The guide aims at hard cases hiding inside stubborn type 2 diabetes, resistant high blood pressure, and adrenal growths.

A simple overnight drug test, where a steroid pill should switch cortisol off, forms the guide's main case-finding tool. Confirmed excess appears in under 4 percent of broad diabetes groups, but about one in four patients in selected high-risk groups fail the test. Mild cortisol excess without classic Cushing signs still raises blood pressure, diabetes, belly fat, and death risk. Surgery cures best when the source can be cut out, and Frias details drug options when it cannot.
pmc-13523279:
Chen Xu and colleagues describe a modified technique for placing an iliac branch device through the same-side leg artery in a 2026 two-center study. Branch devices preserve blood flow to the internal iliac artery during aneurysm repair, yet standard access routes can fail in patients with short or difficult anatomy. Twenty-three patients treated between 2023 and 2024, in whom the opposite leg route was judged unsuitable, received the balloon-anchored approach.

Deployment succeeded in every case, with the branch artery open and no major leaks on early imaging. At one year, the main device was open in all patients and the bridging stent in nearly all. No related reoperations were needed over a median sixteen months. Two minor complications occurred, supporting the technique as feasible for selected difficult anatomies.
pmc-13523379:
Jolanta Guz and colleagues follow chemical changes in DNA during chemotherapy for breast cancer in a 2026 study. Seventy-one patients received standard drug treatment before surgery, with blood and urine collected at four points and tumor tissue taken at operation. Levels of methylcytosine and its oxidized derivatives were measured by advanced chromatography, and activity of the genes that drive this demethylation pathway was assessed.

During treatment, several derivative levels in white blood cell DNA rose, while expression of the pathway genes fell. Patients whose pre-treatment levels of one derivative were lower in blood and urine, and whose tumors showed a particular post-treatment pattern, fared better over six years of follow-up. The authors link the pathway's behavior during therapy to disease-free and overall survival, suggesting prognostic value.
pmc-13523479:
Daryna Maruniak and colleagues examine, in a 2026 retrospective cohort study, risk factors for massive bleeding after heart transplantation. The operation remains the standard for end-stage heart failure, yet heavy bleeding afterward raises illness and transfusion needs. Predictors, especially from bedside clot testing, were poorly described.

The single-center study included 75 adults transplanted between 2019 and 2025 who had preoperative ClotPro viscoelastic testing. Massive bleeding, defined by a standard bleeding scale, occurred in 31 patients, about four in ten. Transfusion use was high, and about one in six patients needed reoperation for bleeding. Many factors linked with bleeding in simple analyses, but only a clot firmness measure from the EX test stayed independent in adjusted analysis. The authors propose it for early risk flagging.
pmc-13524079:
Basu and colleagues showed in 2026 that two plant regulators best known for nitrate sensing also hold back sulfate uptake, linking two nutrient pathways in thale cress. Nitrogen and sulfur work together in crops, but the wiring between their control systems was largely unknown. The regulators, transcription factors TGA1 and TGA4, sit in the nitrate response cascade and also play roles in immunity.

Adding nitrate quickly raised sulfate uptake and use, then a delayed brake cut activity of the main sulfate transporter, and that brake required TGA1 and TGA4. Both factors bind the transporter's control region and dampen it directly. Plants missing both factors took up more sulfate, built more of the amino acid cysteine, and fared better under long sulfur shortage, while sulfur defense compounds also shifted. The authors say the pair keeps nutrient intake in balance and may help breed crops that use fertilizer better.
pmc-13526479:
Fernandez Placencia and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of eosinophilic cellulitis, or Wells syndrome, a rare skin inflammation that mimics bacterial infection. Their patient, a 72-year-old woman with lupus and other autoimmune conditions, first received antibiotics for red, swollen legs and seemed to improve. Three days after finishing the course she returned with itchy red plaques across arms and legs, swelling, and pain, and antihistamines did not help.

Blood tests showed a raised count of eosinophils, a white cell type tied to allergy and inflammation, and a high sedimentation rate, a general inflammation marker. A skin punch biopsy found eosinophil-rich inflammation around and between vessels, matching Wells syndrome, and steroid treatment brought improvement. The authors stress that recurrent cellulitis-like eruptions that answer antibiotics only briefly deserve an early biopsy, since clinic and lab correlation is what separates this mimic from true infection.
pmc-13527479:
Liyang Duan and Xianjie Wu describe, in a 2026 case report, treating a child's severe contact dermatitis from lacquer tree exposure with abrocitinib, a targeted immune drug. Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed T-cell reaction, and standard care relies on avoidance, topical steroids, calamine, and antihistamines, which can fall short in children with widespread disease.

An eight-year-old boy developed intensely itchy red papules and plaques over trunk and limbs for ten days after exposure to Toxicodendron vernicifluum. Three days of topical steroid, emollients, and an antihistamine failed as the rash spread to his face, with a severity score in the severe range. His parents declined systemic steroids over growth concerns, so after counseling the team started daily oral abrocitinib plus nightly cetirizine. Photographs chart facial clearing by day three and near resolution by day eleven.
pmc-13527979:
Emma J. Steel and seven colleagues report a 2026 qualitative evaluation of software that flags chest X-rays for priority reading in a Scottish NHS board. The qXR program from Qure.ai aims to speed lung cancer detection. Staff and patients were asked how acceptable they found it. Sixteen staff took part in interviews before and after rollout. Eight service users joined focus groups.

Staff saw the tool as a helpful adjunct that could shorten the path to scans and treatment. Patients also welcomed faster answers. They preferred brief anxiety with prompt action over long uncertainty. Radiology staff worried about accuracy, over-trust, and biased decisions. The authors say adoption will hold only if the tool fits existing systems and keeps proving itself.
pmc-13528079:
Nicholas C. Nicolaides, James Bradford Kline, and Luigi Grasso develop a blocker drug against a cancer shield protein in a 2026 study. Many tumors release CA125, a protein that coats treatment antibodies. Coated antibodies cannot trigger immune killing well. The team engineered fusion proteins to grab CA125 tightly. Their lead design, NAV-005, bound it with high strength.

In cell tests NAV-005 kept CA125 off treatment antibodies. Immune cells then killed targets at full strength again. A second killing route, driven by complement proteins, also recovered. Antibody-drug conjugates slipped past the shield too. They entered cancer cells and killed as intended. The authors say such blockers could rescue many existing antibody drugs. Clinical testing is the next step they propose.
pmc-13531079:
Jeffrey Yim and colleagues report in 2026 the catheter retrieval of a leg vein stent that migrated into the heart and straddled a valve. The 38-year-old patient felt palpitations and breathlessness one day after vein treatment. Imaging showed the stent crossing the tricuspid valve, causing severe leakage and brief dangerous rhythm bursts.

Two snares, one from each leg vein, gripped both stent ends under ultrasound guidance from within the food pipe, with surgeons standing by. Removal left only mild leakage and no fluid around the heart. The patient recovered smoothly, avoiding open surgery.
pmc-13534179:
Lei Luo and colleagues review in 2026 a long non-coding RNA called HIF1A-AS2 and its role across many human cancers. The RNA does not build proteins, yet raised levels appear in many tumour types and link to poor outlook. Lab studies tie it to cell growth, spread, drug resistance, and cell death control.

The RNA can sponge up smaller RNAs or bind proteins directly, lifting cancer traits through several paths. The review compares patterns across 12 cancer types and weighs barriers to clinical use. Readers see why this RNA draws interest as a diagnostic mark and drug target.
pmc-13536579:
Yunho Jeong and colleagues describe in 2026 a rare skin B-cell lymphoma in a 12-year-old spayed female Shih Tzu dog. Skin B-cell lymphoma is extremely rare in dogs, so single cases still shape what vets know. The dog showed many nodules under the skin across the body.

Stains and flow tests confirmed B-cell type with clonal gene changes, while liver and spleen sampling found no spread. Standard four-drug chemotherapy brought only a brief partial response before fast progression. The case warns that this rare form can behave aggressively and resist usual treatment.
pmc-13536679:
Megha Anand leads a 2026 randomized trial comparing two hands-on approaches for tight hamstrings in desk-based computer workers. Thirty information technology professionals were split evenly between static stretching and myofascial release, a pressure-based soft tissue technique. Each group trained five times a week for three weeks. Knee extension range and a self-rated leg function scale were measured at the start and on three later days.

Both groups gained range and function over the three weeks, with no harmful events reported. Stretching produced slightly larger gains in knee extension by the second and third checks. The authors note those gaps were smaller than the smallest change the knee test can reliably detect, so the practical edge remains unclear. Function gains were also close between groups, and the short follow-up without a control group limits firm conclusions.
pmc-13538379:
Rajesh Kannan Megalingam and Naveen Prasaad Selvarajan present a hybrid network for predicting pedestrian crossing intent on Indian roads in a 2026 study. Crowded, unstructured streets with frequent blocking views and rule-bending walkers challenge models trained abroad. The design mixes image and graph networks with a gate that shifts weight between visual and motion clues by scene, plus a pose tool tuned for distant or partly hidden walkers. A new local road collection supports testing.

Accuracy reached moderate levels on both a standard foreign collection and the new Indian collection, with the fastest response times among compared methods. Extra tests covered blocked views, walker sizes, and cross-collection transfer, plus a run on a small onboard computer showing near real-time speed. The authors argue the trade-off suits driverless use in messy traffic.
pmc-13538479:
Hyun-Jeong Yang and colleagues test a metabolic nutrient for myelin repair after teen social isolation in mice in a 2026 study. Isolation after weaning thins myelin in a social brain hub and dulls sociability. The nutrient, acetyl-L-carnitine, links energy and fat handling. Dish tests traced uptake and conversion in myelin-making cells, while feeding tests in isolated mice checked behavior, myelin protein, and fat profiles in a major white matter tract.

In dishes, the nutrient widened myelin sheaths without boosting early cell growth, switched on growth signals, and raised breathing power in mature cells. Feeding restored social preference and myelin protein in isolated mice, while a myelin poison erased those gains. Fat chain patterns in the tract also normalized. The authors frame the nutrient as a metabolic lever for myelin disorders.
pmc-13539879:
Heidi Kruit, Mika Gissler, and Leena Rahkonen analyse, in a 2026 cohort study, how the reason for starting labour artificially relates to how the birth turns out. Inductions keep rising as mothers get older and heavier, so clinicians need reason-specific evidence.

Hospital records from Helsinki covered 16,377 induced births at term between 2017 and 2021. Going past the due date and waters breaking early were the commonest reasons. Caesarean rates peaked when induction followed blood pressure disorders, while poor newborn outcomes clustered in inductions done for fetal concerns. First-time motherhood, an unready cervix, older age, shorter height, and higher body weight each raised caesarean risk.
pmc-13540279:
Annagowni and colleagues review nanotechnology platforms that combine ultrasound and photoacoustic imaging with treatment, an approach called theranostics, in 2026 medical research. Photoacoustic imaging fires light pulses into tissue and listens to the faint sound waves produced, marrying light's sensitivity with sound's depth. Natural tissue components such as hemoglobin, lipids, and melanin already absorb light and give signals, but engineered nanoparticles sharpen targeting and signal strength for diseased tissue.

The review explains the physics of the combined ultrasound and photoacoustic method, lists contrast agents both natural and manufactured, and surveys uses across diseases. Designed nanomaterials can also carry drugs, so the same particle that lights up a tumor on the scan can deliver therapy to it under image guidance. Remaining difficulties include weak signals from deep tissue and proving safety of new particles. Annagowni presents the pairing as a pillar of precision nanomedicine still maturing toward routine care.
pmc-13540879:
Kristine Mørch leads a 2026 prospective study of giardiasis that refuses to clear with standard nitroimidazole drugs, an intestinal parasite infection increasingly seen in travellers. Four centres in Norway and England enrolled 120 adults between 2009 and 2024, fifty-nine of them with resistant disease.

A treatment ladder gave a repeat nitroimidazole course first, which cured only about a quarter of those who tried it. Pairing the drug with albendazole cured roughly three quarters, and quinacrine, an older medicine, worked in every case where it was used. Infection caught in India and a more recent diagnosis year predicted standard treatment failure. Parasite strain patterns varied by travel region.
pmc-13542079:
Vijay Kumar and seven colleagues run, in a 2026 engine study, a single-cylinder diesel engine on blends of Karanja biodiesel while tracking vibration alongside performance and exhaust. Biodiesel from this non-edible seed oil may cut emissions, yet shaking behaviour affects engine life and comfort.

Blends of twenty and thirty percent biodiesel were tested across loads, compression ratios, and recirculated exhaust settings. Vibration rose with load, fell with higher compression, and dipped then climbed as exhaust recirculation grew. Both blends vibrated less than plain diesel, and the stronger blend cut hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide, and smoke noticeably. Fuel efficiency dropped and nitrogen oxides rose, marking the trade-off.
pmc-13543479:
Fen Liu and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study of early-onset dyslipidemia, abnormal blood fats arising in younger adults, using health check-up data from more than 3.5 million people in northwest China during 2019. The region lacked high-quality figures of its own. Everyone received questionnaires, physical examination, and laboratory tests including a full lipid profile, allowing the team to count each abnormality type and test which traits travelled with them.

One in four participants, 25.7 percent, had dyslipidemia. Low protective cholesterol was the commonest single fault at 14.5 percent, followed by high triglycerides at 10.6 percent, while most affected people had only one abnormal measure. Male sex, older age within the adult range, diabetes, hypertension, smoking, drinking, and excess weight all raised the odds independently. Screening should focus on those combined risks, the authors conclude, even though regional prevalence sits below the national level.
pmc-13544079:
Steven Lâm and colleagues published a 2026 evaluation of OHRECA, a six-year One Health centre. It worked across several African countries from 2020 to 2025 to build capacity against diseases jumping between animals, people, and environments. Africa carries the world's heaviest load of such threats, yet how capacity programmes achieve lasting results is poorly documented. The evaluators used a realist mixed-methods design, asking not just what changed but how and why.

The centre contributed to scientific output and workforce growth in its target countries. Two mechanisms did the work: learning by doing, and genuine partnership, both sustained by long time horizons and institutions that stayed the course. With no baseline or comparison group for many outcomes, the authors present the findings as an explanatory case study rather than proof of effectiveness. They offer design lessons for similar programmes in lower-income settings.
pmc-13548579:
Vincenzo Quagliariello and colleagues review whether a class of diabetes drugs could protect the hearts and metabolism of breast cancer survivors, in a 2026 narrative review. Hormone-driven breast cancer is common, and hormone-blocking treatment saves lives while raising fat around the organs, disturbing lipids, and inflaming blood vessels. Heart disease has become a leading non-cancer killer in this group, prompting interest in sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors.

These drugs, first made to lower blood sugar, also guard the heart and kidneys. The review gathers laboratory, animal, and observational evidence that they calm insulin signaling, fat tissue inflammation, liver fat, and vessel dysfunction, and may even counter hormone therapy resistance. Matched patient studies in cancer populations are summarized with caution. The authors frame the drugs as a targeted candidate strategy needing direct trials in survivors on hormone therapy.
pmc-13550479:
Liang Zhao tests a video intelligence system that watches volleyball practice and turns what it sees into tailored drills, in a 2026 study. The pipeline detects players with a standard object detector and tracks their trajectories with a sorting algorithm. A neural network then reads body keypoints. From those it judges jump mechanics, approach angles, and arm-swing and block timing. Fifty-six competitive athletes trained for six weeks, half with the system's real-time feedback and half with standard coaching.

The supported group improved more across transition speed, serve-receive accuracy, rotation speed, defensive coverage, jump height, and timing consistency. Match-like indicators such as side-out rate and attack efficiency also rose further, and several gains survived one to two weeks later. Zhao concludes that fused trajectory and keypoint data can sharpen coaching decisions, pending tests in other venues and competitions.
pmc-13550579:
Liang Liang, with four colleagues, published a 2026 atlas of how male and female mouse brains respond differently to repeated stress. Depression is more common in women, so the team exposed mice to sub-chronic variable stress and then sequenced single nuclei from the hippocampus, a brain region tied to mood. Behavior was checked with tests for loss of pleasure.

Females showed stronger loss of pleasure and a drop in blood serotonin, while males changed little. Sequencing 31,256 cells revealed about three times as many altered genes in females, with little overlap between sexes. Female changes centered on support cells called oligodendrocytes, their energy-producing genes, and weakened oxytocin signaling, which the authors offer as leads for sex-specific depression treatments.
pmc-13551779:
Shen Chen and eight colleagues reported in 2026 on how mixing two nitrogen forms affects strawberry growth in protected cultivation. Growers know ammonium plus nitrate usually beats either form alone, yet the mechanism was unclear. Using the cultivar Benihoppe at a fixed total nitrogen level, the team varied the ammonium-to-nitrate ratio and measured growth, hormones, and gene activity.

A ratio of seven to three ammonium to nitrate promoted height and stalk growth and raised fruit yield without changing fruit size in the reported results. At the green fruit stage that mix raised auxin, cytokinin, and gibberellin levels, and gene analysis highlighted hormone signaling pathways. The authors propose the ratio coordinates nitrogen uptake with hormone signals, offering a basis for precise fertilizer management.
pmc-13551979:
José Manuel García-Heredia, Sara M Ortega-Campos, and Amancio Carnero published a 2026 study of gene splicing in tumors. The gene is called NUMB. It makes four protein versions through alternative splicing, the reshuffling of gene parts. NUMB has been cast as both tumor blocker and tumor helper. The team mined public databases for version levels in tumors and healthy tissue. They grouped samples by which versions ran high.

Two versions rose in tumors, while two others ruled healthy tissue. The two clusters tied to distinct activity in four key signaling paths. A score built on version balance split breast cancer cell lines by biology and drug response. High scores linked to worse patient survival. The team proposes version balance as a marker for precision cancer care.
pmc-13554079:
Marion Ferreira leads a seven-author team showing that how immune drugs reach the lung changes their safety and power in a 2026 mouse study. Lung cancer drugs that rouse the immune system can work well yet cause harsh side effects. The team gave three such agents through the airway or into a vein in healthy mice. They then tested one antibody given each way in mice with lung tumours.

Airway dosing spared the liver and calmed body-wide inflammation compared with vein dosing. Weight held steadier and blood markers looked calmer under airway care. Airway dosing also drew more immune cells into the lung, in step with dose. In tumour-bearing mice, airway delivery filled lungs with helper and killer cells and gave better tumour control.
pmc-13554279:
Kirsten O'Brien leads a seven-author team testing tiny perfluorocarbon droplets for bone work in a 2026 study. These droplets, smaller than a cell, carry a liquid core in a fatty shell and may deliver gases or drugs. Related bubbles already aid bone repair research, yet droplet effects on bone cells were untested. The team tracked droplet contact with bone-forming cells and bone-eating cells, under normal and low oxygen.

Long exposure over twelve days cut the number of bone-eating cells in both oxygen settings. Short exposure under low oxygen instead boosted their formation. Bone-forming cells from several sources stayed healthy throughout. The authors call the droplets compatible with key bone cells, with effects that depend on timing and oxygen, a base for targeted bone delivery.
pmc-13554379:
Iqra Farzeen leads an eight-author team reviewing chemical modulators of synaptic plasticity as a route to treat Alzheimer's disease in a 2026 paper. Synapses strengthen or weaken with experience, and that flexing underlies learning and memory. The disease creeps in years before symptoms, marked by amyloid plaques and tangles of the tau protein. Failing synapses and shrinking synapse counts track the loss of thinking power.

Damage signals from amyloid are thought to rouse immune cells in the brain, whose chemicals then push tau toward its harmful form. The review surveys compounds that tune synapse strength as candidate medicines. Aiming at plasticity offers a target earlier than late-stage damage. Readers get the biology of memory formation beside the case for such drug strategies.
pmc-13555879:
Tom Caput leads a six-author team pooling studies that compare two fixes for a collapsed lung in a 2026 analysis. Air leaking into the chest space can be drawn out by simple needle aspiration or by a chest tube left to drain. Nineteen studies, trials and comparisons alike, entered the pool. Outcomes covered instant success, side effects, hospital stay, and pain.

Success rates matched between the two approaches overall. Aspiration brought far fewer side effects than tube drainage. Patients treated by aspiration left hospital about two and a half days sooner. They also reported clearly lower pain scores. The authors back aspiration as the first strategy, echoing international guidelines, since equal success comes with a gentler course.
pmc-13556079:
Lulu Li and five colleagues sequenced in 2026 the full genome of an industrial bacterium used to make 2-ketogluconic acid, a building block for a common food antioxidant. The strain, Pseudomonas plecoglossicida JUIM01, produces the acid through fermentation, and knowing its genes should help engineers improve it. The team read the whole chromosome and annotated what each predicted gene likely does.

The genome is a single circular chromosome carrying more than four and a half thousand predicted proteins. Annotation revealed a control network of 75 core regulators grouped into six cooperating modules that seem to manage metabolism and stress responses. Pathways for glucose use, fat metabolism, and energy generation tied to acid production were mapped in detail. The authors offer the sequence as a resource for building hardier, higher-yielding production strains.
pmc-13559079:
Ye and colleagues build the first chemical atlas of histone marks in this 2026 study of fetal Down syndrome brains, hunting epigenetic changes beyond the extra chromosome 21 itself. Using advanced mass spectrometry on fetal cortex tissue, they catalogued the modifications decorating all four core histones, then zoomed in on the mark that moved most.

Healthy fetal cortex carried 172 distinct histone modifications against 168 in Down syndrome samples. Of the quantifiable marks, one acetylation, H3K79ac, fell furthest, down 34 percent in syndrome tissue in the comparison. Genome mapping placed the depleted mark at three neurodevelopmental genes, and its loss paired with abnormal activity in each: one gene silenced, two overexpressed. The authors nominate this single depleted mark as a candidate driver of the syndrome's brain development differences and a possible drug target.
pmc-13560079:
Siika and colleagues report in 2026 on how strongly the width of the lower aorta runs in families, using Sweden's Stockholm screening program. The program ultrasound-scans men for abdominal aortic aneurysm, a dangerous ballooning of the body's main artery. The question was whether siblings share not just aneurysms but subtler width patterns.

Linking screening records for over sixteen thousand 65-year-old men to the national multigeneration registry yielded nearly nine thousand sibling pairs. Aortic width correlated modestly between full siblings, weakly between half siblings, and strongly between twins, in line with shared genetics. If one sibling had an aneurysm-width aorta, the estimated chance that a brother's aorta was at least borderline wide ran about five percent for full siblings. For twins it ran twenty-one percent. Heritability estimates came out around four tenths for width itself and six tenths for aneurysm-range categories.
pmc-13560279:
Alhassan Sibdow Abukari, Shelley Schmollgruber, and Emmanuel Kwame Korsah develop an instrument to measure family-centered care in neonatal intensive care units in low-resource settings. Their 2026 three-phase study begins with a scoping review, interviews, and focus groups that drafted forty candidate items. Surveys of 346 family members and one hundred clinicians then fed factor analysis for item reduction.

The final tool holds twenty items across four domains: family acceptance, education, environmental design, and sufficient resources. Psychometric checks came out strong, with reliability coefficients above 0.94 across the reported indices. A two-round expert Delphi panel confirmed content validity for every item. The authors note that no validated measure previously existed for family-centered care in resource-limited newborn units. They offer the FEES instrument to guide nursing adjustments and future research design in neonatal care.
pmc-13562379:
Jessica Campisi and three colleagues present two patients with adventitial cystic disease, a rare condition where jelly-filled cysts grow in an artery wall and squeeze the vessel shut. The disorder usually strikes the artery behind the knee in healthy middle-aged men, causing leg pain when walking. Open removal of the cyst has been the classic fix. Their 2026 report sets a catheter-based repair against open surgery, one patient each.

A young, healthy patient received a stent placed through a catheter for disease in the thigh artery. An older patient with other illnesses received a vein bypass around the blocked knee artery. Both were free of symptoms one year later. The authors argue that the choice should follow the lesion site and the patient's overall health. Stenting may serve selected cases, while open repair stays vital where a stent cannot go.
pmc-13562579:
Yangyang Gao and Shuxian Liu design a detector that finds tiny objects in drone photographs, where people and vehicles shrink to a few pixels. High-altitude views pack small targets densely against cluttered ground, and deep networks often wash their outlines away. Their 2026 network, EDC-Net, adds three parts. An edge-aware module feeds contour cues back into learning, a context module gathers wide scene information cheaply, and a detection head uses flexible convolution that follows bent, irregular shapes.

Tested on the VisDrone2019 benchmark, the network beat its YOLO11s baseline by 4.5 points on the looser accuracy measure and 3.0 points on the stricter one. It did so with 29.8 percent fewer parameters. A second test on the TinyPerson dataset, built around very small people, confirmed the skill transferred. The authors aim the design at traffic watching, power-line inspection, farming, and fire patrol from the air.
pmc-13563779:
Li Wang and four colleagues test a teamwork model for the hardest COPD admissions: flare-ups in patients juggling heart failure, diabetes, and more. Clashing treatments for clashing diseases sink outcomes under routine care. The 2026 study, at a Chinese tertiary hospital, compared routine care with a doctor-nurse integrated model built on joint rounds, one shared plan covering lungs and companions, and discharge planning done together. Records ran from 2022 to 2025, and statistical matching produced 52 pairs.

The integrated group fared better on the combined measure of death or cardiopulmonary readmission within a year, with a hazard ratio of 0.58. Stays shortened from about eleven days to about eight on average. Symptom scores improved more, and in-hospital complications fell from 29 to 12 percent, led by fewer sugar crises and heart failure episodes. The authors argue that managing the whole patient jointly, rather than each disease in turn, is what moves the needle.
pmc-13563979:
Dai Mengting and colleagues track, in a 2026 retrospective study, how gut microbes change as chronic liver disease worsens toward liver failure. Samples from 947 patients covered early disease, two stages of cirrhosis, and acute-on-chronic liver failure, with ten common gut bacteria measured by a targeted genetic test.

Four patterns of change emerged, and a ratio favoring harmful over helpful bacteria rose more than fivefold across the stages. Computer models predicted each stage change well, best for the step into liver failure. A simple ratio of two bacteria also separated stages. The results suggest stool testing might one day warn clinicians that a patient's liver disease is about to turn dangerous.
pmc-13570479:
Megan Noda, Mathew Ghodsian, and Jonathan Chan survey, in a 2026 international study recruited through Facebook support groups, how vitiligo affects daily and emotional life. Vitiligo is the skin condition that removes pigment in patches. One hundred eighty-one adults, mostly women from the United Kingdom and Australia, completed a fifteen-item quality-of-life scale and open questions during late 2023 and early 2024.

Stigma and sun exposure topped the challenges named. Patches on the head and neck tied to changed grooming and clothing, trouble making friends, and limits on daily activities. Men reported stronger emotional impact than women in this sample. The patient-voiced results argue that care should treat social burden as part of the disease.
pmc-13570879:
Jing Lu and colleagues present, in a 2026 data paper, a benchmark set for detecting flight anomalies in small training aircraft, built because real abnormal flight data are scarce. One hundred twenty real flights from two common trainer models yielded about a million data points. A physics-based method injected four fault types: throttle surge, path deviation, engine misfire, and pitch excursion.

Normal and fault versions of the same flights sit side by side, organized by fault and aircraft, so detection algorithms can be compared fairly. Statistical checks and baseline detectors validate the set. Aviation safety researchers gain shared ground truth for building monitors that warn before small-plane accidents develop.
pmc-13572479:
Silvia Torrents, with 14 colleagues, reports a 2026 case series on stem cell therapy for graft-versus-host disease that resists steroids. In this illness, donor immune cells attack the patient after a transplant. Cells from the jelly of donated umbilical cords may calm that attack, but batch quality varies.

The series covers 49 patients, median age 10 years, treated at four hospitals from 2018 to 2022. Patients got a median of four infusions, and batches were classed by a lab potency test that gauges how well they calm immune reactions. In all, 71.4 percent responded by day 28, and one-year survival was 55.1 percent. In patients under 12, stronger batches went with better responses. The link backs potency testing as a release check for future cell products.
pmc-13573479:
Xinwei Zhang, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 investigation of AI-measured heart artery plaque and bad heart events. Scans can now gauge plaque load and a computed flow score, yet which measure warns best was open. The team followed patients who had CT angiography of the heart arteries at one centre.

Of 381 patients, 67 had a major event within 18 months at most, from death to repeat artery procedures. All six plaque measures tied to events. The share of soft, non-calcified plaque stood out as the strongest single warning once other factors were counted. Adding the flow score to plaque data did not lift the joint model in a real way. One vessel, the right coronary artery, carried the most weight in side checks. The authors call those side findings early and in need of outside proof.
pmc-13574879:
Ondine Walter, with five colleagues, reports on a 2026 study of poverty and sickle cell disease across mainland France. This inherited blood disorder brings painful vessel-blocking crises and slow organ wear. Whether living in a poor area worsens its course in a rich country was unsettled.

Insurance records followed 17,315 patients for a median of just over eight years, with each home area scored on a national hardship index. Patients in the hardest-hit areas had slightly more blocking crises and spent more days in hospital for them. Long-term organ damage showed no gap between areas. Death leaned higher in poor areas, though the gap fell short of firm proof. Use of vaccines, vitamins, and preventive drugs was even across areas. The authors read the pattern as a crisis burden, not a care-access one.
pmc-13575179:
K K D A Wijesekara leads a 2026 safety study of breakwater blocks made from two waste streams. The binder uses sodium silicate drawn from old television tube glass, an electronic waste product. The aggregate comes from construction and demolition rubble, bound into a geopolymer, a cement-like material.

Blocks were soaked in pure water and seawater for 64 days in standard leaching tests, then results were projected across a 50-year service life. Heavy metals such as lead, cadmium, and nickel stayed far below Dutch safety limits in the projections. Pure water drew out more sodium and calcium than seawater did. The authors judge the material safe for marine use, while recommending field trials under real wave forces.
pmc-13576779:
Gustavo Schiavone Crestana leads a 2026 report on a Brazilian workshop that teaches Python programming to bioscientists. Modern biology produces huge datasets, and Python is now a core tool for handling them, yet training lags in many countries. The workshop covers basic coding and data handling with popular libraries.

The paper reviews changes made in the 2021 and 2022 editions after feedback from earlier rounds. New committees, a code of conduct, and live feedback forms improved organisation. Teaching pairs, code clubs, and classroom technology were added to lift learning. Good practice and reproducibility were pushed through talks and hands-on work following the PEP8 style guide. Outreach grew through social media and international events. The authors close with updated advice for anyone planning a similar school.
pmc-13576879:
Esra Yildirim-Manav and three colleagues test which glue and filling choices make a glued-back tooth fragment strongest, in a 2026 dental study. When a front tooth breaks and the piece is saved, reattaching it keeps the natural shape and look. The team broke 72 extracted human front teeth in a standard way and reattached the pieces six ways.

Groups combined three adhesive curing modes, light, self, and dual, with two filling thicknesses, runny flowable and firm packable. After 5,000 heating and cooling cycles, a machine measured the force needed to break each repair. Both choices mattered on their own. Dual-cure glue with packable filling gave the strongest repairs, while light-cure glue with flowable filling gave the weakest. Packable material beat flowable under every glue mode. The authors recommend the dual-cure and packable pairing for fragment repairs.
pmc-13578279:
Norbert Wronski and co-authors link a protein called RIPK4 to energy use and spread in melanoma, in a 2026 cell study. Melanoma is a skin cancer that rewires how it burns fuel as it turns invasive. The team used two melanoma cell lines with the protein deleted, plus versions where the gene was switched back on.

Cells without RIPK4 breathed and burned sugar more weakly, and two fuel gate proteins fell. In ball shaped cell clusters the same cells pushed fewer arms into gels and slipped into vessel like channels less often. Lung growths in mice held less of one fuel gate protein when RIPK4 was absent. Restoring the protein fixed some signals but not the fuel burn itself, hinting at more paths at work.
pmc-13579879:
Godson Emeka Anyanwu and colleagues test a mango compound against ketamine driven brain harm in rats, in a 2026 study. Ketamine scrambles the balance between go and stop signals in the brain, faking features of schizophrenia and burning tissue through stress chemistry. Rats dosed for a week were then treated for two weeks with the compound at three strengths, or with a standard psychiatric drug.

Ketamine wrecked maze learning, spiked movement, and warped signal chemical levels across three brain zones. The mango compound restored learning, memory, and calm movement in step with dose, the top doses nearing normal. Signal chemicals settled back, cell loss eased under the microscope, and a key antioxidant switch lit up in cell cores. Scar like support cell overgrowth also receded.
pmc-13584379:
Maoyao Ling and colleagues probe how a breathing machine can injure the lungs it is meant to save, using mice in this 2026 study. Strong air pressure can trigger fierce inflammation in lung tissue, a problem called ventilator-induced lung injury. The team focused on two pathways: a cell-stress pathway named PERK and an immune sensor named NOD1, each feeding a master inflammation switch.

Mice breathed at high volume for four hours and came out with damaged, leaky lungs and high levels of inflammatory signals. Mice bred without the NOD1 sensor fared better, and a drug that blocks the PERK pathway also eased the harm. Using both blocks at once protected the lungs most of all, which hints that care may need to hit more than one pathway.
pmc-13587379:
Yibin Cai and colleagues test a blood inflammation score as a forecast tool in esophageal cancer. The cancer, of the squamous type in the food pipe, is often found at a locally advanced stage, where chemo plus radiation is the main hope of cure. Outcomes still scatter widely, so the team asked whether the pan-immune inflammation value, a score built from routine blood counts, could sort patients before treatment began.

Their 2026 study covered 696 patients who received that combined treatment. Higher scores traveled with bigger tumors and, in both simple and adjusted models, with shorter overall and cancer-free survival. The link bent rather than running straight, and it held in nearly every subgroup. Blending the score with standard staging split patients into three risk bands more sharply than staging alone. The authors offer the pairing as a cheap guide for tailoring care.
pmc-13593579:
Martyniuk and McNeil appraise in 2026 OpenEvidence, a web-based artificial intelligence tool that answers clinicians' questions at the point of care. The product presents itself as an AI copilot for doctors facing high-stakes decisions.

The review describes how the tool works. A clinician types a question in natural language, even a long one carrying full patient case details. The answer is a synthesized summary of the research with a linked reference list, plus suggested follow-up questions. Its maker stresses that sources accompany every answer and calls the product a search engine rather than an answer engine. Access is free for verified health professionals and students in Canada and the United States, with occupational proof required. The appraisal walks through the registered and public versions and the audience the product targets.
pmc-13593679:
Xiaoxiao Li and a sizable team examined whether chrysophanol, a natural compound from the anthraquinone family, can protect the kidneys during sepsis, the body's overwhelming response to infection. Their 2026 work paired cell experiments on human kidney cells with a mouse model in which a bacterial toxin triggers septic kidney injury.

In the cell tests, pretreatment with chrysophanol kept more cells alive. It lowered the output of inflammatory signals such as IL-6 and TNF-α, raised the calming signal IL-10, and cut levels of damaging reactive oxygen. In the mice it reduced tissue damage, cell death, and scarring in the kidneys, and standard blood measures of kidney function improved. The authors present the compound as a promising protective candidate, while noting that exactly how it works at the molecular level remains to be pinned down.
pmc-13594479:
Daisuke Yoshimoto and co-authors describe a simple electrical trick for placing a pacing lead in the Bachmann bundle, the bridge that carries signals to the left atrium. Pacing there may cut the onset and persistence of atrial fibrillation. Their 2026 single-center series covers fifty patients. In each, the approach was attempted during pacemaker or defibrillator implantation.

Operators advanced the lead delivery system from the great vein toward the atrium and fixed the lead just below the spot where the atrial signal abruptly grew stronger. Every patient received a septal lead, and in forty-four the paced tracing met the criteria for true bundle capture, with mapping taking only a couple of minutes. Thresholds improved by the end of the procedure and stayed stable over six months, with no dislodgements, fluid around the heart, or infections.
pmc-13599579:
Michael E. Cloesmeijer and colleagues ask in 2026 why people with milder hemophilia A respond so differently to one drug. Hemophilia A is an inherited bleeding disorder caused by low levels of clotting factor VIII. Desmopressin can raise those levels, but the size of the rise varies by person, and the gene variant each patient carries plays a large part. Doctors now test each person before relying on the drug.

The team applied machine learning to a population model built from 1,441 patients carrying 55 different variants in the F8 gene. Ten variants shifted the response in a clear way. Three blunted the rise, one cutting it by more than half. Seven boosted it, the strongest reaching over three times the typical level. Delivery route mattered too: nose and skin routes peaked lower than a vein drip. Adding patient factors cut unexplained variation nearly in half, toward predicting response without a test dose.
pmc-13600579:
Michael G Ross, writing alone, examines how weak science enters obstetric malpractice cases about brain injury in newborns. Claims that a baby's brain damage was caused during pregnancy or delivery must rest on sound proof of cause, he argues. Yet cerebral palsy cases are among the costliest in medicine, and they attract theories built on shaky ground. Judges decide which expert claims count as science under standards such as Daubert and Frye.

Ross walks through popular theories blaming newborn brain injury on events around birth, critiquing each against basic physiology. Either side can promote such theories, he notes, and sued doctors face heavy pressure toward defensive practice. His remedy is educational: stronger teaching of basic science and human physiology during obstetrics training. That grounding, he argues, would help doctors answer unfounded claims with confidence in court.
pmc-13602379:
Papezikova and colleagues test in 2026 whether rainbow trout bred for disease resistance actually resist three major pathogens, a bacterium and two parasites, under laboratory challenge. Fish farming increasingly breeds for resistance as drug treatments face limits.

Three genetic lines were exposed to Flavobacterium psychrophilum, which causes coldwater disease, and to two parasites of skin and kidney, while the team tracked deaths, immune measures, and pathogen loads. Two lines carried known resistance markers. Surprisingly, the line declared genetically resistant died most after the bacterial challenge, hinting that strain virulence or environment overcame its genetics. Against one parasite that line first carried more parasites but then cleared them most efficiently. The authors conclude that resistance is a joint product of genes, pathogen, and setting, so lines must be tested at each farm before adoption.
pmc-13612279:
Liguang Wang leads a six-author team building a blood test panel for the commonest lung cancer. Non-small cell lung cancer is usually found late, and the standard serum markers CEA and CYFRA21-1 miss many cases. Tiny RNA molecules called snoRNAs ride stably inside small vesicles in blood. The team screened vesicle RNA from patients and controls, then validated four candidate snoRNAs by PCR in 240 untreated patients and 205 healthy people.

The four-snoRNA panel alone scored an area under the curve of 0.924, edging past the two standard markers at 0.903. Combining all six markers lifted accuracy to 0.970, with sensitivity near 87 percent and specificity near 97 percent. Performance held in early-stage disease and in matched subsets. No single snoRNA tracked tumor features after corrections, so the value lies in the panel. The authors frame the work as exploratory, a candidate for validation rather than a clinic-ready test.
pmc-13614179:
Ananya Pal, Nicole Leifer, and Daphna Shimon probe how sodium ions are stored in a bowl-shaped porous carbon material designed for sodium-ion batteries, a cheaper cousin of the lithium battery. Earlier work used hard carbons with messy, poorly known structure, so the link between shape and storage stayed blurry. This material has layered pores at several scales and a surface area of 917.5 square metres per gram.

It delivered a reversible capacity of 250 milliamp-hours per gram in a salt water based cell. Using two magnetic resonance methods, the team found four distinct places where sodium ions sit inside the carbon. Watching how those signals changed with heat added clues about how the ions move. Knowing exactly where sodium rests helps engineers design carbon shapes that store more and waste less.
pmc-13616579:
Inês Camarinha and colleagues present a case report of a 26-year-old professional volleyball player. His back-of-shoulder pain turned out to be a torn serratus anterior. That muscle hugs the ribs and steadies the shoulder blade. Such tears are rare and usually announce themselves with pain at the front-side chest wall and a palpable lump, mostly in rowers and throwing athletes. This player felt only posterior shoulder pain after a serve, worse when spiking, lasting two weeks.

His cuff tests were normal, and a bedside ultrasound showed nothing, so the first suspicions fell on joint damage inside the shoulder. An MRI then revealed the traumatic muscle tear. The case warns sports doctors that a normal shoulder work-up with lingering back-of-shoulder pain deserves a wider look, since a chest wall muscle can masquerade as a joint problem.
pmc-13618979:
Julian Devigne and two colleagues describe an arthroscopic technique for rebuilding the superior capsule of the shoulder when a massive rotator cuff tear cannot be repaired. That is a hard problem in younger patients without much arthritis. Instead of harvesting graft tissue elsewhere, the method reroutes the shoulder's long head of biceps tendon onto the greater tuberosity, using it as graft material. Fixation uses knotless anchors, not tied sutures.

The construct uses two low-profile anchors to maximize contact between tendon and bone, achieving strong compression while letting the surgeon fold the posterior cuff into the repair. Prerequisites are strict: an irreparable tear, an intact biceps tendon, and satisfactory bone quality. The authors trace the lineage from fascia lata reconstruction to biceps rerouting with knotted sutures. They present the knotless version as faster, more versatile, and gentler on bone. The article is a technique guide, not an outcomes study.
pmc-13619779:
Renan Prado and Melissa Lou Silva compared health outcomes for adults who live with both type 2 diabetes and celiac disease against matched patients with diabetes alone. Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten that damages the gut lining. Using a large electronic health record network, the team matched 8,760 patients in each group on demographics, heart risk factors, medicines, and lab values.

Patients carrying both conditions faced higher hazards across a long list of problems: protein in the urine, severe high blood sugar, eye and nerve complications, kidney disease, and a combined heart outcome. Depression and anxiety hazards were also higher. Hospitalization risk, notably, did not differ between the groups. Follow-up stretched past four years on average. The authors argue that the pairing deserves closer monitoring in diabetes care, since the added burden spans body and mind.
pmc-13620179:
Kwon and colleagues chart a decade of cardiovascular change in Korean adults with dyslipidemia, abnormal blood lipids. Their 2026 nationwide cohort study uses national health insurance sample data from 2010 to 2019. It tracks disease incidence and lipid-lowering prescriptions in adults aged twenty and over. Rates were standardised for age and sex.

Overall cardiovascular incidence among people with dyslipidemia fell markedly, from about 37 to about 21 cases per thousand person-years. The drop was driven by ischemic heart disease, down about 49 percent, and ischemic stroke, down about 47 percent, while heart failure incidence crept upward. Statin use reached about 95 percent of patients by 2019, yet high-intensity statins remained rare at under five percent of users. Ezetimibe prescribing roughly quadrupled. The authors read the trends as progress with unfinished business on treatment intensity.
pmc-13620279:
Elisa Suter and seven colleagues asked whether inherited variants in two immune brake genes predict how myeloma patients fare on CAR T-cell therapy. The treatment reprograms a patient's own T cells to hunt a marker on myeloma cells, yet responses vary and relapse is common. Records covered eighty-seven patients treated at one center between 2021 and 2025.

Patients carrying the minor variant of a CTLA4 change relapsed less and died less than those with two major copies, and their progression-free and overall survival ran longer. A LAG3 variant showed a similar pattern, strongest in patients carrying two minor copies. The authors are careful to call these findings suggestive only. They propose the two variants as candidate biomarkers that prospective studies should test before any clinic uses them to pick patients.
pmc-13623379:
Adonay Ferreira Lisboa and Marcelo Falcão de Santana review the nutritional health of patients after endoscopic gastroplasty, a stomach-shrinking procedure done through a scope for obesity. Sewing the stomach smaller helps people eat less, and doctors worry such procedures might also starve the body of vitamins and minerals. Records came from a private service in Salvador, Bahia.

The retrospective study covered twenty-seven patients, most of them women, with an average age near forty-four. Before the procedure a handful already showed low iron, B12, vitamin D, zinc, or calcium, or high blood sugar. Six months later the lab profile looked much the same, with no new harm showing in follow-up. Weight loss was solid and held steady across the period. Starting body mass showed no link to the lab values. The authors caution that the small sample limits the strength of the reassurance.
pmc-13623979:
Rasmus Reinke and colleagues published a 2026 study of a glowing dye test used during total thyroid removal to predict parathyroid trouble afterward. The four small parathyroid glands sit behind the thyroid and control blood calcium; if their blood supply is damaged, hormone levels crash. Injecting indocyanine green dye makes well-fed glands light up under a special camera.

From May 2021 to June 2023, 124 patients had the dye assessment during surgery, and each visible gland was scored by glow strength. Patients with at least one strongly glowing gland needed calcium-regulating medicine at discharge far less often than those without. The dye still missed some future cases, and six patients developed permanent gland failure; all six had shown a steep hormone drop during surgery, a sharper warning sign. No dye side effects or liver harm appeared. The authors call the test safe and useful, while noting the scoring rests on human judgement.
pmc-13624279:
Xavier Eduardo Garzon Garzon leads a clinical test of a microneedling radiofrequency device aimed at double chins and jawline definition. The treatment drives fine needles into the skin while heating the tissue. The device used here works at several depths at once, reaching fat under the chin muscle as well as the skin layers above.

Sixteen volunteers with graded levels of under-chin fat received three sessions spaced four weeks apart, and ultrasound measured the fat layers before and after. Both the fat under the skin and the deeper fat layer shrank measurably, and the jaw angles slimmed on both sides. Two-thirds of participants improved by at least one grade on the photographic scale, and nearly all reported satisfaction. No severe side effects appeared. The authors present the multilayer approach as an effective office-based alternative for patients avoiding surgery.
pmc-13624779:
Rayhaan Gerard Pais and co-authors introduce TattleTail, a rule-based computer tool that finds pyocin gene clusters in the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Pyocins are virus-tail weapons that kill rival bacteria, and their genes look so much like virus genes that standard tools often mislabel them as dormant viruses.
