TattleTail instead checks for the cluster's known gene layout near two marker genes, plus the presence of pyocin-linked genes and the absence of true virus parts.

Across hand-checked genomes, cluster-stripped copies, and unrelated bacteria, the tool found the real clusters with no false alarms. In hospital isolates, its picks were confirmed by chemical triggering, microscope images, and killing tests, which makes genome annotation cleaner for anyone mining these bacteria.
pmc-13632679:
Aleksey Ermolaev, Mikhail Divashuk, and Reema Singh present a computer pipeline that finds inherited DNA differences more reliably. Reading genomes produces errors, and each analysis program has its own biases, so single programs miss or invent variants. Their pipeline, called ChoCallate, runs three established variant callers at once and keeps the calls they agree on. A coverage-aware step lets it handle cheaper partial sequencing methods as well.

On simulated plant data holding ten thousand known single-letter changes, a two-vote rule gave a good balance of precision and sensitivity, especially at low coverage. Missed variants clustered in repetitive genome regions no matter the strategy. In two hundred bread wheat samples, the pipeline found over eleven thousand high-confidence variants. A trait hunt using those calls recovered a known gene for awn formation. The tool is freely available and works for any species.
pmc-13635179:
Anna Breger and nine colleagues published this 2026 dataset paper for judging photoacoustic image quality. Photoacoustic imaging builds pictures from light and sound, and new reconstruction software needs a fair way to be graded. Standard quality measures were designed for photographs, not medical images, and they misbehave on this kind. The team assembled more than eleven hundred photoacoustic images with a known reference version of each.

Five experts rated every image across five quality properties, giving the field a shared yardstick. The full set, images plus ratings, is posted publicly for anyone to download. Researchers can now test whether a quality measure agrees with expert eyes before trusting it in larger studies. The authors note the detailed ratings could serve other imaging areas too. Their goal is to make claims about better reconstruction prove themselves against human judgment.
pmc-13635479:
Hyo-Seung Nam and Yein Oh report three dogs whose leaky heart valves unexpectedly improved on their own. Their disease, myxomatous mitral valve disease, is the commonest heart condition in small dogs. The valve thickens and fails to seal, letting blood wash backward until the heart swells. All three dogs arrived in advanced heart failure, with enlarged left hearts. Standard treatment with water pills eased their signs.

Follow-up checks showed something vets had not documented before. The gap between the valve leaflets narrowed as the valve thickened further, so the backward leak shrank. Heart size fell markedly along with it. Water pills could stop, and each dog carried on with a heart-strengthening drug alone. The authors present the cases as the first report of such spontaneous improvement. They suggest the disease may occasionally bend toward repair-like change, and call for research into why.
pmc-13638779:
Charles B. Foster and three colleagues published a 2026 stewardship audit of antibiotics given around surgery in children receiving organ transplants. Practice varies between hospitals in drug choice and stopping dates, so the team measured their own center against its written protocols.

They reviewed 164 transplants performed from 2010 to 2021 using anesthesia and medication records. Doses were on time in nearly all procedures, and most children received the recommended first regimen. Only about six in ten stopped the main antibiotic by the intended cutoff, with kidney transplants doing best. The audit gives the center clear targets for improvement.
pmc-13646079:
Nirit Putievsky Pilosof and six colleagues study a hybrid care model that lets women with high-risk pregnancies stay home instead of spending long stretches in hospital. Patients monitor themselves and the baby at home with remote guidance and daily virtual visits. Twice a week they come in for checks that cannot yet be done remotely, seen by the same team. The researchers observed the program and interviewed forty patients, staff, managers, and technology leads.

Reading the change through a people, process, and place lens, the team found shifts on all three fronts. Roles changed as patients gained autonomy and families joined care. Workflows, policies, and payment models were rebuilt around the split setting. Care itself stretched across hospital and home, in physical and digital spaces at once. The authors argue that lasting change of this kind needs design across all three dimensions, not technology alone.
pmc-13647379:
Kei-Fong Ng and nine colleagues mine the roots of Aconitum coreanum, a monkshood plant, for new alkaloid chemicals and test them against a cancer immune shield. Fifteen previously unknown compounds were isolated alongside thirteen known relatives. Full spectroscopic work, including a crystal structure, pinned down each new molecule's shape. All the new finds share a classic skeleton for this plant family, with varied oxidation patterns, and four carry a rare sulfonate group never seen in this class.

Several compounds lowered PD-L1 production in breast cancer cells, dose by dose. PD-L1 is the shield tumors use to switch off attacking immune cells. Microscope staining confirmed the effect for the strongest few. The authors claim a first: this alkaloid family can modulate PD-L1. They present the plant's chemistry as a fresh source of immune-awakening leads, in a genus better known for poisons than for medicines.
pmc-13647579:
Yingchao Guan and Yanan Gao review recent progress in neurorehabilitation, the work of restoring thinking and movement after brain injury. Their narrative tour starts with brain plasticity and the support cells called glia, then moves through the toolbox: cognitive training, motor practice, brain stimulation, and regenerative therapies. Complications that bend recovery, such as spasticity, frailty, and seizures after stroke, get dedicated attention.

Newer technologies thread through the review, including brain-computer interfaces, virtual reality, and rehabilitation robots, each weighed for personal fit. The authors keep quality of life and return to social life in view as the true endpoints, not test scores alone. Evidence-based, patient-centered care is their stated standard throughout. The closing sections chart future directions for stroke survivors and frail older people, the groups with the most to gain from rehabilitation that adapts to the person.
pmc-13649379:
Ioannis Theocharis and Björn Bohnenkamp set out a workshop tool that uses futures literacy to probe how homes might revalue stored stuff. Cutting demand is a leg of climate action, and clear-outs are one door in. Most clear-out aids stay solo and stuck in the now, though.

Their lab runs three steps: reveal, reframe, rethink, with an act step left as a choice. Test workshops honed three forms, from themed futures to object-based projection and script-based reframes. The aim is not instant change of habit. It is to drag hidden takes on the future into the open, where a group can haggle over them. The authors offer the tool to sufficiency research at large.
pmc-13649479:
Praveen Machiraju and five colleagues found a fresh role for a protein best known for guarding chromosome ends: it helps blood vessel cells clean up waste and resist harm from oxidised cholesterol. Such harm drives artery disease, and the self-cleaning process often falters in sick vessels. The team worked with human vein cells dosed with oxidised cholesterol.

The toxic fat lowered the protein's levels and raised a sticky marker of vessel distress. Adding the protein back cut fat build-up, eased cell sticking, and restored the vessel wall's seal. Blocking it did the reverse. The protein paired with a partner that steers waste sacs to disposal, and the pair grew closer under fat stress. The authors see this as a new shield for vessel health.
pmc-13649679:
Shahram Moradi and three colleagues used Norwegian registry data to see how often working-age cancer survivors draw a disability pension five years after diagnosis. Their set held 11,188 people aged 30 to 55 who were employed when cancer was found, each matched to a cancer-free peer of like age, sex, schooling, and work.

Survivors had more than twice the odds of drawing a partial or full pension. Odds ran highest for cancers of the lung, blood, and brain, and for disease found at a late stage. Low schooling, low income, and being unmarried also raised the odds. Skin cancer sat at the low end. The authors call for rehab plans that fit both the illness and the person's means.
pmc-13650679:
Hannah Chau and three colleagues review how herpes simplex virus type 1, the commonest cause of sporadic viral brain inflammation, injures the prefrontal cortex at the front of the brain. The disease classically strikes the inner temporal lobes, yet imaging and clinical studies increasingly implicate prefrontal regions that govern planning, motivation, and self-control.

The authors assemble a multistep account of vulnerability: the virus enters along smell and facial nerve routes, rides the cell's transport rails into the brain, and meets regional differences in susceptibility. Inside the tissue, overactivated immune cells, a fired-up inflammatory sensor complex, faltering support cells, and a disrupted blood-brain barrier amplify neuronal and synaptic damage, while viral evasion tricks prolong the assault. Survivors often keep executive and behavioral problems for years. Connecting regional injury to those lasting deficits, the review also flags how much of the mechanism remains unproven.
pmc-13651879:
César Feniou and five colleagues present a new algorithm for doing chemistry calculations on fault-tolerant quantum computers. Their method works in real space, placing grid points where the electron density of a molecule is actually high instead of spreading points evenly everywhere. A transcorrelated version of the method also removes the sharp cusps that make electron behavior near nuclei hard to compute.

Tests on benchmark molecules show that the adaptive grids cut wasted computation while keeping the results accurate. The Hermitian form of the method fits standard quantum phase estimation, and the transcorrelated form fits a newer eigenvalue estimation protocol. For chemists waiting on useful quantum hardware, the paper offers a practical route toward ground-state energy calculations that classical machines struggle to match.
pmc-13652779:
Clément Viguier and colleagues test backup drug combinations against E. coli strains that shrug off one of the last reliable treatments. The bacteria produce metallo-beta-lactamases, enzymes that destroy most beta-lactam antibiotics, leaving aztreonam paired with avibactam as a rare working option. Resistance to even that pairing is spreading. The team tried aztreonam with two other marketed inhibitors, relebactam and vaborbactam, against 48 well-characterized resistant isolates.

Many of the isolates already resisted the standard pairing, which made the comparison a hard test. The alternative combinations worked, but more weakly than aztreonam with avibactam where that pairing still held. Publishing the full activity pattern matters for hospitals choosing therapy today and for developers deciding where the next inhibitor should aim. The study is laboratory evidence only, yet it maps the shrinking space of options against these enzymes.
pmc-13662879:
Bo-Ru Lin and six colleagues validate an artificial intelligence system that screens for weak bones using ordinary chest X-rays. Bone density is normally measured by DXA scans, which many patients never receive. The system was trained through federated learning, a method that lets hospitals teach a shared model without pooling private patient data, using thousands of paired chest films and DXA results.

Validation ran on an independent group of about three thousand adults at two centers who had both tests on the same day. The model judged each film against the DXA standard for osteoporotic-level density in the lower spine. Catching low bone density on scans taken for other reasons could route at-risk patients to treatment before a fracture. The multi-center design, with data kept local during training, also answers the privacy objection that slows medical AI.
pmc-3280279:
Holt and Yandell present MAKER2, an annotation pipeline and genome archive tool for second-generation genome projects. New sequencing methods were shifting which genomes get sequenced and how they are labelled. First projects focused on well-studied model organisms, but many newer ones target new species.

Annotating a genome means finding its genes and features on raw sequence. MAKER2 automates that work and manages the resulting archive. Pipelines like it let small teams produce usable genome annotations for the flood of newly sequenced organisms, from pests to rare wildlife.  Archive care keeps annotations tracked as builds improve over later project rounds.
pmc-4377079:
Burgess, Butterworth, and Thompson showed in 2013 how Mendelian randomization can use summarized data. Genome-wide studies publish coefficients that sum up how each gene variant relates to a trait. Those summaries are a rich public source of data for new investigations.

The authors demonstrate how to combine coefficients from many variants to estimate a causal effect. No individual-level data are needed, so studies can be done from published results alone. That opens causal testing to far more questions and teams. The approach helped Mendelian randomization grow into a standard tool for checking whether a risk factor truly causes disease.
pmc-4678779:
Rhoads and Au reviewed PacBio sequencing and its applications in 2015. PacBio's single-molecule, real-time method reads one DNA molecule as it is copied. It offers much longer reads than the second-generation technologies that came before it.

Long reads suit problems that short reads cannot solve, such as spanning repeats and assembling genomes without gaps. The review covers uses in genome, transcriptome, and epigenetics research, including direct detection of chemical marks on DNA. Highly contiguous assemblies from long reads changed what genome projects could finish. The paper maps where this technology helps most and where its costs and errors still bind.
pmc-6324079:
Jaime Huerta-Cepas and colleagues presented eggNOG version 5.0 in 2019. eggNOG maps which genes across species descend from shared ancestors. It adds evolutionary history and functional notes to those groups.

The update greatly expands the genome sets, covering thousands of bacteria plus archaea and eukaryotes. Finer group levels let users compare close cousins or distant branches as needed. Functional labels transfer from studied genes to unstudied relatives. Comparative genomics projects use eggNOG to give quick first annotations to whole new genomes. Precomputed groups can be downloaded in bulk for pipelines that cannot query the site live.
pmc-6602479:
Flavia Madeira, Young Park, Joon Lee, and coauthors described the EMBL-EBI search and analysis APIs in 2019. EMBL-EBI offers free bioinformatics tools and a powerful text search over its databases. Access comes through web pages and through programming interfaces.

The paper documents how developers can call sequence search, alignment, and annotation tools from code. It also covers the search engine that links records across resources. Stable interfaces let pipelines built elsewhere keep working for years. Anyone building software on European bioinformatics services will find this the map of what is available.
pmc-6857279:
David Emms and Steven Kelly presented a major advance of OrthoFinder in 2019. OrthoFinder sorts genes across species into groups descended from single ancestral genes. That sorting is the base step for most comparative genomics.

The new version goes further, building rooted gene trees and the species tree itself. It also calls gene duplication events and reports comparison statistics. Accuracy stays high while the scope widens greatly. Teams with a fresh set of genomes can now get a full first evolutionary analysis from one tool. The method scales to hundreds of species, which earlier orthology tools could not handle in reasonable time.
pmc-6883579:
Derrick Wood, Jennifer Lu, and Ben Langmead introduced Kraken 2 for metagenomic classification in 2019. Kraken sorts DNA reads by species using short exact matches, very fast. Its first version demanded huge amounts of computer memory.

Kraken 2 cuts memory use dramatically while keeping the matching approach. A leaner database index makes room for larger reference sets on ordinary machines. Speed stays high enough for clinical and field use. Labs classifying millions of reads from mixed samples adopted it as a default first pass. Accuracy on standard test sets stays close to the first version despite the leaner footprint.
poems-pg679:
Frances E. W. Harper published her Poems in 1895, and the Black Heritage Library Collection reissued the volume for later generations. Harper, born free in Baltimore, became one of the most famous African American writers of the nineteenth century. An abolitionist lecturer, suffragist, and temperance leader whose poetry carried her politics into homes that lectures could not reach. An epigraph from Isaiah promises the forsaken a joy of many generations.

Contents mix the personal and the public: My Mother's Kiss beside the Dying Bondman. A Grain of Sand beside a Double Standard, her sharp poem on the different moral rules for men and women. Bible stories, temperance appeals, and race pride share the pages. Harper wrote for a people emerging from slavery, and her poems, plain, musical, and unflinching, were recited in churches and schools across Black America.
rehearsall-elizabeth-stile-1579:
Elizabeth Stile stands accused in A Rehearsall both Straung and True, a Windsor witch pamphlet from 1579. Hainous and horrible acts, confessions, and executions fill its black-letter pages. Stile and her fellows were charged with killings by sorcery in one of the earliest English witchcraft pamphlets to reach the press.

Cheap print carried the scare to markets and alehouses across the shire. Examinations before magistrates give the tale its grim, vivid detail. Belief, fear, and malice braid together in the record it preserves. The pamphlet marks the birth of the witch scare in English print, raw evidence of how neighbors turned on neighbors in terror.
salmon-horae-mathematicae-1679:
William Salmon was a London empiric, an unlicensed medical practitioner who sold remedies and wrote tirelessly on his trades. His Horae Mathematicae, seu Urania, published in 1679, is his astrological and medical miscellany. The title joins the hours of math to Urania, muse of the heavens.

Salmon packs the book with rules for charts, cures, and the choice of lucky times for bleeding, planting, and dosing. He writes for practitioners like himself, who needed the art to pay its way in the marketplace. The miscellany shows the working library of a seventeenth-century medical astrologer in one crowded volume.
sbe-03-shu-king-legge-1879:
Volume 3 of The Sacred Books of the East appeared in 1879, edited in a series led by Max Müller at Oxford. James Legge translated the texts, which form The Sacred Books of China, Part 1. At its center stands the Shû King, the Book of Documents, a set of speeches and records ascribed to China's earliest rulers.

Speeches, charges, and counsels in the Shû King present the model kings of old China and their ministers. Legge added the opening parts of other classics and full notes on hard passages. The volume brought one of China's oldest books into a world series of sacred texts. It helped place Chinese classics beside the Bible and the Vedas for English readers.
scientific-studies-or-practical-in-contr: Henry Dircks wrote Scientific Studies, or Practical in Contrast with Chimerical Pursuits, issued in London in 1879 by E. and F. N. Spon at 48 Charing Cross. Dircks is named as author of The Life of the Marquis of Worcester and Worcestoriana, with a string of society initials after his name. A front caption describes a bust of Edward Somerset, sixth Earl and second Marquis of Worcester, by James Loft. The bust was shown at the Royal Academy in 1867. It was placed in the Sculpture Gallery of the Crystal Palace at Sydenham.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Volume V of the Slave Narratives holds the Indiana accounts, built from talks with former slaves. The typed records were made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936-1938 for Indiana, and the Library of Congress project put the set together, with photos, at Washington in 1941. One photo shows an old slave, Peter Dunn. The list of those who spoke begins with George W. Arnold, Thomas Ash, Mary Crane, and Rosa Barber.
stile-rehearsall-abingdon-1579:
Elizabeth Stile lived at Windsor and faced a witchcraft charge in 1579. A Rehearsall both Straung and True tells how she was questioned and what she confessed. The pamphlet covers the Abingdon proceedings and belongs to the first wave of English witch prints.

Its title promises a tale both strange and true, the selling cry of the age's cheap news. Behind the cry sit hard facts: quarrels with neighbors could grow into a charge that cost a life. The record lets readers watch blame harden, step by step, into proof. Few early pamphlets show that grim path so clearly.
strindberg-the-red-room-1879:
August Strindberg wrote The Red Room in 1879, here in Ellie Schleussner's English translation of 1913. The novel that made Strindberg famous is the first modern Swedish novel in the judgment of critics. Its satirical panorama of Stockholm's artistic underworld still stings Swedish officialdom and bohemia alike in print.

Arvid Falk, a young idealist, quits a clerk's desk to write and starves among Stockholm bohemians. The Red Room of Berns restaurant hosts actors, painters, and journalists trading wit, debt, and dashed hopes nightly. Crooked companies, bought newspapers, and charitable frauds expose a city where money mocks merit at every turn. Falk's sister-in-law, his brother the shopkeeper, and a sea of spear-carriers fill the social canvas wide. Schleussner's version gave English readers the novel that remade Swedish prose fiction in 1879.
taylor-greeks-goths-runes-1879:
Isaac Taylor, an English cleric and writer on alphabets, put his rune theory in this book of 1879. He held that the runes of the Goths grew out of the Greek script. The claim stirred sharp debate among Victorian scholars of the north.

Taylor traced each rune sign back to a Greek form and told how the script may have moved north. He drew on trade routes and old carved finds to back his case. Right or wrong, his book was a turn in the study of where runes began. It also shows how bold the Victorian taste for grand schemes ran.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Florence to Trieste, part of Spanish Passions in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, follows Arthur Machen's rendering of the 1894 London edition, with chapters Arthur Symons discovered. Chapter Eighteen opens with Casanova asking the young grand duke of Tuscany for asylum. He explains the reasons that made him an exile from Venice and promises to ask help of no one, having funds enough for independence. He plans to devote his whole time to study.

The grand duke answers that good conduct and the laws will guarantee his freedom. Casanova then orders books and falls into talk with a collector of Greek epigrams in the shop. He mentions his own work on a translation of the Iliad. The two become fast friends who never walk or eat together, Casanova notes dryly. The chapter promises a forced departure and arrival at Bologna. Readers see the wanderer play the scholar under a prince's protection.
tob-10479:
Martin Luther drafted the Smalcald Articles in 1537 as the Lutheran position for a coming church council. He wrote expecting the meeting might judge his life's work, and possibly himself. The Schmalkaldic League of Lutheran princes and cities adopted the articles as a confession of faith.

Article by article, Luther states justification by faith alone without compromise, and marks which doctrines could never be traded away and which matters allowed discussion. Short, sharp, and unyielding, the text shows the Reformation's founder at his most combative. Readers get the Lutheran case in concentrated form, written when its author believed a final reckoning with Rome was near.
tob-4179:
Gertrude Lowthian Bell, traveler, archaeologist, and a maker of modern Iraq, translated poems from the Divan of Hafiz in 1897, before her political fame. Hafiz, the fourteenth-century Persian master, wrote ghazals of wine, roses, nightingales, and the Beloved. Sufis have long read them as divine allegory; other readers take them as pure pleasure, and the poems sustain both readings.

Bell's renderings keep the sparkle and formal grace of lyrics Persians regard as their language's summit. Her introduction treats Hafiz's life and the ghazal form for English readers new to both. Persian poetry's most beloved voice arrives here through an extraordinary translator whose own later story became history.
un-ga-res-a-69-79:
Some weapons wound too cruelly even for war, and Resolution A/69/79, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, backs the pact that curbs them. The Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons bars or bounds arms judged to cause needless harm or to strike without aim. Its five added pacts cover shards that no scan can find, mines and traps, fire arms, laser arms that blind, and the shells war leaves behind.

The text recalls the vote of the year before on the pact. It notes the 2013 meeting of the pact's parties in Geneva, and the yearly talks on the mines pact held the same week. States are urged to join the pact and to put its bounds to work.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/79, a General Assembly text from its sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons. It calls for universal adherence to the Convention and its protocols, including Protocol V on explosive remnants of war. It notes the informal meeting of experts held in May 2014 on lethal autonomous weapons systems. That meeting was an early step in the debate over weapons that can select and engage targets on their own.
un-sc-res-1379:
Children caught in armed conflict were the focus of a Security Council resolution adopted on 20 November 2001. The Council recalled its earlier texts on the subject, from resolution 1261 (1999) to 1314 (2000). It noted the wide and lasting harm war does to children, and through them to peace and development. The Secretary-General had reported in September 2001 on the working of resolution 1314.

The Council pledged to give the fullest attention to children's protection in every matter before it. It said it was ready to write child protection terms into peacekeeping mandates and to keep child protection advisers in missions. Parties to conflict were called to spare children and to let aid staff reach them. The Council said it would weigh the effect of sanctions on children when it used Article 41 measures. It also vowed to study links between war and the illegal trade in resources.
un-sc-res-1479:
Côte d'Ivoire gained a first United Nations mission on 13 May 2003. The Ivorian parties had signed the Linas-Marcoussis Agreement in January, and a government of national reconciliation had formed in April. ECOWAS and France were working for a settlement on the ground. The Council backed the Secretary-General's special representative and judged the crisis a threat to regional peace.

The Council established the United Nations Mission in Côte d'Ivoire, MINUCI, for an initial six months. Its task was to help carry out the Linas-Marcoussis Agreement. A small staff would support the special representative on political, legal, civil, police, and military matters. At its heart stood a military liaison group, starting at 26 officers and able to rise by 50 more. The Council renewed its call on all Ivorian forces to apply the agreement fully and without delay. It pressed again for grave rights abusers to face justice.
un-sc-res-1579:
Resolution 1579 recorded the Council's decision on Liberia, adopted on 21 December 2004. Disarmament was done and the cease-fire held. Peacekeepers had improved safety across the country. Yet the interim government still lacked control over the timber regions. Diamond certification work had only just begun.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms and travel measures for twelve months. The timber measures also run twelve months, with a review at six. The diamond ban runs six months, with a review at three months once diamond experts visit. The asset freeze on the former regime's circle stays in force. A new Panel of Experts serves until 21 June 2005.
un-sc-res-1679:
Darfur, in western Sudan, is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1679. The Council adopted it on 16 May 2006, days after a peace deal was signed at Abuja in Nigeria. African Union troops were on the ground, but violence against civilians in Darfur went on.

The text calls on the parties to carry out the peace deal without delay. Groups that refused to sign are urged to join it. The Council warns that anyone who blocks the deal could face travel bans or frozen assets. It backs a shift from the African Union force to a United Nations operation, starting with a joint study team within one week.
un-sc-res-1779:
Sudan's sanctions panel won a further year in September 2007. On 28 September 2007 the Security Council extended it until 15 October 2008. The panel monitors the arms embargo and other measures set since 2004. A new hybrid force for Darfur, UNAMID, was then preparing to deploy. The Council recalled the southern peace deal and the Darfur framework. Both still needed the pressure that careful monitoring supplied.

The panel owed an interim report within ninety days. A midterm briefing was due by 29 March 2008. It also had to coordinate with the African Union mission and with UNAMID. States and United Nations bodies were urged to share facts with it. The final report would close the term.
un-sc-res-179:
Resolution 179, adopted on 11 June 1963, backs a peaceful settlement in Yemen. It notes with satisfaction the Secretary-General's work on parts of the Yemen situation that came from outside the country. The parties directly concerned had accepted the same terms for pulling forces apart, known as the terms of disengagement.

Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Republic agreed to pay the costs, over two months, of the UN observation work the terms required. The Council asks the Secretary-General to set up that observation operation as he defined it. It urges the parties to keep to the terms in full and to avoid any act that would raise tension in the area.
un-sc-res-1879:
UNMIN was extended as Nepal's parties quarreled on 23 July 2009. The constituent assembly was writing the new constitution inside its set time frame. The special committee on the Maoist army needed to be rebuilt and set to work. The president's statement of 5 May had taken up the troubles.

The Council extended UNMIN's mandate in line with the government's request and the Secretary-General's advice, for six months. It agreed with his view that the current arms monitoring arrangements should stay while the integration question lasted. All parties were called to use the mission's expertise and readiness to help. The government had to take the steps needed to create the conditions for the mission's eventual end. The Secretary-General owed a report by the mandate's midpoint. Unity among the parties was urged as the only way to finish the peace.
un-sc-res-2679: Resolution 2679 is a formal act of the Security Council, preserved here in official-record wording sourced from English Wikisource. Its high number places it in the Council's recent output within this collection's long sequence. The text is complete at that place: the members' findings first, then their numbered decisions, exactly as the record holds them.
un-sc-res-379: Dated 1975 in the catalog, Resolution 379 records formal action by the United Nations Security Council. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-479:
War erupted between Iran and Iraq in September 1980. The Council took up the item on 28 September 1980. It reminded all states of their Charter duty to settle disputes by peaceful means. Force against another state's land or independence was barred. The Council noted its own chief role in keeping world peace. It said it was deeply concerned at how events were moving.

Iran and Iraq had to stop any further use of force at once. They should settle the dispute by peaceful means under law and justice. Both sides should accept a fitting offer of mediation. Other states had to show restraint and avoid widening the war. The Secretary-General's good offices received the Council's support.
un-sc-res-79: Arms cuts in standard arms were sent for more study in Security Council Resolution 79, passed on 17 January 1950. The General Assembly had passed a text on the ordering and general cut of such arms in December 1949. The Council rules that the text go to the Commission for Conventional Armaments. There it will be weighed in line with the body's own plan of work. The Soviet member was absent from the vote, and the Yugoslav member took no part in it.
un-sc-res-979: Within the United Nations official record, Resolution 979 is the Security Council text catalogued for 1995. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Children caught in war are the subject of Resolution 1379. It passed by a full vote on 20 November 2001. War harms children in wide and deep ways, the Council said. The harm casts a long shadow on peace and growth. States bear the chief duty to shield children. All who fight must obey the laws made to guard them.

The text's keenest tool was a public list. The UN chief was asked to name, in his next report, the groups that recruit or use child troops. The list would draw on wars the Council deals with, and on other dire cases too. That list grew teeth in later years. Groups named on it face strong pressure to free the children they hold.

Resolution 1479, adopted unanimously on 13 May 2003, plants a UN flag in Côte d'Ivoire's peace process. Ivorian parties had signed the Linas-Marcoussis Agreement in January, and a government of national reconciliation had finally met in April with all political groups present. West African and French forces were already on the ground trying to hold a ceasefire.

The Council created a UN mission for Côte d'Ivoire, called MINUCI, for an initial six months. Its job was to help the Ivorian parties carry out the peace agreement, and it included a small military component working alongside the French and regional forces. A special representative received full authority over all UN activity in the country.

Liberia's sanctions are renewed with an eye to lifting them in Resolution 1579, adopted on 21 December 2004. Disarmament was complete and the ceasefire held. But the National Transitional Government still lacked control of the timber areas. Diamond certification was only being prepared. Associates of the former regime were accused of undermining stability. UNMIL's deployment had improved security.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms and travel measures for 12 months and the timber measures for 12 months. It renews the diamond measures for six months only. A review after three months aims at lifting them once an effective, internationally verifiable Certificate of Origin regime exists. It confirms the Resolution 1532 (2004) asset freeze remains in force. The Panel of Experts is re-established until 21 June 2005, with a preliminary report on diamonds due by 21 March 2005 and a full report by 7 June 2005.

The Darfur Peace Agreement, signed in Abuja in May 2006, is the pivot of Resolution 1679, adopted on 16 May 2006. The African Union Mission in the Sudan, AMIS, had cut large-scale violence in Darfur. The African Union had decided that a UN operation should follow AMIS. Sudan and Chad had grown hostile toward each other, adding risk to the region.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council calls on the parties to keep their promises under the peace deal without delay and urges those who have not signed to sign. It warns it may use travel bans and asset freezes against anyone who breaks or blocks the deal. It backs the African Union's plan to move from AMIS to a UN operation and calls for a joint AU-UN assessment mission within one week. Advice on the new force's shape and cost is due within a week of that mission's return.

Some guides bill this text as the birth of the Darfur hybrid force. It is not. That force was set up two months past, in July 2007. This text keeps a probe team on Sudan's bans. War still scarred Darfur. Bomb raids from the air drew fresh blame. Talks in Libya were set for 27 October. Resolution 1779 passed on 28 September 2007.

The sleuth team's term grew to 15 October 2008. It would brief by 29 March 2008. Its work had to mesh with the peace forces on the ground. It would judge if raids and bans breaches had eased. States and UN arms were told to help the team in full. The force on the ground gets warm words in the text. But the act here is time for the watchers, not the birth of a force.

A United Nations observation operation in Yemen is set up on 11 June 1963. Civil war had drawn in outside powers, and Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Republic had accepted matching terms to disengage. Both governments had also agreed to pay the costs of the observation work for two months.

The Secretary-General is asked to establish the observation operation as he had defined it in his April report. The parties are urged to observe the disengagement terms in full and to avoid any step that would raise tension in the area. The Secretary-General is to report on how the decision is being carried out. The mission became the United Nations Yemen Observation Mission.

Nepal's peace process reaches another renewal in Resolution 1879, adopted on 23 July 2009. The Constituent Assembly chosen in April 2008 was writing a new constitution. The government and the Unified Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) had agreed to start discharging and settling disqualified Maoist army personnel, including minors. Nepal asked for six more months of the UN Mission in Nepal, UNMIN.

The Council renews UNMIN until 23 January 2010. It urges all parties to use UNMIN's help to finish the leftover parts of its mandate by that date. It agrees with the Secretary-General that the arms monitoring setup was a short-term measure that cannot go on forever. It asks Nepal to shape the terms that will let UNMIN finish and withdraw, and seeks a report by 30 October 2009 on progress toward those terms.

Afghanistan under the Taliban is the subject of Resolution 2679, adopted on 16 March 2023. The Council expressed concern that the Taliban had made no progress on the expectations set for them. It stressed the full and equal participation of women in public life. Respect for the rights of women, children, and minorities was also stressed.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to carry out an independent assessment of Afghanistan. The full assessment was due by 17 November 2023. It would be prepared after talks with Afghan political actors and other interested parties. The study had to offer practical advice for the way forward. Political, aid, and development actors, inside and outside the United Nations, needed a joined-up approach. The goal was to meet the country's current challenges together.

The Secretary-General's mission on Western Sahara reported back in the autumn of 1975, but the situation stayed grave. Spain had written to the Council again on 1 November. Resolution 379, adopted by consensus on 2 November 1975, follows up the mission sent under Resolution 377.

The Council urged all the parties concerned to avoid one-sided action. Any step that might raise tension in the area further was to be avoided. The Secretary-General was asked to continue his consultations with the parties. He also had to step them up and report back as soon as he could. His report would help the Council decide what further measures might be needed. The text kept the matter firmly on the Council's agenda.

War between Iran and Iraq had just erupted in September 1980. Iraq's forces had crossed into Iran days earlier. Resolution 479, adopted unanimously on 28 September 1980, was the Council's first response. The agenda item was bluntly titled the situation between Iran and Iraq.

Both countries were called on to stop using force at once. They had to settle their dispute peacefully, under law and justice. Mediation offers should be accepted, the text urges. Other states were warned to show restraint. Nothing should widen the conflict. The Secretary-General's good offices won support. He had to report back within forty-eight hours. The war, tragically, ran for eight more years.

Arms control paperwork moved one step forward on 17 January 1950. The General Assembly had passed a resolution in December 1949 on the regulation and general reduction of conventional arms and armed forces. Resolution 79 does a single thing with that text. The Council decided to transmit the Assembly's resolution to the Commission for Conventional Armaments. The commission would study it further, in line with its own plan of work. That transmission is the whole content of the resolution.

A judge of the International Court of Justice died in February 1995, leaving his seat empty. Judge Roberto Ago, named in the text, had died on 24 February. The rest of his term had to be filled under the Court's Statute. Resolution 979, adopted on 9 March 1995, fixes the date of the vote.

Under Article 14 of the Statute, the Security Council sets the date of such an election. The Council chose 21 June 1995. The vote would take place at a meeting of the Security Council. A meeting of the General Assembly, during its forty-ninth session, would vote on the same occasion. Both bodies have to agree on a judge for the appointment to be made. The decision is one of the small, regular acts that keep the World Court at full strength.
upanishads-muller-vol1-1879: The Upanishads, Part 1 forms volume one of The Sacred Books of the East, the great Oxford series edited by F. Max Muller and issued by the Clarendon Press in 1879. Muller himself made the English rendering, and the work was planned in two parts. The pages present here hold the title page and the start of a dedication to the Marquis of Salisbury, so the sacred texts themselves do not appear. The series title page notes that many scholars shared the work of rendering the East's holy books.
